scope: Every protein that would be a Target candidate while its rare-cell signal is dismissed, or after release from the pooled 1% detection flag, and every Target candidate of the 2026-11-10 catalog.

rubric.R1: A primary source reports the human gene in a panel organ by a gene-specific assay, and donor-level single-cell data detect it in that organ in at least 1% of one donor population. The rare-cell grade becomes established.
rubric.R2: A primary source reports the human gene, RNA or protein, by a gene-specific assay in normal adult tissue that the tissue-tier registry or its updates tier Vital or Protected, and no gene-specific multi-tissue panel or reliable IHC contradicts it. Unsafe.
rubric.R3: Human loss of function causes disease of a Vital tissue, and the ortholog is expressed in that adult tissue. Unsafe.
rubric.none: No publication, restriction to germline, placenta or embryo, conflicting reports, assays shared with paralogs, cultured or diseased samples, other species alone, or database annotation alone. Recorded; no category effect.
rubric.recorded: A finding that a second reader confirmed as human, adult, normal-tissue and gene-specific but that does not meet R1 to R3: cultured or induced cells, database annotation alone, a family-level source, no retrievable quote, or a Manageable or Disposable tissue. Recorded with its tissue and tier. No category effect; the candidate filters can act on it.

method: Web literature search by Claude subagents on 2026-11-10, and on 2026-11-11 for the 21 proteins whose signal the whole-body panel dismissed, and for the 3 proteins released when two lone donors in different cell types stopped counting as replication; each claim carries the URL opened and the quote returned. Candidate sweep: on 2026-11-12, 37 Claude research agents searched the literature for normal-tissue function or expression of every Target candidate of policy oncoref.target-selection.2026-11-10.1, 25 proteins each, and 36 second readers each tried to refute one batch's findings. On 2026-11-13 the abstract, open full text or supplementary table behind each proposed exclusion was retrieved from PubMed, PMC or the publisher and the quote recorded; an exclusion without a retrieved quote was not made.
limitations: Many pages were read through a fetch tool that summarizes, so quotes are as that tool relayed them
Several papers were read at abstract level because full text was blocked; each evidence item says so
PubMed was reached through Europe PMC or E-utilities
A null result means nothing was found in this search, not that nothing exists
HPA and GTEx bulk values are numeric filters elsewhere and were not counted as literature
Candidate-sweep findings other than the exclusions carry the second reader's paraphrase, not a quote
A candidate-sweep null is one agent's search, not proof of absence; FSCB was not searched
Olfactory, taste and hair-keratin family rules rest on family-level sources and were not reviewed gene by gene
Tiers for olfactory epithelium, taste buds, nasal mucosa, lacrimal gland, sensory ganglia, bone and tooth come from the 2026-11-13 registry updates, written from abstracts

evidence.source_title: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4972530/ (PMID 27333034)
evidence.tissue: brain; neurons (inferred from the mouse overexpression model, not shown for endogenous human protein)
evidence.finding: Human: Letronne et al. 2016 (EBioMedicine, PMID 27333034) report from brain transcriptomics that ADAM30 expression is about 50% lower in Alzheimer's disease brains and inversely correlates with amyloid load, which implies measurable ADAM30 mRNA in non-diseased adult brain. The functional work (cathepsin D activation, APP lysosomal sorting) used neuronal overexpression in mice and cells.
evidence.limitations: Letronne et al. 2016 (PMID 27333034, full text PMC4972530) says what is claimed, and the full text is stronger than the abstract. ADAM30 mRNA was measured in human frontal cortex on a custom oligonucleotide array (12 AD cases, 12 controls) and validated with a Quantigene probe assay (51 AD, 42 controls), showing about 50% lower expression in AD and an inverse correlation with amyloid load. The paper also reports neuronal immunostaining for ADAM30 in human frontal cortex (Brodmann area 10) with a polyclonal antibody; the claim listed neurons as inferred only from the mouse model. Caveats: values are arbitrary units normalised to housekeeping genes, so the absolute level is unknown and may be very low, consistent with near-zero atlas values; controls are aged post-mortem brains; antibody validation was not checked; and the paper notes ADAM30 is not expressed in mouse brain.

evidence.source_title: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7966854/ (mouse); GTEx v8 median expression for ENSG00000182035.11 via gtexportal.org API (human, adipose near zero)
evidence.finding: Mouse: Adig is predominantly expressed in the adipocyte fraction of adipose tissue (and testis); Adig-null mice show altered fat mass accrual and impaired leptin secretion, and a later study reports adipocyte-specific knockout disrupts lipid droplet formation in brown fat with impaired cold tolerance. Human: no adipose expression confirmed here (HPA and NCBI call human ADIG testis-enriched), though the knockout paper cites a human GWAS linking ADIG to BMI-adjusted leptin.
evidence.limitations: The Cell Reports 2021 paper (PMC7966854) exists and says what is claimed: mouse Adig is most highly expressed in adipose tissue, mainly the adipocyte fraction, and Adig-null mice are leaner on a high-fat diet with reduced fat-mass-adjusted leptin and impaired leptin secretion from explants. All of it is mouse knockout work. The only human data is a GWAS locus near ADIG for BMI-adjusted leptin, where the implicated SNP (rs6071166, near SLC32A1) was not linked to expression of nearby genes in human adipose. I queried GTEx v8 directly: ADIG median is 86.6 TPM in testis, 1.2 in thyroid, and no adipose or breast tissue appears in the top 12 (all others at or below 0.14 TPM). HPA calls it testis-enriched with no protein data. UniProt's human entry describes a seipin-binding lipid-droplet function, but gives no human tissue evidence. The bioRxiv brown-fat/cold-tolerance source was not opened. No human adult adipose expression is supported.

evidence.source_title: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4059656 (PMID 24933156)
evidence.tissue: tooth and alveolar bone; also reported in brain, bone marrow, long bone and cartilage; ameloblasts; bone-lining cells; glial cells; macrophages, megakaryocytes and some CD34+ marrow cells
evidence.finding: Mouse (15 weeks): AMELX mRNA by RT-qPCR and protein by western blot in mandibular alveolar and basal bone, with low and inconsistent RT-PCR signal in eye, ovary, tongue, heart, colon and kidney (Jacques 2014, PMID 24933156). That paper cites earlier immunohistochemistry reports of amelogenin in brain glial cells and hematopoietic cells (Deutsch 2006, PMID 16674683) and in long bone, cartilage and marrow stromal cells (Haze 2007, PMID 17393535); those two were seen only as citations and search snippets, and species was not confirmed.
evidence.limitations: Jacques 2014 (PMC4059656) exists and matches the claim, but it is entirely mouse. AMELX mRNA was found in mandibular alveolar and basal bone at 1 and 15 weeks, falling with age; protein was a roughly 26 kDa band in alveolar bone and near the detection limit in basal bone. Bone-section staining was in 1-week-old mice. Soft-tissue RT-PCR at 15 weeks was low or inconsistent (eye and ovary positive; tongue, testicle, heart, colon, kidney inconsistent; liver, lung, muscle negative). No human tissue was studied. The paper cites Deutsch 2006 and Haze 2007 without stating species; I could not open either abstract (PubMed rate-limited), so the brain, hematopoietic, long bone and cartilage claims remain unverified. Mouse has no Amely, so the mouse data are gene-specific there, but the human AMELX/AMELY distinction is unaddressed and the antibodies are cross-species.

evidence.finding: Human: the cloning paper (Jonsson 2004, Genomics 84:859-866, 'Hash4, a novel human achaete-scute homologue found in fetal skin') found Hash4/ASCL4 expression restricted to skin by real-time PCR, about 7-fold higher in fetal than adult skin, so adult skin is positive at a lower level. The PubMed abstract says Hash4 expression was restricted to skin among the tissues and cells tested by RT-PCR, with about 7-fold higher expression in fetal than adult skin by real-time PCR, so adult skin is positive at a lower level. UniProt Q6XD76, citing the same paper, reads: expressed in skin, 7-fold higher in fetal than adult skin, weak expression also in fetal lung, aorta and brain and in adult stomach, kidney, ovary and breast. The assay is gene-specific PCR on human tissue. Caveats: no absolute adult level is given, the full text was not opened so the provenance and normality of the adult skin RNA is unchecked, and the mouse Ascl4-null statement was not verified.

evidence.source_title: https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/K7ELQ4.fasta vs P17544 and O15130; https://www.proteinatlas.org/ENSG00000170653-ATF7/tissue
evidence.tissue: all tissues (via ATF7 sequence identity); ubiquitous
evidence.finding: Human: the readthrough protein (UniProt K7ELQ4, 463 aa) is identical to canonical ATF7 (P17544) over its first 411 residues and shares no segment of 8+ residues with the NPFF precursor (O15130), by direct sequence comparison in this session. HPA classes ATF7 as 'low tissue specificity, detected in all', so nearly every peptide from this candidate is also made by a ubiquitously expressed transcription factor.
evidence.limitations: Re-ran the comparison on the UniProt FASTA files: K7ELQ4 is 463 aa and identical to ATF7 (P17544, 483 aa) over residues 1-411 (88.8%). It shares no 8-mer with the NPFF precursor O15130. 403 of its 455 possible 9-mers are also ATF7 9-mers; only the 52-residue C-terminal tail is unique. The HPA ATF7 page reads 'Low tissue specificity' and 'Detected in all'. The expression evidence is for ATF7, not the readthrough transcript, so this is a peptide-sharing problem and not evidence that the readthrough gene itself is expressed.

evidence.source_title: He et al. 2013, Cell 154:1085: Beclin 2 functions in autophagy, degradation of G protein-coupled receptors, and metabolism
evidence.tissue: human fetal and adult brain lysates
evidence.finding: Beclin 2 protein in adult human brain.
evidence.quote: We also detected human Beclin 2 protein expression (predicted molecular weight 49 kD; apparent molecular weight 53 kD) in samples from human fetal and adult brains using an antibody generated against amino acids 49-67 of human Beclin 2
evidence.limitations: Single blot; the tissue RNA panel in the paper is mouse.

evidence.source_title: PMID 23954414 (PMC4231430, Fig. 1C); UniProt A8MW95
evidence.finding: Human: UniProt (A8MW95) curates Beclin 2 as present in fetal and adult brain at protein level, citing He et al. 2013, even though the catalog shows 0.0 TPM off-target.
evidence.limitations: UniProt A8MW95 carries 'Present in fetal and adult brain (at protein level)' with experimental evidence from PMID 23954414. The full text (PMC4231430, Fig. 1C) shows a western blot of human Beclin 2 in fetal and adult human brain lysates. The antibody was raised against Beclin 2 residues 49-67, and siRNA against beclin 2 reduced the band without affecting Beclin 1. Caveats: it is a single western blot from one lab with a custom peptide antibody, with no independent replication found and no cell-type resolution. The mRNA tissue panel in the paper (Fig. 1B) is mouse, not human.

evidence.finding: Mouse: Beclin 2 is required for ligand-induced lysosomal degradation of several GPCRs via GASP1. Heterozygous knockout mice have defective autophagy, increased brain cannabinoid 1 receptor, elevated food intake, obesity and insulin resistance; homozygotes have decreased embryonic viability.
evidence.limitations: The abstract of PMID 23954414 says exactly what is claimed: GASP1-dependent GPCR degradation, heterozygous knockouts with defective autophagy, raised brain CB1R, increased food intake, obesity and insulin resistance, and reduced embryonic viability in homozygotes. The knockout is gene-specific, but the phenotype is mouse-only and no human loss-of-function disease was found. Mouse RT-PCR in the same paper shows beclin 2 in brain, skeletal muscle, thymus, placenta and uterus. It becomes relevant mainly alongside the human brain western blot in the same paper.

This is mouse-only. UniProt Q8NDY6 gives the human function only 'by similarity' (ECO:0000250) and has no human tissue-specificity annotation. The source describes the role as maturation during postnatal development, so it does not show adult human expression. No human expression source was opened here.

evidence.source_title: PMID 27515280, Additional files 2 and 3 (12864_2016_2960_MOESM2_ESM.xlsx, MOESM3_ESM.xlsx); UniProt P59826
evidence.finding: Human: UniProt P59826 records BPIFB3 as detected in nasal septal epithelium (Bingle and Craven 2002). RNA-seq of human olfactory epithelium against 16 control tissues found BPI-fold proteins, together with lipocalins, to be the most over-expressed non-receptor gene families.
evidence.limitations: UniProt P59826 does carry 'Detected in nasal septal epithelium' with experimental evidence from PMID 11971875. That paper's full text is paywalled; its abstract is family-level only. I opened the per-gene supplementary tables of Olender 2016, which the original researcher had not: BPIFB3 is 648, 333, 242 and 1234 FPKM in the four human olfactory epithelium samples, 0.06 in respiratory epithelium, and at the 0.003 floor in nearly all 16 control tissues (testes 0.14). Fold change is about 49,000 and it is in the 194-gene overexpressed list. Samples were biopsies and autopsies from elective-surgery donors; ages are not stated and respiratory contamination is variable. The paralogs are separate rows with different profiles, so this is gene-level RNA-seq.

evidence.source_title: PMID 27515280, Additional files 2 and 3 (12864_2016_2960_MOESM2_ESM.xlsx, MOESM3_ESM.xlsx)
evidence.tissue: olfactory epithelium, tongue, minor salivary gland
evidence.finding: Human: a 2025 preprint, citing the human olfactory transcriptome study, lists BPIFB6 with BPIFB3 and BPIFB4 among the most tissue-enriched, highly expressed genes in olfactory epithelium. Olender et al. state in their abstract that BPI-fold proteins show the highest over-expression there. UniProt Q8NFQ5 records only tonsil expression.
evidence.limitations: The cited preprint returned HTTP 403. Its published version (Cells 2025, PMID 41369347, PMC12691349) lists BPIFB6 only in a sequence-identity table and names BPIFB3 and BPIFB4, not BPIFB6, as olfactory-expressed. The claim is nonetheless supported by the Olender 2016 supplementary tables: BPIFB6 is in the overexpressed gene list with fold change about 9,000, at 9.9, 5.0, 6.8 and 224 FPKM in the four human olfactory samples, 0.07 in respiratory epithelium and about 0.003-0.03 in controls. 'Highly expressed' is overstated: three of four samples are 5-10 FPKM and one is 224, well below BPIFB3 and BPIFB4. Donor ages are not stated. Only olfactory epithelium is supported; no source was found for tongue or minor salivary gland, and UniProt Q8NFQ5 records tonsil only.

evidence.finding: Human cell lines: BPIFB6 silencing fragments the Golgi, alters retrograde and anterograde trafficking, and suppresses enterovirus replication, indicating a secretory-pathway function in somatic cells.
evidence.limitations: The abstract of PMID 26962226 confirms the claim: BPIFB6 is ER-localised, and RNAi silencing causes Golgi fragmentation, altered retrograde and anterograde trafficking, and suppressed replication of coxsackievirus B, poliovirus and EV71. The RNAi is gene-specific and the phenotype is opposite to BPIFB3's. The evidence is from cultured cell lines only, which says nothing about which normal adult tissues express the protein. It is a mechanism, not normal-tissue expression.

evidence.tissue: breast (lactating and virgin mammary epithelium); mammary secretory epithelial cell
evidence.finding: Mouse: BTN1A1 is required for milk lipid secretion (null mice release lipid droplets with damaged membranes, per OMIM 601610 summarising Ogg et al. 2004), and transcripts are also present in virgin mammary tissue. UniProt annotates the human protein for milk-fat droplet secretion by similarity.
evidence.limitations: The knockout requirement for milk-lipid droplet secretion is real and gene-specific, but it is mouse. PMID 20208008 only restates it; the primary source is Ogg et al. 2004 (PMID 15226505, title verified). UniProt gives the human function 'by similarity'. Whether this is a gap depends on policy: lactation is a reproductive-cycle function and the catalog already seems to count breast as reproductive. The virgin mammary transcripts are also mouse-only in the cited source.

evidence.source_title: PMID 20208008; UniProt Q13410 (by similarity)
evidence.finding: Mouse: Btn1a1 transcripts were found in spleen and thymus as well as virgin mammary tissue, and BTN1A1 protein was detected in thymic epithelial cells. BTN1A1-Fc bound activated T cells and inhibited CD4/CD8 proliferation, IL-2 and IFN-gamma secretion; UniProt Q13410 carries this function for the human protein by similarity.
evidence.limitations: The abstract of PMID 20208008 supports the claim: mouse Btn1a1 transcripts in virgin mammary tissue, spleen and thymus; BTN1A1 protein in thymic epithelial cells; BTN1A1-Fc binds activated T cells and inhibits CD4/CD8 proliferation, IL-2 and IFN-gamma. All of it is mouse, and the T-cell inhibition uses recombinant immobilised Fc fusion protein in vitro. UniProt Q13410 carries the function for human only 'by similarity'. No human thymic epithelial data were found.

evidence.tissue: salivary gland (submandibular), saliva, serum; salivary duct epithelium, serous and mucous acini; also nerves and some endothelium within the gland
evidence.finding: Human: CABS1 protein was detected in submandibular gland by Western blot, immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence with monoclonal antibodies, and in saliva and serum by Western blot. The authors flag antibody caveats: several bands were nonspecific, isotype controls were not clean, and mass spectrometry failed to sequence CABS1 from gland or saliva.
evidence.limitations: Source opened (Reyes-Serratos et al., PLoS One 2024) and it says what the claim says, caveats included: human submandibular gland by Western blot, IHC and IF; saliva and serum by Western blot only. Weakened rather than confirmed because the protein identity is not orthogonally established: the authors could not sequence CABS1 from gland or saliva by mass spectrometry, many monoclonal bands in saliva looked nonspecific, and the 13G3 isotype control gave a band at 64 kDa overlapping the signal. The tissue is adult human but not from healthy donors: Western blot and IHC used grossly or morphologically normal areas of glands resected for squamous carcinoma, and IF used two carcinoma resections plus two Sjogren's syndrome glands. Serum was a pilot on one pooled sample from a single 30-year-old man. I read only the first 100,000 characters of the page.

evidence.source_title: PMID 25632019, PMC4386001, DOI 10.1152/ajpregu.00153.2014 (abstract only read); follow-up PMID 38753592
evidence.finding: Human: an earlier paper from the same group reported that CABS1, previously thought testis-only, is also expressed in salivary glands and lung, and that peptides from its C-terminal region are anti-inflammatory in rodent models. I saw this only as a search-result summary; the lung claim was not confirmed in the 2024 follow-up that I did read.
evidence.limitations: The paper exists (St Laurent et al., Am J Physiol Regul Integr Comp Physiol 2015, PMID 25632019). I could read only the abstract via Europe PMC; full text was blocked. The abstract states: 'Using Western blot and PCR, we discovered that the human protein CABS1, previously thought to only be expressed in the testes, is also expressed in the salivary glands and lung, in a tissue-specific manner.' So the claim matches the abstract and is about human CABS1. Weakened because I could not check tissue source, donor status, antibody type or whether PCR products were sequenced, and the same group's 2024 follow-up did not study lung and raised specificity problems with their CABS1 antibodies. The lung claim rests on this one unreplicated report; human/adult/normal is assumed from the abstract, not verified.

evidence.source_title: PMID 28381457, PMC5495925, DOI 10.1152/ajpregu.00393.2016 (abstract only read); contradicted in part by PMID 38753592
evidence.finding: Human: a 27 kDa salivary CABS1 band was reported to rise with salivary cortisol during acute and exam stress. The 2024 follow-up from the same group could not confirm that this 27 kDa form is CABS1, so the stress link is weak. Seen only as a search-result summary.
evidence.limitations: The paper exists (Am J Physiol Regul Integr Comp Physiol 2017, PMID 28381457); only the abstract was readable. It reports a CABS1-immunoreactive 27 kDa band in saliva of all volunteers, acute stress increasing the 18, 27 and 55 kDa bands, and changes in the 27 kDa band positively associated with salivary cortisol in both acute and academic stress. So the claim matches. Weakened because the evidence is an immunoreactive band only, and the same group's 2024 paper states they are 'unable to confirm the presence of a relatively abundant 27 kDa CABS1 form in human saliva'. The stress-induced form is therefore not established as CABS1. It is also a secreted fluid, not a tissue of expression.

entries.summary: The discovery paper (SEREX, lung cancer sera) reports testis-specific expression among normal tissues, and UniProt and HPA repeat this (HPA: testis-enriched, spermatid/spermatocyte cluster, no IHC tissue profile). A mouse study places the protein in the acrosome of spermatids and spermatozoa. No opened source reports CAGE1 in adult brain or any other non-reproductive normal tissue; the discovery paper does note expression in non-cancerous tissue surrounding tumours, lower than in the tumour.
entries.decision_reason: Sources describe germline, placental or embryonic restriction, or did not test adult somatic tissue.

evidence.finding: Human: the Human Protein Atlas single-cell page lists CAGE1 as 'cell type enriched' in skeletal myofibers at the protein level in its deep visual proteomics data (protein tau 1.00), with no matching RNA value reported. This is a single atlas annotation with no primary paper found.
evidence.limitations: The HPA single-cell page was opened and does list protein specificity 'Cell type enriched (Skeletal myofibers)' with protein tau 1.00 in its deep visual proteomics section. One detail of the claim is wrong: that section does report RNA values (RNA tau 0.70, 'Cell type enhanced (T-cells)'); the gene-level single-cell RNA call is group enriched in early spermatids and late primary spermatocytes (tau 0.84). Weakened because this is a single atlas annotation with no primary paper, the supporting peptides and their uniqueness could not be inspected, and a tau of 1.00 may simply mean the protein was detected in only one profiled cell type in a sparse dataset. Gene specificity is unverified, and the gene is already flagged mapping_risk. Adult normal status of the tissue is assumed from HPA practice, not checked.

evidence.tissue: brain and multiple somatic tissues (mouse); somatic cells generally; shown in NIH3T3 fibroblasts at the centrosome
evidence.finding: Mouse: nested RT-PCR with sequencing found Ccdc42 transcript in brain and in all adult tissues tested except kidney, and endogenous CCDC42 protein localised to the centrosome in NIH3T3 fibroblasts. The full-length isoform was testis-only, so somatic cells may express a different isoform; the knockout paper (Pasek 2016) reports brain plus developing sperm expression with no phenotype beyond male sterility.
evidence.limitations: Source opened (Tapia Contreras and Hoyer-Fender, Front Cell Dev Biol 2019). It is mouse only, with no human expression data. The claim is slightly overstated: the first RT-PCR (exons 5-7) gave strong testis and epididymis signal and only weak brain signal; the nested PCR (exons 6+7) gave a product in all tissues except kidney. Sequencing confirmed the testis and epididymis products, and the ovary and NIH3T3 products, but the brain and other somatic tissue products are not reported as sequenced. Nested PCR detects trace transcript and says nothing about level. Full-length isoform 203 was testis-only, and the authors could not verify the short isoforms (201 not amplified; the 202 primer amplified an unrelated sequence). Endogenous centrosome staining in NIH3T3 is by antibody in a cell line with a no-primary control only. I did not open Pasek 2016. I read the first 100,000 characters of the page.

evidence.source_title: Sen et al. 2004, Arthritis Rheum 50:488: WISP3-dependent regulation of type II collagen and aggrecan production in chondrocytes (PubMed abstract)
evidence.finding: WISP3 (CCN6) protein in midzone chondrocytes.
evidence.quote: WISP3 protein is expressed in the midzone chondrocytes of normal adult articular cartilage
evidence.limitations: Abstract only; antibody validation against other CCN proteins not checked.

evidence.finding: Human: biallelic loss-of-function mutations in CCN6 (WISP3) cause progressive pseudorheumatoid dysplasia, a postnatal disorder with onset at about 3 to 8 years and continued cartilage loss, so the gene is needed for cartilage maintenance after birth. The mouse knockout reportedly has no skeletal phenotype (seen only as a search-result title, not opened).
evidence.limitations: PubMed abstract of PMID 10471507 (Hurvitz et al., Nat Genet 1999) read: nine different WISP3 mutations in unrelated patients with autosomal recessive progressive pseudorheumatoid dysplasia; symptoms start at 3 to 8 years, with continued cartilage loss and joint replacement by the third decade; no extraskeletal manifestations; authors conclude the gene is essential for normal postnatal skeletal growth and cartilage homeostasis. Positional cloning is gene-specific. The evidence is human genetics in a childhood-onset disease that progresses into adulthood, not an expression measurement in normal adult tissue. UniProt O95389 also cites this paper for expression in synoviocytes and articular chondrocytes. The mouse-knockout part of the claim was not checked (I did not locate that paper).

evidence.finding: Human: immunohistochemistry shows WISP3 protein in midzone chondrocytes of normal adult articular cartilage, and WISP3 raises type II collagen and aggrecan expression in chondrocyte lines.
evidence.limitations: PubMed abstract of PMID 14872491 (Sen et al., Arthritis Rheum 2004) read: immunohistochemistry with an anti-WISP3 antibody shows WISP3 protein in midzone chondrocytes of normal adult human articular cartilage (also in osteoarthritic clusters and fetal growth cartilage); WISP3 transfection raises type II collagen and aggrecan in human chondrocyte lines C-28/I2 and T/C-28a2, and a PPRD mutant is impaired. Caveat: only the abstract was read, so antibody validation against other CCN family members was not checked; it is a single 2004 IHC study.

entries.summary: No gene-specific study of CDCP2 in normal adult human tissue was found. evidence.finding: Mouse: Cer1 is expressed in bone and growth plate by RT-PCR, immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridisation. Human: a nonsynonymous CER1 SNP (rs3747532) is associated with low bone mineral density and vertebral fracture in southern Chinese women. No adult human expression data were found.
evidence.limitations: PubMed abstract of PMID 19113921 (Tang et al., J Bone Miner Res 2009) read and matches: Cer1 expression in mouse bone and growth plate by RT-PCR, IHC and in situ hybridisation; human nonsynonymous SNP rs3747532 associated with low BMD in premenopausal women (OR 2.2, 95% CI 1.0-4.6, borderline) and vertebral fracture (OR 1.82, p = 0.025) in a 1083-subject cohort. Expression is mouse only (age of the mice not stated in the abstract; growth plate implies young animals), and the human link is a weak single-cohort candidate-gene association, not expression or function in adult human bone.

evidence.tissue: retina; rod and cone photoreceptors (connecting cilium / transition zone)
evidence.finding: Mouse: centrin 1 protein localises to the photoreceptor connecting cilium and is lost in Cetn1 knockout retina. The knockout has no retinal degeneration and its only overt phenotype is male infertility, so the retinal function looks redundant with other centrins.
evidence.limitations: Source exists: Avasthi et al., J Cell Sci 2013, PMID 23641067 / PMC3711207; abstract read. It says CETN1 is expressed in male germ cells and photoreceptors and resides in the photoreceptor transition zone and connecting cilium; Cetn1 knockout mice are viable with no retinal degeneration, normal phototransduction-component localisation and normal transducin translocation; the only phenotype is male infertility. Mouse only, and the retinal role is non-essential. The specific statement that centrin 1 staining is lost in knockout retina is not in the abstract and was not verified. No human retina evidence was found.

evidence.tissue: inner ear (vestibular maculae); extrastriolar vestibular hair cells
evidence.finding: Mouse: Cib3 transcripts are highly expressed in extrastriolar vestibular hair cells; Cib3 knockout mainly affects those cells, and Cib2/Cib3 double knockout disrupts stereocilia maintenance in all vestibular hair cells with severe balance deficits. UniProt annotates human CIB3 as an auxiliary subunit of the hair-cell mechanotransduction channel (by similarity).
evidence.limitations: PubMed abstract of PMID 37001993 (Wang et al., J Neurosci 2023) read and matches the claim: Cib3 transcripts are high in the extrastriolar region of mouse vestibular maculae, Cib3 knockout mainly affects extrastriolar hair-cell stereocilia, and Cib2/Cib3 double knockout abolishes MET currents and causes severe balance deficits. Knockouts are gene-specific, but CIB3 is redundant with CIB2 for MET. All of it is mouse; the UniProt Q96Q77 function line for human CIB3 is 'by similarity' only. No human expression or human loss-of-function evidence was found.

evidence.source_title: PMID 12039054; UniProt Q6PB30
evidence.finding: Human: Lin et al. 2002 detected CSAGE (CSAG1) and TRAG-3 by RT-PCR in normal cartilage as well as testis, but in no other normal tissue; OMIM 300944 records one study finding it absent from normal cartilage and another finding it in normal chondrocytes.
evidence.limitations: PubMed abstract of PMID 12039054 (Lin et al., Gene 2002) read: 'CSAGE and TRAG-3 are expressed in chondrosarcoma, melanoma, and cartilage and testis, but not in other normal tissues.' UniProt Q6PB30 repeats this, citing the same paper. So the source says it, in human. Weakened because: only the abstract was read, so donor age and how normal the cartilage was are unverified; the gene was cloned by differential display between chondrosarcoma lines and normal cartilage, which implies lower expression in cartilage; RT-PCR within a highly homologous family (CSAGE vs TRAG-3, with splice variants) may not separate paralogs; it is a single 2002 study with no replication found. The OMIM 300944 statement about conflicting studies could not be checked.

evidence.tissue: anterior pituitary; gonadotrophs (colocalises with LH-beta in secretory granules)
evidence.finding: Mouse only: Cres (Cst8) mRNA and protein are expressed in anterior pituitary gonadotrophs, where it colocalises with LH-beta and is regulated by GnRH and androgens; CRES inhibits prohormone convertase 2. One correction to the claim: the 2006 abstract says GnRH and estradiol negatively regulate Cres mRNA, while androgens restore CRES protein. No human pituitary evidence was cited or found, and the catalog's human RNA is near zero, so this stays a mouse-only possibility.

evidence.tissue: stomach (non-tumor gastric mucosa, pyloric glands); pyloric gland epithelium; more frequent with intestinal metaplasia
evidence.finding: Human: CT83 (KK-LC-1) mRNA was detected by RT-PCR in 7% of stomachs without gastric cancer (115 non-GC patients), and every positive case carried Helicobacter pylori; in stomachs with a tumor, 77% of non-tumor sites were positive. A companion study (PMID 29666402) localised the non-tumor signal to pyloric glands of the lower corpus (59% of pyloric-gland samples, none in fundic glands).
evidence.limitations: Both sources exist and the numbers match: PMID 36484013 abstract gives 77% of non-tumor sites in tumor-bearing stomachs vs 7% in stomachs without tumors (118 GC, 115 non-GC patients), all positives H. pylori carriers; PMC5904109 full text gives 45/76 (59.2%) pyloric gland samples and 0/13 fundic, 76.6% in lower-corpus pyloric glands. CT83 is single-copy so RT-PCR is gene-specific. But the tissue is not normal: all positives are H. pylori-infected, atrophic/metaplastic or tumor-adjacent mucosa (the authors call it a pre-cancerous marker), and 93% of cancer-free stomachs were negative. Assay is 40-cycle end-point RT-PCR with gel readout, mRNA only, no protein in non-tumor tissue, one research group. Field cancerization is an alternative explanation. Real as a disease-state/induced signal, not as healthy-tissue expression.

entries.reported_tissue: brain (single RT-PCR report, contradicted by other sources)
entries.summary: The original LAGE-1 paper found testis as the only positive normal tissue, UniProt adds very low placenta and some uterus, and HPA IHC (reliability Enhanced) shows protein only in testis seminiferous ducts with other staining disregarded as off-target. One Brazilian multiple-myeloma group, however, reports normal brain positive for LAGE-1 by RT-PCR in an 18-tissue panel; the brain sample age is not stated and discrimination from CTAG1A/B (NY-ESO-1) is not explicitly documented, although NY-ESO-1 was scored negative in the same brain sample. No source opened reports CTAG2 in lung or alveolar cells. Because of the brain report this is classed as conflicting rather than silent.
entries.decision_reason: Reports conflict, cannot separate the gene from paralogs, or come from cultured, diseased or fetal samples.

evidence.assay: RT-PCR (per abstract; details not in abstract)
evidence.finding: Only testis positive among normal tissues.
evidence.quote: The only normal tissue that expressed the gene was testis.
evidence.limitations: Abstract only; full text not opened, so the tissue list and primer specificity versus NY-ESO-1 were not verified. Authors cloned both genes and treat them separately.

evidence.assay: RT-PCR, 18 normal tissues (data from the group's earlier study, Andrade et al., ref 7)
evidence.finding: Normal brain positive for LAGE-1; all other normal tissues negative; NY-ESO-1 positive only in mammary gland.

evidence.limitations: Paper says primers amplify both LAGE-1a and -1b isoforms but does not state they exclude NY-ESO-1 (NY-ESO-1 was negative in brain, suggesting they do). Donor age, brain region and number of brain samples not given; the underlying Andrade et al. paper was not opened; end-point RT-PCR without quantitation.

evidence.limitations: HPA does not say whether the antibody cross-reacts with NY-ESO-1 (CTAG1A/B); 'off target' staining in other tissues was dismissed by curators, not shown absent.

evidence.source_title: De Smet C et al. DNA methylation is the primary silencing mechanism for a set of germ line- and tumor-specific genes. Mol Cell Biol 1999 (PubMed abstract)
evidence.tissue: somatic tissues vs male germ cells
evidence.finding: LAGE-1 promoter highly methylated in somatic tissues, unmethylated in germ cells (supports silencing).
evidence.quote: those of MAGE-A1 and LAGE-1 were highly methylated in somatic tissues. In contrast, they were largely unmethylated in male germ cells.
evidence.limitations: Abstract only; methylation is indirect evidence for absence of expression.

evidence.source_title: PMID 14734521 (Gotter et al., J Exp Med 2004, PMC2211762); abstract only, no CTAG2-specific mTEC source found
evidence.finding: Human, family-level only: purified medullary thymic epithelial cells promiscuously overexpress more than 400 genes, including cancer-germline genes. The abstract does not name CTAG2/LAGE-1, and I could not open the full text or find a gene-specific mTEC study, so this is only a plausible explanation for the thymus value already in the CSV (3.9 TPM, 24.9 nTPM).
evidence.limitations: Source exists and the abstract says human mTECs overexpress >400 genes including cancer-germline genes, but it does not name CTAG2/LAGE-1; the attribution to CTAG2 is inference at family level. I did not open the full text, so whether CTAG2 appears in the gene lists is unverified. Human thymus samples in such studies are typically from paediatric cardiac surgery, so not adult. Even if true, mTEC promiscuous expression bears on central tolerance rather than on-target toxicity, so it is not a normal-tissue function finding.

entries.toxicity_reports: No on-target normal-tissue toxicity attributable to LAGE-1/NY-ESO-1 recognition was found in the one clinical paper opened: Lopez et al. 2025 phase 1 of IMCnyeso (NY-ESO-1/LAGE-1A x CD3 bispecific; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12047507/) states 'There are no treatment-related discontinuations or deaths. The most common adverse events are grade 1/2 cytokine release syndrome and associated symptoms.' Web-search snippets (not opened) for lete-cel and the NCI NY-ESO-1 TCR trial likewise describe no off-tumor target toxicity; these therapies target the shared SLLMWITQC/HLA-A*02 epitope, so they inform on LAGE-1A as well as NY-ESO-1.

evidence.source_title: PMID 14532297 (Taimi et al., J Biol Chem 2004, doi:10.1074/jbc.M308337200)
evidence.tissue: skin (keratinocytes); keratinocyte (HPK1a transformed human keratinocyte line)
evidence.finding: Human: the cloning paper states CYP26C1 is not widely expressed in the adult but is inducible by retinoic acid in a transformed human keratinocyte line. It is a functional retinoic-acid-catabolising enzyme. Biallelic loss causes focal facial dermal dysplasia type IV (PMID 29263414), a congenital developmental skin defect, which is an expected embryonic role and not counted as a finding.
evidence.limitations: Source exists and the abstract says exactly this: 'CYP26C1 is not widely expressed in the adult but is inducible by RA in HPK1a, transformed human keratinocyte cell lines.' The evidence is a transformed (HPV-immortalised) cell line treated with exogenous retinoic acid in vitro, not normal adult skin in vivo; the same sentence actually supports low adult expression. Paralog specificity is not established from the abstract (CYP26A1/B1 are also RA-inducible in keratinocytes), though the cloning paper presumably used CYP26C1-specific probes. Not evidence of normal-tissue expression.

entries.toxicity_reports: No CYP26C1-targeted therapy toxicity found. (A pan-CYP26 inhibitor, talarozole, appeared in search results for topical skin use; I did not open it for safety data and it is not CYP26C1-selective.)

Retinal expression is therefore plausible but unconfirmed by any gene-specific assay; HPA has no IHC annotation.

evidence.finding: Human: DCST1 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that negatively regulates type I interferon signalling by ubiquitinating STAT2 for degradation (Nair et al. 2016). UniProt records it as induced by IFNB1. The work was done in cell lines and gives no normal-tissue expression data.

UniProt Q5T197 carries 'INDUCTION: Induced by IFNB1'. All of it was done in HEK293T cells, largely with ectopic expression plus siRNA; there is no normal-tissue or primary-cell data, so it does not show expression in any normal adult tissue.

evidence.source_title: Terkawi et al. 2017, Sci Rep 7:41772, PMID 28181499, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5299406
evidence.tissue: blood / tissue macrophages; monocyte-derived macrophages (activated, phagocytosing)
evidence.finding: Human: Terkawi et al. 2017 (Sci Rep) found DEFB130 among the top three genes upregulated in macrophages phagocytosing Plasmodium falciparum-infected red cells; expression was higher in differentiated macrophages than in monocytes, knockdown increased parasite biomass, and synthetic DEFB130 peptide had modest anti-plasmodial activity.
evidence.limitations: I opened the paper (Terkawi et al. 2017, PMC5299406) and it supports the claim as stated. DEFB130 was one of the top three upregulated genes (about 4.6-fold by microarray, validated by qRT-PCR) in human donor macrophages phagocytosing P. falciparum-infected red cells. ELISA and confocal immunofluorescence showed protein, and levels were higher in differentiated macrophages than in monocytes or THP-1. esiRNA knockdown raised parasite biomass, and the synthetic peptide had modest activity (IC50 about 43-49 uM). Caveats: the macrophages were differentiated in vitro with GM-CSF and IFN-gamma, not taken from tissue; it is a single unreplicated study; absolute expression is not given; the antibody is not knockout-validated. The paper does not distinguish DEFB130A from DEFB130B (it cites NM_001037804), which does not matter for a combined A/B entry.

evidence.source_title: Ottolenghi et al. 2002, Genomics 79:333-43, PMID 11863363 (primary, full text not opened); cited in Zhang et al. 2014, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4197572
evidence.finding: Human: Zhang et al. 2014 (Development), summarising earlier RT-PCR work, state that DMRT6/DMRTB1 is strongly expressed in adult testis and weakly in human adult ovary and pancreas; in mouse, fetal Dmrt6 mRNA is mainly in brain. The mouse knockout phenotype is confined to spermatogonial differentiation and meiosis, with no somatic requirement reported.
evidence.limitations: Zhang et al. 2014 (PMC4197572) does say Dmrt6 'is strongly expressed in adult testis in mouse and human and weakly in human adult ovary and pancreas', citing Ottolenghi et al. 2002 (Genomics, PMID 11863363). That is a secondary one-line citation. The Ottolenghi abstract does not mention tissue expression and I could not open its full text, so the assay, its specificity among DM-domain paralogs and whether it was quantitative are unverified. The same paper reports Dmrt6 knockout mice as 'otherwise normal and healthy' outside spermatogenesis, with females normal and fertile, so there is no somatic function. Pancreas is already sampled by the bulk and rare-cell panels at about zero, so this is a weak, unreplicated 2002 RT-PCR signal.

evidence.source_title: Xiao et al. 2001, Nat Genet 27:201-4, PMID 11175790, https://www.nature.com/articles/ng0201_201
evidence.finding: Human: DSPP encodes the major non-collagenous dentin matrix proteins made by odontoblasts; heterozygous DSPP mutations cause dentinogenesis imperfecta type 1/2 and dentin dysplasia (Xiao et al. 2001, Nat Genet). Odontoblasts persist and secrete dentin throughout adult life, so this is a constitutive adult non-reproductive function.
evidence.limitations: The Xiao et al. 2001 abstract (PMID 11175790) confirms three DSPP mutations segregating with dentinogenesis imperfecta 1 in three Chinese families. This is human germline genetics, so it is gene-specific. Two caveats: the paper shows a developmental dentin disease, not adult expression, and the statement that odontoblasts keep secreting dentin through adult life is general dental biology the paper does not itself show. The mutations are dominant (splice-site and missense), not simple loss of function. Tooth is absent from every panel the screen uses, so the gap is real.

evidence.source_title: Xiao et al. 2001, Nat Genet 27:201-4, PMID 11175790
evidence.finding: Human: in two of three families in Xiao et al. 2001, DSPP missense mutations segregated with dentinogenesis imperfecta plus progressive high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (DFNA39). Secondary sources (MedlinePlus) say DSPP is active in the inner ear, with transcripts detected in mouse inner ear, but a causal role in hearing is described as unresolved.
evidence.limitations: The source exists and says this: two of three families had DGI1 plus progressive high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (DFNA39) with DSPP missense mutations. But the only expression evidence is in mouse inner ear ('transcripts of DSPP ... are also detected in the inner ear of mice'), with no human cochlear expression data. The human link is co-segregation in two families from one study, with no demonstrated causal role. I did not open the MedlinePlus statement. A PubMed search for DSPP and inner ear or cochlea returned no later study showing human inner-ear expression.

evidence.source_title: Ogbureke et al. 2016, J Histochem Cytochem 64:623-36, PMID 27666430 (PMC5037501); Ogbureke and Fisher 2004, J Dent Res 83:664-70, PMID 15329369; Prasad et al. 2011, PMC3261624 (mouse)
evidence.tissue: kidney, salivary gland (also cartilage, liver, brain and bone in mouse); ductal / tubular epithelium (proximal, distal and collecting tubules; salivary striated and interlobular ducts)
evidence.finding: Human and monkey: Ogbureke and colleagues report DSPP protein by immunohistochemistry in salivary gland ducts (Ogbureke and Fisher 2004) and in kidney tubules, where it co-localises with MMP20 (2016). Mouse: Prasad et al. 2011 detected DSPP by RT-PCR, in situ and IHC in salivary gland, cartilage, liver, kidney and brain, but not heart or spleen, at levels far below dentin.
evidence.limitations: All three sources exist and broadly say what is claimed. Ogbureke and Fisher 2004 (PMID 15329369) report DSPP in human and mouse salivary glands, and Ogbureke et al. 2016 (PMID 27666430) report DSPP with MMP20 in human and monkey kidney tubules by IHC, proximity ligation and immunofluorescence. The human evidence is antibody-only, from one group, with no knockout or orthogonal RNA validation. The Human Protein Atlas lists DSPP RNA as 'Not detected' with IHC 'Pending normal tissue annotation', so there is no independent protein confirmation. Prasad et al. 2011 is mouse-only, and the claim misdescribes it: the methods were RT-PCR, real-time PCR, Western, IHC and a lacZ knock-in (not in situ), and the abstract compares levels to bone (higher in salivary gland, cartilage, liver and kidney), not to dentin. I read abstracts only for all three papers.

evidence.source_title: He et al. 2016, Int J Mol Sci, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4848891
evidence.finding: Human cell lines only: shRNA knockdown of EBLN1 in human oligodendroglia cells reduced proliferation and induced apoptosis (He et al. 2016, Int J Mol Sci), and siRNA knockdown in HeLa impaired cell-cycle transit and increased DNA damage (Sci Rep 2016). Protein existence is still contested (UniProt transcript-level evidence only) and another study reports the locus is epigenetically repressed in most tissues.
evidence.limitations: The source (He et al. 2016, PMC4848891) exists and reports that shRNA knockdown of EBLN1 (81% mRNA reduction) in human OL cells suppressed proliferation, caused G2/M arrest and roughly doubled apoptosis (5.8% vs 3.0%). But OL is a permanent line established from human fetal brain, not normal adult tissue. EBLN1 protein was not measured and there was no rescue experiment, so off-target shRNA effects are not excluded. I did not open the HeLa knockdown paper or the epigenetic-repression study mentioned in the claim. This is not evidence of a physiological role in adult brain.

evidence.source_title: https://rest.ensembl.org/sequence/id/ENSG00000267618?type=protein;multiple_sequences=1 ; https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/O75771.fasta ; https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q8WZ73.fasta ; HPA RAD51D ENSG00000185379 and RFFL ENSG00000092871 (https://www.proteinatlas.org): both Low tissue specificity, detected in all, protein-level evidence
evidence.finding: Human. Ensembl annotates this gene as a RAD51L3-RFFL readthrough. Its three protein isoforms are built almost entirely from RAD51D (UniProt O75771, DNA repair) sequence, and the longest (272 aa) continues into the C-terminal RING region of RFFL (UniProt Q8WZ73, E3 ubiquitin ligase rififylin). Only short junction or tail segments are unique, so most peptides are shared with two normally expressed proteins. This is a sequence comparison done in this session; I did not look up RAD51D or RFFL tissue expression.
evidence.limitations: Could not refute. Ensembl describes ENSG00000267618 as 'RAD51L3-RFFL readthrough' (havana, protein_coding) with three protein products, which I re-fetched and aligned by eye against UniProt. (1) ENSP00000466834 (272 aa): after the initiator Met, residues match RAD51D (O75771) from about residue 171 (AEALRRIQ...) to 301 (...LAKSSRQ), then continue in RFFL (Q8WZ73) from SIDSEDSFVPG to the C-terminal RING end (...RAVHVFRS). It skips the RFFL segment VSGAEDQN, which may match another RFFL isoform, so the only unique peptides are those spanning the RAD51D/RFFL junction and possibly that skip. (2) ENSP00000467986 (128 aa): RAD51D sequence from MLDVLQEL to LAKSSRQ plus SIDS from RFFL. (3) ENSP00000464799 (204 aa): RAD51D from residue 120 (MAANVAHGL...) to SSRQ, skipping one RAD51D segment (TQDEEEQ then AEALRR), with a unique 20-aa tail ILSCGQPAATGSAWMDSLRRSH. One wording correction: the longest isoform is roughly half RAD51D and half RFFL rather than 'almost entirely RAD51D', but the claim does say it continues into the RFFL RING region, so the substance stands. The claim left parent expression unchecked; HPA lists both RAD51D (ENSG00000185379) and RFFL (ENSG00000092871) as 'Low tissue specificity', 'Detected in all', with protein-level evidence. Caveats: this is sequence identity, not an expression measurement of the readthrough, and it cannot distinguish the readthrough from its parents (gene_specific=false). The readthrough itself has transcript-level evidence only in HPA.

evidence.source_title: https://rest.ensembl.org/sequence/id/ENSG00000273155?type=protein ; https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q8TCC3.fasta ; HPA MRPL30 ENSG00000185414 (https://www.proteinatlas.org/ENSG00000185414-MRPL30/tissue): Low tissue specificity, detected in all, protein-level evidence
evidence.tissue: all tissues (ubiquitous mitochondrial ribosomal protein); all nucleated cells
evidence.finding: Human. Ensembl annotates this gene as a novel LIPT1-MRPL30 readthrough, and its 131-aa protein (ENSP00000387111) is identical to the first 118 residues of MRPL30 (UniProt Q8TCC3, 161 aa); only the last 13 residues (FVVSSQLFLKCIA) are unique. MRPL30 is a mitochondrial ribosomal protein, so nearly every peptide from this candidate is also a normal self peptide. This is a sequence comparison done in this session, not a published expression result; I did not check MRPL30 expression itself.
evidence.limitations: Could not refute. Ensembl describes ENSG00000273155 as 'novel LIPT1-MRPL30 readthrough' (havana, protein_coding). Its only protein, ENSP00000387111 (131 aa), is identical to MRPL30 (UniProt Q8TCC3, 161 aa) over residues 1-118; it then diverges into a unique 13-aa tail, FVVSSQLFLKCIA, where MRPL30 continues IKPLKLPQ... I re-fetched both sequences and the claim holds exactly. The claim left MRPL30 expression unchecked; HPA lists MRPL30 (ENSG00000185414) as 'Low tissue specificity', 'Detected in all', with evidence at protein level, so the shared 118 residues are normal self sequence in essentially every adult tissue. Caveats: this is a sequence-identity argument, not an expression measurement of the readthrough transcript, and by its nature it cannot distinguish the readthrough from its parent (hence gene_specific=false). Only peptides overlapping the 13-residue tail or the junction at residue 118/119 would be candidate-specific, and the readthrough protein itself has transcript-level evidence only in HPA.

entries.summary: All gene-specific literature places EXD1 in the male germline: mouse studies define it as a piRNA-biogenesis partner of TDRD12 in the PET complex localised to intermitochondrial cement of spermatocytes, and two human genetics papers link EXD1 variants to male infertility, one measuring EXD1 mRNA by RT-qPCR in human testis biopsies. No publication reporting EXD1 RNA or protein in normal adult human brain or any other somatic tissue by a gene-specific assay was found, and equally no gene-specific multi-tissue panel showing its absence there. UniProt has no tissue-specificity or disease comment; HPA has no antibody or IHC, calls bulk RNA testis enriched (11.7 nTPM) but summarises single-nuclei brain RNA as 'Low cell type specificity / Detected in many', which is database count data in line with, not independent of, the donor-level signal.
entries.decision_reason: Sources describe germline restriction or did not test adult somatic tissue; the only brain statement is HPA database RNA annotation. Human loss of function causes male infertility (testis, not a vital tissue), so R3 does not fire.

evidence.finding: Human: mature FAM237A (also called neurosecretory protein GL, NPGL) binds and activates human GPR83 at nanomolar concentrations in transfected HEK293T cells, and the authors describe it as a neuropeptide ligand of a brain-specific receptor. This is in vitro receptor pharmacology, not a measurement of FAM237A in human tissue, and the pairing is not yet officially accepted.
evidence.limitations: The source exists and says what the claim reports (Li et al., FEBS J 2023): mature human FAM237A binds and activates human GPR83 at nanomolar range in transfected HEK293T cells, and the abstract calls FAM237A a 'so far rarely studied neuropeptide' and GPR83 'brain-specific'. The ligand is recombinant FAM237A itself, so it is gene-specific and not the paralog FAM237B (NPGM). But it is in vitro receptor pharmacology only: nothing in it measures FAM237A RNA or protein in any human tissue, adult or otherwise, and the abstract says the pairing had not been reproduced by other laboratories and GPR83 is still officially an orphan. It supports a plausible neuropeptide role, not demonstrated expression in normal adult human hypothalamus.

evidence.source_title: PMID 35742932 (Narimatsu Y et al., Int J Mol Sci 2022;23:6488, PMC9223635)
evidence.tissue: brain (hypothalamus); effect on adipose tissue; hypothalamic neurons
evidence.finding: Mouse: NPGL (the Fam237a product) is described as a small secretory protein identified in the hypothalamus of birds and mammals; transgenic overexpression of Npgl in ICR mice increased white adipose tissue mass. Evidence is gain-of-function in rodents only; no loss-of-function model was found.
evidence.limitations: The source exists and matches the claim (Narimatsu et al., Int J Mol Sci 2022): NPGL is 'a small secretory protein identified in the hypothalamus of birds and mammals', and Npgl-transgenic ICR mice had increased white adipose tissue mass. The evidence is mouse-only and gain-of-function by transgenic overexpression, so it does not show an endogenous requirement or any human expression. The abstract contains no human data and no loss-of-function model. The transgene is Npgl specifically, so it is not paralog-ambiguous.

The 1998 cloning paper states FKBP6 is expressed in testis, heart, skeletal muscle, liver and kidney (the source of the UniProt comment), whereas a 2006 RT-PCR panel of 15 adult human tissues detected a band only in testis, and HPA IHC (reliability Enhanced) summarizes protein only in spermatogonia and ovarian follicle cells. A 2015 study measured FKBP6 mRNA by qRT-PCR in non-cancerous liver of an HCV-infected patient, i.e. diseased tissue with virus-induced expression. None of the papers discusses discrimination from the FKBP6P1/FKBP6P2 pseudogene copies.

evidence.source_title: PMID 9782077 (Meng X et al., Genomics 1998;52:130-7) for the claim; PMID 12764197 (Crackower et al., Science 2003;300:1291-5) as the gene-specific knockout counter-evidence
evidence.finding: Human: the 1998 paper that first cloned FKBP6 states it is expressed in testis, heart, skeletal muscle, liver and kidney, and proposes that hemizygous deletion may contribute to hypercalcemia and growth delay in Williams syndrome. Only the abstract was read, the assay is not stated there, and later databases describe the gene as testis-restricted, so this may reflect low-specificity early methods.
evidence.limitations: The source exists and the abstract says verbatim 'FKBP6 is expressed in testis, heart, skeletal muscle, liver, and kidney' and that hemizygous deletion 'may contribute to certain defects such as hypercalcemia and growth delay in WS' (Meng et al., Genomics 1998). It is about human FKBP6. The abstract does not state the assay, relative levels, or whether the tissues were adult; I did not read the full text. A 1998 cloning paper most likely used hybridisation or RT-PCR, which could cross-detect other FKBP family members, so I marked gene-specificity as unestablished and adult-normal as presumed. The Williams syndrome link is speculation in the abstract, not a demonstrated somatic function. Later gene-specific loss-of-function evidence points to a germline role: Fkbp6 knockout mice and as/as mutant rats have male sterility from a meiotic defect, females are fertile, and that abstract reports no somatic phenotype (Crackower et al., Science 2003). This is an unreplicated early report that conflicts with the modern atlases, not evidence of a somatic function.

evidence.source_title: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8559929/ (Mota et al., PLoS Genet 2021)
evidence.finding: Mouse: Foxr1 knockout gives about 23.5% survival to postnatal day 21, lower body weight, a thinner cortical plate and enlarged ventricles; mouse qPCR detected Foxr1 mRNA in heart, liver and lung as well as brain. Human: one proband with a de novo M280L variant had postnatal microcephaly and progressive brain atrophy (confounded by a co-occurring ATP1A3 variant), and the paper cites Human Brain Transcriptome data that brain expression is maintained throughout life.
evidence.limitations: The source exists and the stated numbers check out (Mota et al., PLoS Genet 2021, first 100k characters read): about 23.5% of Foxr1 knockout mice survive to P21, they weigh 24.5% less, the cortical plate is about 11.3% thinner and ventricles are 34.6% larger. Mouse qPCR detected Foxr1 mRNA in heart, liver and lung, with higher expression in brain at embryonic day 17. The human proband has a de novo M280L variant with postnatal microcephaly and progressive brain atrophy, and the ATP1A3 variant was returned to the family as a partial diagnosis. The paper cites Human Brain Transcriptome data that brain expression 'is maintained throughout life'. As a normal-adult-human finding it is weak: the knockout phenotype is mouse and developmental, the highlighted brain qPCR signal is embryonic, the single human case is confounded, and the only adult human evidence is a secondary citation of an array atlas at low level, not a gene-specific assay in adult tissue. The paper itself says FOXR1 is expressed at low levels in most tissues and mainly in brain and reproductive organs.

Low-level normal expression in a few cell types is supported; the specific tissues are not.

entries.summary: No GAGE10-specific expression study was found; the three PubMed hits for GAGE10 concern promoter polymorphism, methylation and copy number. Family-level sources describe GAGE as germ-cell restricted: IHC with pan-GAGE monoclonals on 24 normal tissues was positive only in testis and ovary (oocytes), and normal lung was negative. These antibodies were characterized on GAGE-1 to -8 and do not address GAGE10 specifically.

entries.decision_reason: The assay detects alarin, a splice product sharing only the peptide's first residues with GALP; antibody specificity is not established.

evidence.tissue: eye (cornea, iris, retina, choroid); corneal epithelium and endothelium, perivascular cells of iris and retina, intrinsic choroidal neurons
evidence.finding: Alarin, a peptide made from a GALP splice variant lacking exon 3, shows immunoreactivity in human corneal epithelium and endothelium, around iris and retinal blood vessels and in intrinsic choroidal neurons; quantitative RT-PCR confirmed alarin mRNA in human retina and choroid. Reviews also place alarin around blood vessels in human and mouse skin.
evidence.limitations: Abstract of PMID 23178871 read: alarin-like immunoreactivity in human corneal epithelium and endothelium, around iris and retinal blood vessels and in intrinsic choroidal neurons, with quantitative RT-PCR confirming alarin mRNA in human retina and choroid. Caveats: the abstract does not state donor age or health (normal adult donor eyes are assumed, not verified); the authors call it 'alarin-like' immunoreactivity, so antibody specificity is not established beyond the qPCR in retina and choroid; cornea and iris are antibody-only. Alarin is a GALP splice product, so this is the GALP gene and not a paralog, but it bears on only the shared N-terminal residues of the GALP peptide. The skin statement comes from reviews and was not checked.

evidence.source_title: PMID 11861493 (macaque ISH); PMID 14962070 (rat ISH)
evidence.tissue: hypothalamus (arcuate nucleus, median eminence) and posterior pituitary; arcuate neurons; pituicytes of the neurohypophysis
evidence.finding: In adult macaque, GALP mRNA is confined to the arcuate nucleus, median eminence and neurohypophysis (PMID 11861493); in rat it is in arcuate neurons and pituicytes (PMID 14962070) and is induced by leptin, so expression is state-dependent. No human-specific expression paper was found in this session.
evidence.limitations: Both abstracts were read and say what the claim reports: in situ hybridisation confines GALP mRNA to arcuate nucleus, median eminence and neurohypophysis in macaque (PMID 11861493), and to arcuate neurons and pituicytes in rat (PMID 14962070). The evidence is macaque and rat only; no human expression data. The state-dependence in the rat paper is thyroid hormone and lactation (lactation raises neurohypophysis GALP), not leptin; leptin regulation is only cited as background in the macaque abstract. In situ probes are gene-specific, and the pattern is conserved across primate and rodent, so human arcuate expression is plausible but unshown.

evidence.assay: mRNA detection, method not stated in the abstract
evidence.finding: GALR3 mRNA detectable in adrenal gland and pancreas.
evidence.quote: GALR3 mRNA was highly expressed in human testis and was detectable in adrenal gland and pancreas.
evidence.limitations: Detectable only; no cell type and no protein.

evidence.source_title: PMID 9832121; rat distribution PMID 9722565
evidence.finding: The human cloning paper reports GALR3 mRNA highly expressed in human testis and detectable in adrenal gland and pancreas. Rat data (same era, PMID 9722565 abstract seen in search results only) describe a widely distributed, low-abundance transcript highest in hypothalamus and pituitary.
evidence.limitations: Abstract of PMID 9832121 read: 'GALR3 mRNA was highly expressed in human testis and was detectable in adrenal gland and pancreas.' The rat statement also matches PMID 9722565 (widely distributed, low abundance, highest in hypothalamus and pituitary by RNase protection). Caveats: 'detectable' only, a 1998 assay whose method and tissue source (probably commercial adult RNA) are not given in the abstract, with no cell-type localisation and no protein. It supports a low-level signal, not a functional role.

evidence.finding: Mouse: MGI states that Galr3-null mice show increased anxiety-like behaviour and abnormal social investigation, and a separate report describes an alcohol-preferring phenotype; a 2023 review abstract describes GALR3 as broadly expressed in the nervous system including the retina and as a modulator of immune and inflammatory responses (a murine colitis study, PMID 33436730, was listed but its abstract was not read).
evidence.limitations: PMID 36693600 abstract read: it states GALR3 is 'broadly expressed in the nervous system, including the retina' and modulates immune and inflammatory responses. It is a primary mouse study, not a review, and the functional data are mouse disease models (light damage, P23H Rho), where GALR3 loss or the antagonist SNAP-37889 was protective, plus ARPE19 cells. The MGI behavioural phenotypes and the alcohol-preference report were not opened and remain unverified. All mouse; no human normal-tissue expression or loss-of-function evidence. The knockout is gene-specific, but SNAP-37889 selectivity was not assessed here.

evidence.quote: GDF-9 mRNA was observed in ovary and testis and, surprisingly, in diverse nongonadal tissues, including pituitary, uterus, and bone marrow.
evidence.limitations: Abstract only (via NCBI E-utilities); signal levels, which tissues were positive by Northern vs only RT-PCR, and probe/primer specificity versus GDF9B/BMP15 not visible. evidence.tissue: thyroid gland; calcitonin-producing parafollicular C cells
evidence.finding: Human: OMIM and UniProt summaries of Lindahl et al. 2001 state GFRA4 transcripts are highly expressed in adult human thyroid, with RT-PCR and in situ hybridisation localising it to C cells (normal and medullary carcinoma). The primary paper was not opened in this session.
evidence.limitations: The primary paper was found and its abstract read (Lindahl et al. 2001, PMID 11116144). The title and abstract state that human GFRA4 splice forms are 'predominantly expressed in the thyroid gland' and that RET and GFRA4, but not other GFRA mRNAs, overlap in 'normal and malignant thyroid medullary cells'. That is human, includes normal tissue, and distinguishes GFRA4 from GFRA1-3. The 'adult thyroid' and 'RT-PCR and in situ' details come from the OMIM summary seen in search results; the abstract does not give the methods or donor age. No human protein-level evidence in normal C cells was seen.

evidence.finding: Mouse: GFRalpha4 is produced only in thyroid C cells and they express functional receptor throughout postnatal development. Knockout mice have 60% less thyroid calcitonin as newborns and increased juvenile bone formation, but adult calcitonin levels, C-cell number, growth and viability are normal.
evidence.limitations: Abstract of PMID 16497798 read and it matches the claim: by in situ and immunohistochemistry the functional GPI-anchored GFRalpha4 is made in mouse only in C cells (not parathyroid or brain); knockouts have 60% less thyroid calcitonin as newborns and 45% less at 3 weeks, increased juvenile bone formation, and normal adult calcitonin, C-cell number, growth and viability. Mouse only, hence weakened. It supports the human C-cell finding and shows the adult loss-of-function phenotype is mild.

entries.decision_reason: Evidence is from another species, a database annotation or an assay shared with a paralog, or the tissue is reproductive.

evidence.tissue: olfactory epithelium, vomeronasal organ; olfactory sensory neurons
evidence.finding: Mouse: Goofy is a Golgi membrane protein expressed specifically in olfactory and vomeronasal sensory neurons; knockout mice have mislocalised adenylyl cyclase III, shortened olfactory cilia and a raised odour detection threshold. No human olfactory expression data were located (search budget ran out).

Mouse only; no human olfactory expression data. Humans lack a functional vomeronasal organ, so only the olfactory epithelium part could carry over.

evidence.source_title: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2719720
evidence.finding: Mouse: connexin 23 (Gje1) is expressed in lens fibre cells and the Aey12 point mutant arrests lens development with small eyes, although a targeted null has transparent lenses. For human, the search results state that the ortholog carries a stop mutation at the start of exon 3 and that no Cx23 mRNA was found in human eye, so this is likely not a human liability.
evidence.limitations: PMC2719720 opened (Sonntag et al., 'Mouse lens connexin23 (Gje1) does not form functional gap junction channels but causes enhanced ATP release from HeLa cells'). It confirms the mouse part (Cx23 in newly formed lens fibre cells) and the human part: a stop mutation at the start of exon 3, 'No Cx23 mRNA was found in human eye', no transcript by RT-PCR or Northern in human lens and retina, and the conclusion that Cx23 is a pseudogene in primates. The statement is accurate as written, but as a human normal-tissue liability it is negative: the only human evidence argues against lens expression. PMC4920263 (Aey12 mutant and null) was not opened.

evidence.source_title: PMID 25287256; doi:10.1007/s00726-014-1847-3 (Got1l1 knockout, contradicts PMID 20133766)
evidence.tissue: brain (cortex, hippocampus, pineal gland); cortical pyramidal neurons, hippocampal CA3/CA2 neurons, pinealocytes
evidence.finding: Mouse, disputed: Kim et al. (PNAS 2010) reported the enzyme as an aspartate racemase present in cortical and hippocampal neurons and pinealocytes, with knockdown impairing adult hippocampal neurogenesis. A later knockout study (Tanaka-Hayashi et al., Amino Acids 2015) found Got1l1 mRNA high in testis but not detected in brain, no racemase activity, and unchanged D-aspartate in knockout hippocampus. The weight of evidence favours testis-restricted expression.
evidence.limitations: Both sources exist and are described accurately, but together they refute brain expression rather than support it. Kim et al., PNAS 2010 (PMID 20133766) reported a cloned mammalian aspartate racemase that colocalizes with D-aspartate in brain and neuroendocrine tissues, with shRNA depletion in adult hippocampal newborn neurons impairing dendritic development and survival; this rests on antibody staining and shRNA, both prone to off-target effects. Tanaka-Hayashi et al., Amino Acids 2015 (PMID 25287256), using a Got1l1 knockout, found the mRNA 'highly expressed in the testis, but it is not detected in the brain and submandibular gland', no difference in D-aspartate between wild-type and knockout testis or hippocampus, and recombinant Got1l1 with aminotransferase but no racemase activity. The gene-specific knockout evidence agrees with the low human brain RNA. All data are mouse. The finding's own text concedes it is not a real screen gap; it should not count as normal-tissue expression. The cortex/CA3/pinealocyte localisation detail was not checked (abstracts only; PMC full text blocked by captcha).

evidence.source_title: PMID 20921407; doi:10.1073/pnas.1012764107 (abstract read via PubMed E-utilities)
evidence.tissue: brain (midbrain interpeduncular nucleus); interpeduncular nucleus neurons
evidence.finding: Mouse: Gsc2 (Goosecoid-like, Gscl) expression in adult brain is restricted to the interpeduncular nucleus. Knockout mice have reduced REM sleep, fewer REM episodes, lower REM theta power and lose Dgcr14 expression in that nucleus, with apparently normal anatomy (Funato et al., PNAS 2010). Mouse only; the gene lies in the human 22q11 deletion region.
evidence.limitations: Source exists and its abstract matches the claim: Funato et al., PNAS 2010 (PMID 20921407) states that Gscl expression is restricted to the interpeduncular nucleus, and that Gscl-/- mice have apparently normal IP anatomy and connections but reduced total REM sleep time, fewer REM episodes, reduced REM theta power, increased arousability during REM, and loss of Dgcr14 expression in the IP. Gscl is the mouse ortholog of human GSC2 (not GSC), and the knockout is gene-specific. Weakened because it is mouse only: no human adult expression or protein data are given, and the phenotype is a mild sleep-architecture change, not a vital-tissue defect. Only the abstract was read (PMC full text blocked by captcha).

entries.summary: Human sources describe GSX2 as an embryonic ventral-telencephalon (ganglionic eminence) patterning factor; no opened source reports GSX2 RNA or protein in normal adult human tissue by a gene-specific assay, and nothing was found for retina or RPE. Caveat: in adult mouse brain Gsx2 protein is expressed in a restricted subset of subventricular-zone neural stem cells (antibody and knock-in reporter), and HPA bulk RNA lists human brain at 1.1 nTPM, so a small adult human SVZ population cannot be excluded. HPA has no tissue IHC and UniProt has no tissue-specificity comment.

evidence.source_title: De Mori R et al. Agenesis of the putamen and globus pallidus caused by recessive mutations in the homeobox gene GSX2. Brain 2019 (PubMed abstract)

evidence.source_title: Lopez-Juarez A et al. Gsx2 controls region-specific activation of neural stem cells and injury-induced neurogenesis in the adult subventricular zone. Genes Dev 2013 (PubMed abstract)
evidence.assay: immunostaining / genetic reporter in mouse (per abstract and search summary)
evidence.finding: Gsx2 present in a subset of adult mouse SVZ neural stem cells and induced after injury.
evidence.quote: In the intact brain, Gsx2 is expressed in a regionally restricted subset of NSCs and promotes the activation and lineage progression of stem cells
evidence.limitations: Mouse, not human; abstract only (full text XML could not be retrieved). Implies possible adult brain niche expression but no human confirmation found.

evidence.source_title: Dunwell TL, Holland PWH. Diversity of human and mouse homeobox gene expression in development and adult tissues. BMC Dev Biol 2016
evidence.finding: GSX2 listed among ANTP-class homeobox genes in the 'neural-enriched' set.
evidence.quote: it does include several other ANTP class genes including several implicated in specification and patterning of anterior brain regions in other vertebrates: BARHL1, BARHL2, EN1, EN2, TLX3, NKX6-2, NKX2-2, DLX1, DLX2, HMX1, VAX2, GSX2
evidence.limitations: RNA-seq compendium (includes developmental samples); not a gene-specific assay and I did not determine which samples drove the neural call.

evidence.source_title: Human Protein Atlas gene record GSX2 (JSON)
evidence.finding: RNA tissue specificity 'Tissue enhanced' (brain 1.1 nTPM), cluster 'Brain - Neuronal signaling'; single-cell and single-nuclei brain 'Not detected'; no antibody / no IHC.
evidence.quote: RNA tissue specificity: Tissue enhanced; RNA tissue specific nTPM: brain 1.1; RNA single cell type specificity: Not detected; RNA single nuclei brain specificity: Not detected
evidence.limitations: Count data already used as a numeric filter; no protein data.

evidence.source_title: UniProt Q9BZM3 (GSX2_HUMAN)
evidence.finding: No tissue-specificity comment; function described as brain development.
evidence.quote: regulates the expression of numerous genes including genes important for brain development
evidence.limitations: No adult expression statement.

evidence.source_title: PMID 23723414; doi:10.1101/gad.217539.113 (abstract read via PubMed E-utilities)
evidence.tissue: brain (adult subventricular zone neural stem cell niche); adult neural stem cells / progenitors
evidence.finding: Mouse: Gsx2 is expressed in a regionally restricted subset of adult SVZ neural stem cells in the intact brain, where it promotes their activation and lineage progression. After hypoxia-ischemia or neurotoxic injury it is induced across wide areas of the niche and is required for injury-induced neurogenesis (Lopez-Juarez et al., Genes Dev 2013). Mouse only; not shown in adult human.
evidence.limitations: Source exists and its abstract says what is claimed: Lopez-Juarez et al., Genes Dev 2013 (PMID 23723414) reports that in the intact adult mouse brain Gsx2 is expressed in a regionally restricted subset of SVZ neural stem cells, promotes their activation and lineage progression, is ectopically induced in damaged brains outside its normal domain, and is required for injury-induced SVZ neurogenesis. It is about Gsx2 itself (not Gsx1) and uses mouse genetics, so it is gene-specific. Weakened because it is mouse only, with no adult human data, and adult human SVZ neurogenesis is far more limited than in mouse, so transfer is uncertain. The specific injury models (hypoxia-ischemia, neurotoxic lesion) were not checked: PMC full text was blocked by a captcha and the abstract only says 'damaged brains'.

evidence.source_title: PMID 28234895; doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.1006633 (abstract via PubMed, full text via Europe PMC PMC5345878)
evidence.finding: Mouse: the ortholog H2A.B.3 is most highly expressed in testis, followed by brain. In brain chromatin it is found at transcription start sites of active genes and replaces H2A.Z at intron-exon boundaries, correlating with expression and exon inclusion (Soboleva et al., PLoS Genet 2017). evidence.limitations: Source exists (Soboleva et al., PLoS Genet 2017, PMID 28234895, doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.1006633) and supports the claim. Abstract: H2A.B 'is most highly expressed in the testis followed by the brain in mammals'; H2A.B.3 replaces H2A.Z at intron-exon boundaries in testis and brain, correlating with expression and exon inclusion. Full text: H2A.B.3 ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR in mouse hippocampus show it at the TSS and gene body of active genes, and S3 Fig shows immunostaining in hippocampal neurons. The introduction is more modest than the abstract: 'highly expressed in the adult testis with some expression in the brain'. Weakened because all data are mouse H2A.B.3, with no human tissue. It is also not gene-specific for human H2AB1: mouse H2A.B.3 is one of three mouse H2A.B genes and has no one-to-one mapping to human H2AB1 versus H2AB2/H2AB3, which encode near-identical proteins that an antibody or ChIP cannot separate. The 'no brain phenotyping in the knockout' statement was not checked.

evidence.source_title: PMID 25371201 (PMC4271235), abstract only
evidence.tissue: pancreas (islets of Langerhans); islet alpha and beta cells
evidence.finding: Hes3 is expressed in adult human and rodent pancreatic islets. In mouse, Hes3-null animals show worse beta-cell loss and hyperglycaemia after streptozotocin, expression rises after islet damage, and knockdown in MIN6 cells reduces Pdx1, insulin expression and insulin release.
evidence.limitations: The abstract of PMID 25371201 confirms 'Hes3 is expressed in human and rodent pancreatic islets', mouse co-localisation with alpha and beta cell markers, MIN6 knockdown reducing Pdx1, insulin and evoked insulin release, and increased streptozotocin islet damage in Hes3-null mice. I could not get the full text (JBC returned 403, PMC blocked), so the assay and donor status for the human islet expression, and the claim that expression rises after islet damage, are unverified. evidence.tissue: brain (subventricular zone, dentate gyrus, parenchyma); putative adult neural stem/progenitor cells
evidence.finding: In adult mouse brain, Hes3 marks putative neural stem/progenitor cells in the SVZ, the dentate subgranular zone and the parenchyma. evidence.limitations: The DOI resolves to PMID 30054579 (Nikolakopoulou et al., Sci Rep 2018), an adult mouse brain study. Its abstract supports only that streptozotocin beta-cell damage, high-fat diet and metformin regulate Hes3 levels in mouse brain, and that Hes3 is expressed in neural stem and progenitor cells. The specific anatomical sites, the demyelination/remyelination changes and the Hes3-null culture result are not in this abstract and would rest on the other papers named, which I did not open. Entirely mouse, as the claim itself says; no human adult evidence.
