evidence.finding: Human articular chondrocytes express IL36B (IL-1F8) constitutively, per the UniProt induction annotation citing Magne 2006. UniProt also lists low-level expression in bone marrow, heart, lung and colon (PMIDs 20300079, 21242515, not opened).
evidence.limitations: Magne 2006 does say IL-1F8 mRNA is constitutive in human articular chondrocytes (real-time PCR, six cultures). But these are isolated primary cells in culture from joint-replacement patients (osteoarthritis or femoral neck fracture; the paper does not say which group supplied each experiment), levels are reported only relative to the within-experiment maximum, and IL-1F8 protein was undetectable in chondrocyte supernatants. The authors conclude the joint is not a major source of IL-1F8. The UniProt low-level tissue list (PMIDs 20300079, 21242515) was confirmed only as a UniProt annotation; those papers were not opened.

evidence.source_title: PMID 21881584 (Carrier et al., J Invest Dermatol 2011) for keratinocyte induction; PMID 16646978 / PMC1526623 for synovial fibroblasts only
evidence.tissue: skin (epidermis) and synovium; keratinocytes; synovial fibroblasts
evidence.finding: Human IL36B (IL-1F8) is an inducible pro-inflammatory cytokine: IL-1A and TNF induce it in human keratinocytes, and IL-1A, IL-1B and TNF induce it in synovial fibroblasts (UniProt curated induction, citing Magne 2006). Reviews found in search also report induction in keratinocytes by IL-17A, TNF and IL-36 itself, with keratinocytes the main source in psoriatic plaques.
evidence.limitations: The cited paper (Magne 2006, PMID 16646978) exists but does not test keratinocytes: per its full text (PMC1526623) the cells studied were human synovial fibroblasts, articular chondrocytes, dermal fibroblasts and cell lines. It does show IL-1F8 mRNA induction by IL-1beta/TNF/IL-1alpha in cultured human synovial fibroblasts from joint-replacement patients, but IL-1F8 protein was undetectable in supernatants and not raised in inflamed joint tissue. The keratinocyte statement comes from the UniProt induction line, which misattributes it to this paper. Keratinocyte induction is real but is better supported by Carrier 2011 (cultured primary human keratinocytes, IL-17A and TNF), which is in vitro and psoriatic-lesion evidence, not normal adult tissue. UniProt itself says healthy control skin is low. The Frontiers review was not opened.

evidence.finding: Human: the maternally expressed transcription factor KLF14 is a master trans-regulator of adipose gene expression; its cis-eQTL is associated with type 2 diabetes and HDL cholesterol (Small 2011, MuTHER; replicated in METSIM, PMID 28257690). A stronger source is PMID 29632379 (Small 2018): risk alleles reduce KLF14 expression in adipose, KLF14 knockdown in human pre-adipocytes alters proliferation and lipogenesis, and adipose-specific Klf14 deletion in mice partly reproduces insulin resistance and dyslipidemia, with female-specific effects. KLF14 has no close paralog confounding an eQTL at its own locus. The statement that whole-body knockout males show no phenotype was not checked.

evidence.finding: Human: alpha-lactalbumin is the regulatory subunit of lactose synthase, and its normal expression is confined to the breast during late pregnancy and lactation (UniProt P00709; Tuohy 2016). This is hormone-induced expression in a tissue present in every adult woman, and it is the stated limitation of the alpha-lactalbumin breast cancer vaccine programme.
evidence.limitations: The Tuohy 2016 abstract (PMID 27322324) states alpha-lactalbumin 'expression in normal tissues is confined exclusively to the breast during late pregnancy and lactation', and UniProt P00709 annotates it as 'Mammary gland specific. Secreted in milk.' LALBA is a single well-characterised gene with no paralog ambiguity (its role as the lactose synthase regulatory subunit is textbook). The claim as stated is accurate. Whether it counts as a screen miss depends on whether breast is classed as reproductive in the catalog; it is induced, pregnancy- and lactation-restricted expression in normal adult breast.

evidence.tissue: skin epidermis; oral and oesophageal epithelium; differentiating keratinocytes
evidence.finding: Human: as for LCE3C. LCE3B is a cornified-envelope component detected by quantitative PCR in adult skin, tongue and oesophagus (PMID 15854049), induced in normal epidermis by barrier disruption (de Cid 2009), with antibacterial activity (PMID 28634035). It is deleted together with LCE3C in the common psoriasis risk allele.
evidence.limitations: Same evidence as LCE3C. The sources are real and human, but induction on barrier disruption is reported for LCE/LCE3 genes as a group in the de Cid 2009 abstract, the protein evidence is a pan-LCE3 antibody, and the antibacterial activity is for LCE3 proteins with LCE3A most active. Jackson 2005 describes the group as low-level in barrier epithelia; per-gene LCE3B values in tongue and oesophagus were not verified from the abstract. Strong expression is in injured or psoriatic skin rather than resting normal skin, and the gene is commonly homozygously deleted in healthy people.

evidence.source_title: PMID 19169253 (induction, group-level); PMID 15854049 (group-specific qPCR); PMID 26556599 (pan-LCE3 antibody)
evidence.tissue: skin epidermis; oral and oesophageal epithelium; differentiating keratinocytes (suprabasal and granular layers)
evidence.finding: Human: LCE3 genes are induced in normal epidermis by skin barrier disruption and strongly expressed in psoriatic lesions (de Cid 2009). Quantitative PCR also detects LCE3B/3C in adult skin, tongue and oesophagus with group-wise response to calcium and UV (PMID 15854049), a pan-LCE3 monoclonal antibody stains suprabasal epidermis (PMID 26556599), and LCE3 proteins have defensin-like antibacterial activity (PMID 28634035). Homozygous LCE3B/C deletion is a common psoriasis risk allele in healthy people, so the gene is dispensable.
evidence.limitations: The sources exist and are human. The de Cid 2009 abstract says 'LCE expression can be induced in normal epidermis by skin barrier disruption and is strongly expressed in psoriatic lesions', which is LCE/LCE3-group wording and not specific to LCE3C. Jackson 2005 (PMID 15854049) describes the group-3 genes as 'low-level' in all barrier-forming epithelia including internal ones; I read only the abstract, so the per-gene tongue and oesophagus values are not verified. The antibody in PMID 26556599 is explicitly pan-LCE3, so it does not separate LCE3C from LCE3A/B/D/E. The antibacterial activity in PMID 28634035 is for LCE3 proteins, 'LCE3A in particular'. Induction is real at group level, but constitutive normal expression is low, the strong expression is in injured or psoriatic skin, and the homozygous deletion is common in healthy people.

evidence.finding: Human: a bioinformatic survey of GEO and HPA datasets reports LGALS16 detected by microarray in diverse human cells and tissues, with expression changes in brain diseases and diabetes (Kaminker 2021). evidence.limitations: Kaminker and Timoshenko 2021 (PMID 34944551) exists and its abstract says LGALS16 'is detected by microarrays in diverse human cells/tissues and alters expression in association with cancer, diabetes, and brain diseases'. This is a bioinformatic survey of GEO microarray and HPA data; the only wet-lab work is in placental cell lines (BeWo, JEG-3). Microarray probes cannot reliably separate LGALS16 from LGALS13/14, and much of the non-placental signal is from disease datasets and cell lines. It adds no gene-specific evidence beyond the atlases the screen already uses.

evidence.source_title: PMID 22547800, full text PMC3356614, Fig. 4 and Discussion
evidence.finding: Human: UniProt curates LRRC52 tissue specificity as 'mainly expressed in testis and skeletal muscle', citing Yan and Aldrich 2012 (PMID 22547800). The abstract of that paper, which I read, names only testis, so the skeletal muscle statement rests on the UniProt annotation of the paper's tissue panel.
evidence.limitations: The finding said the muscle statement rested only on UniProt. The full text of Yan and Aldrich 2012 (PMC3356614) states it directly: 'LRRC52 is dominantly expressed in testis and skeletal muscle. A much lower level of LRRC52 expression was also detected in several other tissues including placenta, kidney, lung, and some glands' (Fig. 4, TaqMan real-time PCR on a normal human tissue panel, relative to RPLP0). The paralogs LRRC26, LRRC38 and LRRC55 were assayed separately with distinct patterns, so the assay is gene-specific. Caveats: relative mRNA only, plotted on a log scale, no protein, presumably a commercial adult RNA panel, and LRRC38 is also muscle-expressed in the same figure.

evidence.source_title: PMID 31451634 (Lingle 2019, PNAS); supporting PMID 31348683 (Lang 2019, FASEB J)
evidence.tissue: inner ear (cochlea); cochlear inner hair cells
evidence.finding: Mouse: LRRC52 is the BK-channel gamma-2 subunit in cochlear inner hair cells. In Lrrc52 knockout mice, BK current activation shifts by more than +200 mV and BK channel localisation is disrupted (Lingle 2019); nested PCR, immunohistochemistry and proximity ligation independently show LRRC52 transcript and protein with BK-alpha at the hair cell neck (Lang 2019, PMID 31348683). No human inner-ear data found.
evidence.limitations: Both sources exist and say what is claimed: Lingle 2019 (PMID 31451634) shows the >+200 mV BK activation shift and disrupted BK localisation in Lrrc52 knockout inner hair cells (Lrrc26 knockout had no effect), and Lang 2019 (PMID 31348683) shows nested PCR, immunohistochemistry and proximity ligation. The assays are gene-specific, but all evidence is mouse; there is no human inner-ear expression or human hearing-loss data. Real function, mouse-only.

entries.summary: No publication characterising LRRIQ4 (LRRC64) expression or function in any human tissue was found. PubMed returns two title/abstract hits (a mouse telomere-length SNP study and an LRRC8 evolution paper that names the LRRIQ4 family only as a relative), and the roughly 60 Europe PMC hits whose titles I screened are GWAS loci near TERC, methylation or gene-list mentions. UniProt has no tissue-specificity, function or disease comment and NCBI Gene carries only a predicted location. HPA has an antibody used for immunofluorescence only (no tissue IHC), calls bulk RNA testis enriched (2.5 nTPM, early spermatids) and summarises single-nuclei brain RNA as 'Cell type enhanced' in ependymal cells (6.0 nCPM), 'Detected in many' - database counts that neither confirm nor refute the astrocyte signal. No human loss-of-function disease was found.
entries.decision_reason: No gene-specific publication on expression in any tissue; only database RNA annotation. No loss-of-function disease.

evidence.source_title: PMID 14734521, full text PMC2211762 (Fig. 2; Materials and Methods, Tissues)
evidence.finding: Human: RT-PCR on purified medullary thymic epithelial cells detected MAGE-A1 in one of five thymi, at levels much lower than in testis (Gotter 2004, full text read). This is promiscuous tolerance-inducing expression and bears on T cell repertoire more than on on-target toxicity.
evidence.limitations: Gotter 2004 (PMID 14734521, PMC2211762) says this: 'MAGE-A1 was only detectable in one out of five thymi' and 'expression levels were much lower than in the corresponding peripheral tissues', using MAGE-A1-specific primers at 35 cycles. But the thymi were from infants aged 2 to 18 months undergoing corrective cardiac surgery, not adults. Detection was in one of five donors by end-point RT-PCR at high cycle number without sequencing, and it concerns promiscuous tolerance-related expression in a tiny cell population, which bears on the T cell repertoire rather than on-target toxicity.

evidence.source_title: PMID 23377668, full text PMC3581823 (Nanostring and Table 6 RNA-seq sections)
evidence.finding: Human: after fatal neurotoxicity with an anti-MAGE-A3/A9/A12 TCR, quantitative PCR, Nanostring and deep sequencing of human brain showed MAGE-A12 expression 'and possibly MAGE-A1, MAGE-A8, and MAGE-A9'; a pan-MAGE-A antibody stained rare neurons in normal brain (Morgan 2013). The MAGE-A1 signal is described only as possible.
evidence.limitations: Morgan 2013 (PMID 23377668, full text PMC3581823) exists and the abstract wording matches ('MAGE-A12 was expressed in human brain (and possibly MAGE-A1, MAGE-A8, and MAGE-A9)'). The MAGE-A1 evidence is thin on inspection. The neuron staining used antibody 6C1, which the authors verified recognises MAGE-A1, A2, A3, A4, A6, A9, A10 and A12, so it is not gene-specific. The MAGE-A1 RNA signal comes from Nanostring on commercial normal brain RNA against 'an arbitrary cut-off value of 20' (negative-probe mean 8.7 +/- 8.6), described as 'may be present'. The RNA-seq of six control frontal cortices named only MAGE-A12 and MAGE-A8 as expressed, not MAGE-A1. So the one deep-sequencing assay did not support MAGE-A1 in brain; the toxicity is attributed to MAGE-A12.

evidence.source_title: PMID 15684378, full text PMC548016 (Fig. 12B and Discussion)
evidence.finding: Human: UniProt curates MAGEA11 as expressed in testis, ovary, prostate, breast and adrenal tissue, citing Bai 2005, whose abstract states MAGE-11 is expressed in androgen-dependent tissues and acts as an androgen receptor coregulator. Adrenal is the non-reproductive site of concern; I did not see expression levels.
evidence.limitations: Bai 2005 (PMID 15684378, full text PMC548016) supports the UniProt annotation: 'MAGE-11 mRNA was also expressed in samples from testis, ovary, prostate, cancerous prostate, breast, and adrenal tissue, but was weak to undetectable in liver and lung' (Fig. 12B, adult human tissue RNA). The assay is weak, though: non-quantitative end-point RT-PCR at 35 cycles amplifying a 168-bp fragment, with no amplicon sequencing mentioned in the passages I read. The authors state the mRNA 'was not detectable by Northern blotting and required RT-PCR methods', even in testis, 'suggesting that MAGE-11 expression is low'. No protein was shown in normal adrenal, and a 168-bp amplicon in the highly homologous MAGE-A family leaves some paralog risk. Adrenal is the only clearly non-reproductive site; the signal is real but very low and unquantified, consistent with the atlas value near zero.

entries.summary: Morgan et al. 2013 (full text opened, PMC3581823) reported MAGE-A12 RNA in normal human brain by three methods (qRT-PCR with sequencing of products on commercial pooled total-brain and cerebellum RNA and on autopsy brain regions of patients 5 and 8; NanoString on commercial neurological RNAs; RNA-seq of frontal cortex from 6 controls) and rare neurons staining with a pan-MAGE-A antibody (6C1) that cannot identify MAGE-A12; they proposed MAGE-A12 in a subset of neurons as the cause of fatal neurotoxicity. Martin et al. 2020 (PMC7946352) dispute this: GTEx brain maximum 0.3 TPM, no MAGE-A12 RNA above negative-control probe by BaseScope ISH in 8 postmortem brains, the IHC criticized as uncontrolled, and an EPS8L2 peptide proposed instead, while conceding MAGE-A12 cannot be excluded. Classical RT-PCR surveys (De Plaen 1994; UniProt) describe MAGE genes as silent in healthy tissues except testis/placenta.
entries.decision_reason: Sequenced qRT-PCR products in normal brain (Morgan 2013); our donor-level data detect it in brain. A later in situ study found no signal and proposed another peptide, and concedes MAGE-A12 cannot be excluded.

evidence.source_title: Morgan RA et al. Cancer regression and neurological toxicity following anti-MAGE-A3 TCR gene therapy. J Immunother 2013;36(2):133-151 (PMC3581823) - qRT-PCR
evidence.assay: quantitative RT-PCR with gene-specific primers; PCR products sequenced
evidence.tissue: Commercial normal human total brain and cerebellum RNA (pools of 23 and 11 donors); also 11 autopsy brain regions each from trial patients 5 and 8
evidence.finding: MAGE-A9 and MAGE-A12 transcripts amplified from normal brain RNA and confirmed by sequencing; autopsy samples had >20 copies of MAGE-A12 but not MAGE-A3/A6 (fetch tool's reading of the tables: roughly 1-70 copies, e.g. parietal grey matter 70 in patient 8).
evidence.quote: These results demonstrated that the MAGE -A9 and MAGE-A12 transcripts were amplified from these normal human brain samples.
evidence.limitations: Very low copy numbers; pooled commercial RNA. Authors themselves note for the autopsy samples 'the potential for contamination of normal brain tissue from these patients' tumors'. Copy-number values were relayed by the fetch tool from tables, not quoted.

evidence.source_title: Morgan RA et al. 2013 (PMC3581823) - NanoString
evidence.tissue: Commercial RNA from normal human total brain, cerebellum, occipital cortex (brain stem also listed)
evidence.finding: Counts just above an arbitrary cutoff of 20 (negative-probe mean 8.7 +/- 8.6); fetch tool read MAGE-A12 counts as 33, 15, 25, 19.
evidence.quote: Based on an arbitrary cut-off value of 20, these results suggest that MAGE-A1 and MAGE-A12 RNA may be present in commercial samples
evidence.limitations: Signal close to background; authors call the cutoff arbitrary. Probe cross-hybridization among MAGE-A2/A3/A6/A12 not addressed in the text I saw.

evidence.source_title: Morgan RA et al. 2013 (PMC3581823) - RNA-seq
evidence.assay: deep RNA sequencing (>200 million mapped reads per sample)
evidence.tissue: Post-mortem dorsolateral prefrontal cortex from 6 psychiatrically normal controls
evidence.finding: MAGE-A12 and MAGE-A8 reads present at low level (fetch tool: 4-22 MAGE-A12 reads per donor); zero reads for MAGE-A3, A6, A9.
evidence.quote: Data from this large RNAseq database indicated that the MAGE-A12 and MAGE-A8 genes were expressed in samples from human frontal cortex
evidence.limitations: A handful of reads in >200M; multi-mapping among MAGE-A paralogs and the overlapping same-strand CSAG4 locus is not discussed in the text I saw.

evidence.source_title: Morgan RA et al. 2013 (PMC3581823) - immunohistochemistry
evidence.tissue: Biopsy/autopsy brain of patients 5 and 8, plus control patients' brains (figure legend: three control patients)
evidence.finding: Rare positive neuronal cell bodies and processes in patients and controls; no percentage given.
evidence.quote: we verified by western blot analysis that it recognizes MAGE-A1, A2, A3, A4, A6, A9, A10, and A12 (not shown)
evidence.limitations: Antibody recognizes at least eight MAGE-A proteins; cannot attribute staining to MAGE-A12. Authors call for 'large-scale immunohistochemical studies with gene-specific antibodies'.

evidence.source_title: Morgan RA et al. 2013 (PMC3581823) - authors' interpretation
evidence.finding: Authors state this is the first report of MAGE-A12 in human brain, that they have no evidence MAGE-A3 is expressed in brain, and that TCR recognition of MAGE-A12 in a subset of neurons best explains the toxicity.
evidence.quote: This previously unrecognized expression of MAGE-A12 in human brain was possibly the initiating event
evidence.limitations: Hedged by the authors ('possibly'). The TCR also recognized MAGE-A9 and (per Martin et al.) an EPS8L2 peptide.

evidence.source_title: Martin AD et al. Re-examination of MAGE-A3 as a T-cell Therapeutic Target. J Immunother 2021;44(3):95-105 (PMC7946352)
evidence.assay: BaseScope RNA in situ hybridization (ACD) on FFPE sections; GTEx/HPA/FANTOM5 database analysis
evidence.tissue: Brain sections from 8 postmortem donors (5 normal, 3 cancer patients), ~3.2 million cells scanned; GTEx 13 brain regions
evidence.finding: No MAGE-A12 ISH signal above negative-control probe; GTEx brain maximum 0.3 TPM (basal ganglia). Authors criticize Morgan's IHC as lacking controls and propose the EPS8L2 339-347 peptide (EPS8L2 highly expressed in brain) as likely cause.
evidence.quote: No expression of MAGE-A12 was observed above the detection limit determined by the negative-control probe.
evidence.limitations: Authors (employees of a TCR-therapy company) concede: 'it remains possible that despite a thorough search we missed rare MAGE-A12-expressing cells' and RNA instability in FFPE; EPS8L2 is called 'a likely but still unproven source'.

entries.toxicity_reports: Morgan et al. 2013: of nine patients given autologous T cells transduced with an affinity-enhanced HLA-A*0201-restricted anti-MAGE-A3 TCR (also recognizing MAGE-A9 and MAGE-A12 epitopes), three developed mental status changes and two died in coma with necrotizing leukoencephalopathy and CD3+/CD8+ T-cell infiltrates (these outcome details were read from the search-result summary of the abstract plus the opened full text). Authors attribute it to MAGE-A12 in brain ('We propose that the best explanation for the neurologic toxicity observed in three of the nine patients' is recognition of MAGE-A12 in a subset of neurons); Martin et al. 2021 argue an off-target EPS8L2 peptide is the more likely cause. Cause remains unresolved.

evidence.finding: MRGPRX1 in 79% of picked human sensory neurons.

evidence.source_title: PMID 31536477 (PMC6824308), Results section 'Human DRG neurons express TGR5 and MrgprX1', Figures 11-12; also PMID 11850634 (Nat Neurosci 2002;5:201)
evidence.tissue: dorsal root ganglion / trigeminal ganglion (peripheral sensory neurons); small-diameter nociceptor / pruriceptor neurons (TRPV1+)
evidence.finding: Human: qPCR of whole thoracolumbar DRG from 4 donors showed abundant MRGPRX1, and single-cell RT-PCR detected it in about 79% of 85 picked human DRG neurons (about 99% of those co-expressing TRPV1). Cultured human DRG neurons gave calcium responses to the MRGPRX1 agonists BAM8-22 (about 34% of neurons) and chloroquine (about 10%); MRGPRX1 was not detected in human colon biopsies.
evidence.limitations: Opened PMC6824308 (Castro et al., JCI Insight 2019, PMID 31536477). The text matches the claim: MrgprX1 absent in colonic biopsies from 15 healthy subjects; qPCR of T9-L1 whole thoracolumbar DRG from 4 human donors showed TGR5 with greater abundance of MrgprX1; single-cell RT-PCR of 85 human DRG neurons, 79% MrgprX1-positive, 99% of those co-expressing TRPV1; calcium imaging responses to BAM8-22 (34%) and chloroquine (10%). Caveats: the paper is mainly a mouse study with human DRG as one results section; the 85 picked neurons were predominantly small-diameter, so 79% is not a whole-ganglion prevalence; donor age and primer specificity against MRGPRX2-4 were not checked in the methods (tissue is organ-donor DRG, assumed adult). Independent support from Lembo et al. 2002 (PMID 11850634), which localised the family to human small sensory neurons.

evidence.source_title: https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q96LB2 ; underlying primary PMID 11850634 (Lembo et al., Nat Neurosci 2002)
evidence.tissue: dorsal root ganglion / trigeminal ganglion; small-diameter sensory neurons
evidence.finding: Human: UniProt curates MRGPRX1 as a GPCR of small-diameter dorsal root and trigeminal ganglion sensory neurons mediating itch and pain (activated by enkephalin-derived peptides such as BAM8-22 and by chloroquine; Gq coupling sensitises TRPV1). This is a second, curated source for the same function as the primary paper above, not an additional tissue.
evidence.limitations: Fetched UniProt Q96LB2. Function field: GPCR 'specifically expressed in sensory neurons of dorsal root ganglion', involved in itch perception and pain transmission, activated by BAM22/BAM8-22 and chloroquine, Gq coupling sensitises TRPV1. Tissue-specificity field: 'Specifically expressed in small-diameter sensory neurons of dorsal root ganglion and trigeminal sensory neurons' (experimental evidence, PMID 11850634). The claim is accurate as stated. As it says itself, this is a curated restatement of the same function, not an independent tissue; some functional detail in the entry (nasal sneezing) is by similarity to mouse.

evidence.source_title: PMID 23068092 (BBRC 2012, title only); original claim PMID 10191093
evidence.finding: Human NEU2 (cytosolic sialidase) is curated in UniProt (Q9Y3R4) as expressed in skeletal muscle, fetal liver and the NT2-D1 embryonal carcinoma line, based on the original cloning papers (PMID 10191093, PMID 10561456). The enzyme hydrolyses gangliosides and sialylated oligosaccharides.
evidence.limitations: The cloning paper exists and says it: PMID 10191093 abstract, 'Northern blot analysis revealed expression of the NEU2 transcript only in skeletal muscle'. That is a single 1999 Northern blot. The second cited paper (PMID 10561456) is about expression in COS7 cells and E. coli; its abstract has no tissue data, and the 'fetal liver / NT2-D1' wording was not found in either abstract nor in the part of the UniProt entry retrieved. A later paper is titled 'Human cytosolic sialidase NEU2 - low general tissue expression but involvement in PC-3 prostate cancer cell survival' (PMID 23068092, BBRC 2012; title only, not opened), which by its title agrees with the atlases and not with the Northern blot. The skeletal muscle claim is therefore real but old and disputed. A 2022 mouse Neu2 knockout paper (PMID 35217678, title only) reports impaired muscle function, which is mouse-only.

entries.summary: No opened primary paper measured NKX2-6 RNA or protein in normal adult human tissue by a gene-specific assay. The human genetics papers (truncus arteriosus, VSD, atrial fibrillation) cite only mouse embryonic expression in pharyngeal endoderm and outflow-tract/sinus venosus myocardium and did no expression assays. HPA nonetheless classifies RNA as group enriched in heart muscle and salivary gland and in cardiomyocytes, with no IHC profile, so adult cardiac expression is suggested only by sequencing data that cannot be confirmed against NKX2-5 cross-mapping from the literature.
entries.decision_reason: Reports conflict, cannot separate the gene from paralogs, or come from cultured, diseased or fetal samples.

evidence.tissue: blood / immune system; macrophages (primary human and THP-1)
evidence.finding: In human macrophages NLRP11 binds ASC and NLRP3 and is required for NLRP3 inflammasome assembly; NLRP11 deletion blocks NLRP3 activation and siRNA knockdown in primary human macrophages reduces IL-1beta release (Nat Immunol 2022). The gene is absent in mice.
evidence.limitations: Abstract and PMC full text opened. Gangopadhyay et al., Nat Immunol 2022: NLRP11 is 'an essential component of the NLRP3 inflammasome in human macrophages', interacts with NLRP3 and ASC, and its deletion prevents NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, caspase-1 activation, pyroptosis and cytokine release; re-expression rescues. The full text states IL-1beta release (not IL-6) was reduced in primary human macrophages with siRNA-silenced NLRP11. The abstract states NLRP11 is not expressed in mice. Assays are gene-specific (siRNA, CRISPR knockout, rescue). Caveat: the primary cells are in vitro cultured, LPS-primed macrophages, so this is functional evidence in an induced state, not an in situ tissue expression measurement.

The liver part is weak: PMID 27827363 is a TSC22D4 diabetes paper that measured human OBP2A (LCN13) with a single TaqMan assay (Hs01062934_g1) in patient liver biopsies; specificity against OBP2B was not shown and the tissue is not from healthy donors. evidence.source_title: https://www.proteinatlas.org/ENSG00000256574-OR13A1 (JSON: https://www.proteinatlas.org/ENSG00000256574.json)
evidence.finding: Human: the HPA gene record lists OR13A1 under tissue cell type enrichment as 'Spleen - B-cells', with a lymphoma cell-line cluster annotated 'humoral immune response', which suggests the 14.87 TPM blood signal in the CSV is B-lineage transcription. HPA has transcript-level evidence only (no protein data), and its single-cell data show only about 1.6-2.3 nCPM in kidney papillary tip epithelium and cerebellar Purkinje nuclei.
evidence.limitations: The HPA record (ENSG00000256574) exists and does say what was quoted: tissue cell type enrichment 'Spleen - B-cells (Spleen)', cell line cluster 'Cluster 46: Lymphoma - Humoral immune response', transcript-level evidence only, single-cell 1.6 nCPM in papillary tip epithelial cells and 2.3 nCPM in cerebellar Purkinje nuclei. But the inference drawn from it is contradicted by the same record. HPA's sorted blood cell data, which include naive and memory B cells, list OR13A1 as 'Not detected in immune cells' with blood lineage 'Not detected', so the record gives no direct support for the blood signal being B-lineage transcription. The 'Spleen - B-cells' label is not a measurement in B cells: it is a correlation of bulk spleen RNA with B-cell marker genes across samples. The lymphoma signal is a tumor cell line at 4.1 nTPM, which is not normal tissue. Bulk tissue specificity is 'Low tissue specificity', tissue cluster 'Non-specific - Transcription', protein 'Not detected'. All of this is short-read RNA quantification of an olfactory receptor gene with no gene-specific assay (no qRT-PCR, in situ or antibody), so read mis-assignment or an overlapping transcript cannot be excluded. No literature on ectopic OR13A1 expression was checked by the original researcher, and I did not run a literature search either. What survives is a weak, indirect atlas hint of low-level lymphoid RNA, with no protein and no function.

evidence.source_title: PMID 36503361 (Weidinger et al. 2022, Mol Med; PMC9743598)
evidence.finding: Human: functional OR1A2 was reported at mRNA and protein level (RT-PCR, immunostaining, Western blot, Ca2+ imaging) in primary alveolar macrophages from bronchoalveolar lavage, where its activation modulated cytokine release and phagocytosis. The cells came from 50 patients with pulmonary disease, not healthy donors.
evidence.limitations: Source exists and matches the claim (full text opened). All BAL donors were pulmonary-disease patients (COPD, ILD, pneumonia, lung cancer, asthma); no healthy controls for OR1A2. RT-PCR used OR1A2 primers with a no-RT control and OR1A1 was RT-PCR negative, which partly supports gene specificity, but no amplicon sequencing, no knockdown or antagonist; antibodies validated only by heterologous overexpression, and citronellal also activates OR1A1 so function is not gene-specific. But evidence is whole-transcriptome only (hybridisation/sequence-based, not validated per gene), from surface swabs of mixed cell composition (not confirmed taste cells), 166 ORs detected suggests low-level/background signal, and OR1A1 (close paralog) is listed alongside, so cross-mapping is not excluded. No protein or functional data. Only the abstract was verified by me.

This is a cultured cell model (donor/cell-line origin not given in abstract), odorant-induced, RNA only, no protein, no sequencing or paralog control stated (OR2B2/OR2B6 are close family members), and the receptor-ligand link is computational only. Nasal/olfactory epithelium is also the expected canonical site for an olfactory receptor, so it adds little as an off-target safety finding beyond the class-level gap. Abstract only; no open full text found.

evidence.source_title: McRae JF et al. Chem Senses 2012;37(7):585-93, PMID 22714804, PMCID PMC3408771, doi:10.1093/chemse/bjs049 (abstract opened; full text not read). UniProt O76001 is the curated summary of it.
evidence.tissue: olfactory epithelium; olfactory sensory neuron (inferred from odorant-receptor function; cell type not stated in the record)
evidence.finding: Human: UniProt (O76001) curates OR2J3 as a functional odorant receptor for cis-3-hexen-1-ol, citing PubMed 22714804. Human variants Ala-113 and Gln-226 reduce the ability to smell the compound and the combined haplotype abolishes the receptor response, a benign specific anosmia rather than a disease.
evidence.limitations: The source exists and says what is claimed. UniProt O76001 (reviewed) curates OR2J3 as the odorant receptor for cis-3-hexen-1-ol and records that variants Ala-113 and Gln-226 reduce the ability to smell it, with the combined haplotype abolishing the response, all citing PMID 22714804. I opened the PubMed abstract (McRae et al., Chem Senses 2012;37:585-93): it is human, about OR2J3 specifically (coding regions of all 25 receptors in the chr6 cluster sequenced in 52 people; 13 receptors tested in vitro; all 5 OR2J3 haplotypes tested), and the T113A+R226Q haplotype explains 26.4% of variation in detection threshold. Weakened rather than confirmed for three reasons. (1) Neither source measures OR2J3 RNA or protein in olfactory epithelium or any tissue; the tissue and cell type are inferred from odorant-receptor function, as the finding itself admits, and the UniProt record has no tissue-specificity annotation. (2) The evidence is a genotype-to-detection-threshold association plus a heterologous cell assay, not a loss-of-function disease; the phenotype is a benign partial specific anosmia, and two other receptors in the region also respond to the compound, so OR2J3 is not the sole receptor. (3) It is not a vital-tissue function. The finding does stand as gene-specific human evidence that OR2J3 is a working olfactory receptor, in a tissue the screen does not sample.

evidence.source_title: PMID 38069004 (Hirata et al., Int J Mol Sci 2023; PMC10706743)
evidence.finding: Human: OR4E2 circulating RNA was measurable by RT-qPCR and differed between mild gestational hypothyroidism and healthy pregnancy, correlating negatively with TSH and normalising after levothyroxine. This suggests hormone-responsive expression in a blood-derived sample, in pregnant women only.
evidence.limitations: The source exists and the claim is accurately hedged, but it is weak as normal-tissue evidence. Full text (PMC10706743): whole-blood RNA in PAXgene tubes from pregnant women only, 24 subjects (11 healthy-thyroid, 7 untreated mild gestational hypothyroidism, 6 levothyroxine-treated). RT-qPCR relative expression of OR4E2 differed between groups (p<0.05) and correlated negatively with TSH (r=-0.44); OR4E2 was not detectable in one sample. This is a cross-sectional association, not demonstrated hormone induction: the treated group is different women, not the same women before and after. No cell of origin, no amplicon sequencing or protein, and OR4E2 is a single-exon gene so genomic DNA carry-over is a concern. It adds nothing beyond the 0.72 TPM blood value the catalog already has.

evidence.source_title: PMID 40806011 (PMC12348634) for the human biopsy data; the underlying receptor claim is the mouse Olfr734 study by Li et al., Cell Metab 2019 (PMID 31230984, cited from memory, not opened here)
evidence.finding: Mouse and human: OR4M1 (mouse Olfr734) is described as the hepatic receptor for the fasting hormone asprosin, mediating its glucogenic effect; liver knockdown of Olfr734 in diet-induced obese mice increased hepatic lipid content, and OR4M1 was reported as measurable and higher in human liver biopsies from men with type 2 diabetes. The abstract does not say whether the human measurement was RNA or protein.
evidence.limitations: The source exists and says roughly this, but the human evidence is weaker than normal-tissue expression. Full text (PMC12348634): the functional data are mouse Olfr734 liver knockdown, plus OR4M1 siRNA in the immortalised human hepatocyte line THLE-2. The human measurement is mRNA (the discussion says 'mRNA levels of OR4M1'), in liver biopsies from patients with obesity with or without type 2 diabetes; there is no normal-liver group, so it is disease tissue. It is qPCR of a single-exon gene with a near-identical paralog (OR4M2), with no amplicon sequencing or protein data that I found. The 2020 review (PMID 32198197) states asprosin acts through OR4M1 in liver, but this rests on the mouse Olfr734 work, not a human assay. HPA/GTEx liver RNA near zero is not contradicted by any gene-specific human normal-tissue assay.

evidence.source_title: PMID 23241557 (Zhao et al., J Alzheimers Dis 2013; PMC3968322)
evidence.tissue: blood and brain; peripheral blood mononuclear cells; neurons
evidence.finding: Human: OR4M1 and OR11H1 were detected in PBMC and down-regulated after traumatic brain injury; the abstract states these receptors are ectopically expressed in multiple brain regions (species and method not given) and that OR4M1 activation attenuated abnormal tau phosphorylation via JNK signalling (Zhao et al. 2013).
evidence.limitations: The source exists and the expression part is human and normal: full text (PMC3968322) shows OR4M1 mRNA in PBMC of healthy controls (microarray, then SYBR qPCR) and by RT-PCR in postmortem temporal, entorhinal and occipital cortex and hippocampus from 4 neurologically normal cases, so the species and method the claim left open are human RT-PCR. Weaker than claimed in two ways. (1) The tau/JNK result is not endogenous function: human OR4M1 was overexpressed by lentivirus in embryonic mouse cortico-hippocampal neurons and stimulated with acetophenone. (2) Expression rests on SYBR qPCR for a single-exon gene with a close paralog (OR4M2); I found no mention of DNase treatment, no-RT controls or amplicon sequencing, so genomic DNA carry-over and paralog cross-amplification are not excluded. Single lab, small cohorts, RNA only, no protein or cell-type localisation. Consistent with the catalog's very low blood signal rather than a missed function.

evidence.source_title: PMID 17964544 and PMID 37451613 (abstracts only; full texts not opened)
evidence.finding: Human: a common nonsense SNP in OR4X1 (Tyr273Ter) was associated with FEV1/FVC in 2,970 Japanese subjects, and predicted loss-of-function variants in OR4X1 were among 10 genes associated with blood pressure in UK Biobank exomes (n = 454,709). Neither study measured expression; the null allele is common, so the gene is not vital.
evidence.limitations: Both abstracts exist and say what is claimed: rs10838851 (Tyr273Ter) was associated with FEV1/FVC in 2,970 Japanese subjects (P=0.008, among 7 OR nonsense SNPs tested; about 1 percentage point between genotypes), and OR4X1 is one of 10 genes with single predicted loss-of-function variants associated with blood pressure in UK Biobank exomes (n=454,709). Neither measured expression in any tissue, so there is no evidence of normal adult tissue expression or function. The stop allele is the major haplotype in the Japanese cohort (frequency about 0.67), so loss is tolerated. The lung association is a modest candidate-SNP result that I did not find replicated, and the blood-pressure paper notes its genes map near known GWAS loci, so a common stop variant may simply tag a nearby causal signal. The variant is gene-specific, but the finding does not locate OR4X1 in lung or vessels.

evidence.source_title: PMID 37533582 (Murayama et al., JID Innov 2023; PMC10392076)
evidence.tissue: skin (eccrine sweat gland); eccrine sweat gland cells
evidence.finding: Human: OR51A7 (with OR51E2) expression in eccrine sweat glands was confirmed by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry; the ligand beta-ionone activates G-proteins through OR51A7 and topical beta-ionone altered sweating in volunteers (Murayama et al. 2023).
evidence.limitations: Full text (PMC10392076) supports the claim as stated. OR51A7 was higher in hidrotic than anhidrotic laser-microdissected sweat glands from anhidrosis (AIGA) patients by RNA-seq. In situ hybridisation with an OR51A7 antisense oligo probe (sense-probe negative control) detected mRNA in acinar and myoepithelial cells of eccrine glands in AIGA sweating areas and in a healthy donor. IHC detected protein in glands of AIGA patients and a healthy donor. Beta-ionone activated G-proteins through OR51A7 in transfected HEK293T cells (minimum dose 100 uM), and topical beta-ionone changed sweating in volunteers in a sex-dependent way. Caveats that limit weight: normal-tissue evidence is a single healthy donor; the IHC antibody is a commercial Invitrogen antibody with no knockout or peptide-block validation (only a no-primary control, data not shown); the ISH probe is one 42-mer with no test against OR51 paralogs; the functional link is overexpression plus a topical test that cannot attribute the effect to OR51A7 rather than OR51E2. Single lab, not replicated.

evidence.source_title: PMID 15647465 (abstract only)
evidence.finding: Human: OR52D1 was shown by calcium imaging against 100 odorants to be a functional odorant receptor with a narrow ligand repertoire. This supports a physiological role as an odorant receptor, presumably in olfactory sensory neurons, but the abstract reports no tissue expression data.
evidence.limitations: The source exists and its abstract says exactly what is claimed: human OR52D1 is a functional odorant receptor with a narrow repertoire in a calcium-imaging screen of 100 odorants (Sanz et al. 2005). The assay is gene-specific, but it is a receptor-function screen with no tissue data: nothing in the abstract shows OR52D1 expression in human olfactory epithelium or any other normal adult tissue. Expression in olfactory sensory neurons is an inference from the gene class. The general point stands that olfactory epithelium is unmeasured by the screen, but this paper is not direct evidence of normal-tissue expression. I did not look for a human olfactory mucosa RNA-seq dataset that would test it directly.

evidence.source_title: PMID 23778302 / PMC3805820 (full text)
evidence.finding: Human: RNA-seq of peripheral blood from six women with anorexia nervosa found OR52J3 among olfactory receptor genes up-regulated more than two-fold after weight restoration, suggesting state-dependent expression in blood. Patient samples only, no healthy control baseline in the abstract.
evidence.limitations: The source exists (Kim et al. 2013, PMC3805820) and says OR52J3 was up-regulated more than two-fold in whole blood after weight restoration in six women with anorexia nervosa. There are no healthy controls, the authors call the results preliminary, and the full text notes that transcripts with zero read counts at one time point produced large fold-changes, which points to very low absolute counts. There was no qRT-PCR or other orthogonal validation. Three of the four olfactory receptors named (OR51L1, OR51A4, OR51A2) and OR52J3 all sit in the chromosome 11p15 cluster beside the beta-globin locus, so read-through or mis-mapped reads from the very abundant globin transcripts in whole blood are a plausible artifact; that explanation is my inference, not something the paper tests. This is not evidence of physiological induced expression in normal blood cells.

evidence.source_title: PMID 23656994 (abstract only; full text not checked)
evidence.tissue: brain (frontal cortex area 8); not stated in abstract
evidence.finding: Human: OR52L1 is listed among olfactory receptors downregulated in frontal cortex area 8 of Parkinson disease patients versus controls in a transcriptomics study, which implies detectable expression in control adult human cortex. Only the abstract was read; the assay details and control expression level were not confirmed.
evidence.limitations: The source exists and its abstract does list OR52L1 among olfactory receptors downregulated in frontal cortex area 8 in Parkinson disease (Garcia-Esparcia et al. 2013). But expression in normal cortex is only inferred from a disease-versus-control comparison; the abstract gives no control expression level for OR52L1. The cell-level evidence in the abstract (neuronal expression) concerns the downstream machinery (ADCY3, Golf, RTP1/2, REEP1, UGT1A6), not OR52L1. The abstract says only 'a transcriptomics approach'; I did not open the full text, so the platform and whether OR52L1 itself was validated by a gene-specific assay are unverified. Olfactory receptor paralogs are highly similar, so specificity cannot be assumed. The catalog's bulk brain RNA is near zero, so this is at most a hint of low-level transcript.

evidence.source_title: PMID 34070492 / PMC8198027 (full text, section 2.5)
evidence.finding: Human: family-based whole-exome sequencing reported a missense variant in OR52L1 in affected individuals with retinitis pigmentosa, proposed as a candidate alongside OR56A5 and CTSD. This is a genetic association in a small family study with no expression or functional data in the abstract.
evidence.limitations: The source exists (Lin et al. 2021, PMC8198027) and reports an OR52L1 missense variant shared by all five affected members of one retinitis pigmentosa family. The full text states that SIFT, PolyPhen2, LRT and MetaSVM predicted the OR52L1 and OR56A5 variants to be benign and tolerated. So this is not a loss-of-function finding, and the paper's own annotation argues against causality. There is no retinal expression or functional data; the 'detecting visible light' link comes from an in silico protein-interaction network. A shared variant in a single family, with no segregation statistics or replication, is not evidence of a retinal function.

evidence.quote: Systemic Or5v1/Olfr110 deficiency or liver-specific Or5v1/Olfr110 deficiency impaired glucose homeostasis, even after stimulation with 12(S)-HEPE.
evidence.limitations: Abstract only; mouse, not human; the abstract gives no human tissue expression data (human data mentioned are serum activity assays).

evidence.source_title: PMID 41570820, DOI 10.1016/j.cell.2025.12.016; UniProt A2RT31 (mouse, experimental) and Q9UGF6 (human, by similarity only)
evidence.finding: Mouse only: Or5v1/Olfr110 is an oxylipin (12(S)-HEPE) receptor that drives hepatic fatty acid oxidation via PKA/ATF2/CPT1A; whole-body knockout mice develop impaired glucose control, weight gain, fatty liver and insulin resistance, and liver-specific deletion also impairs glucose control (Ge et al., Cell 2026). UniProt transfers this function to human OR5V1 (Q9UGF6) by similarity only; no human liver expression or protein data was found.
evidence.limitations: The source exists and says what the claim reports, but the evidence is mouse-only. PubMed abstract of PMID 41570820 (Ge et al., Cell 2026;189:1481-1498, DOI 10.1016/j.cell.2025.12.016) states that systemic or liver-specific Or5v1/Olfr110 deficiency impaired glucose homeostasis and that 12(S)-HEPE acts through Gs-PKA-pATF2-Cpt1a to promote fatty acid oxidation in liver. UniProt A2RT31 (mouse) carries the function and disruption phenotype with experimental evidence from that paper; UniProt Q9UGF6 (human OR5V1) carries the same function text only 'By similarity' (ECO:0000250 from A2RT31), with no tissue-specificity or disease annotation. The knockout is gene-specific for the mouse ortholog, not a paralog. The only human data in the abstract is that serum from obese patients gave lower Or5v1/Olfr110-Gs activation, which measures ligand activity, not OR5V1 expression in human liver. I read the abstract and UniProt entries, not the full paper, so whether it contains human liver expression data is unchecked.

entries.summary: Otogelin is described as an inner-ear-specific glycoprotein of the tectorial membrane, otoconial membranes and cupulae; in mouse it is still produced by vestibular supporting cells in adults. In the original mouse study, immunoblots of eye, brain, kidney, spleen, liver, intestine and lung were negative. No primary report of OTOG in normal adult human vital tissue was found; HPA lists RNA as pituitary enhanced with no IHC profile, and human loss of function causes non-syndromic deafness (DFNB18B).
entries.decision_reason: Human loss of function causes deafness (DFNB18B); the mouse ortholog is produced in the adult inner ear and nowhere else tested.

evidence.tissue: adipose tissue (brown fat; white fat in obesity); adipocytes
evidence.finding: Mouse Otop1 is expressed in brown adipose tissue and is induced in white adipose tissue by high-fat diet and by TNF; UniProt also lists mouse thymus, heart, kidney, skin, dorsal root ganglion, adrenal, lactating mammary gland and stimulated mast cells.
evidence.limitations: PMID 24379350 exists and its abstract supports induction in obese mouse white fat and by TNF in cultured adipocytes, with a metabolic phenotype in Otop1 mutant mice on high-fat diet. It is mouse only and describes an obesity (disease-state) response. The brown-fat and wider mouse tissue list is not in the abstract and rests on UniProt Q80VM9, which I did not open. No human adipose evidence.

evidence.tissue: inner ear (vestibular utricle and saccule); extrastriolar supporting cells
evidence.finding: Mouse Otop1 is expressed in vestibular supporting cells and is required for otoconia formation; mutant and knockout mice have otoconial agenesis and vestibular dysfunction. UniProt extends the function to human by similarity only.
evidence.limitations: Mouse only, as the claim itself says. PMID 12651873 maps the tilted/mergulhador mutations to Otop1 and reports expression in the macula of the developing otocyst, so part of the evidence is developmental. PMID 20554841 shows OTOP1 at the apex of supporting cells using knockout mice and utricular organ culture. UniProt extends this to human by similarity; no human tissue or human disease evidence is cited.

evidence.source_title: PMID 31543453 (mouse Otop1 knockout, type III taste cells); PMID 37798269 for human channel activity in HEK-293
evidence.tissue: tongue (taste buds); type III acid-sensing (PKD2L1+) taste receptor cells
evidence.finding: OTOP1 is the proton channel that acts as the sour taste receptor; human OTOP1 conducts proton currents and senses ammonium chloride (UniProt Q7RTM1, PMID 29371428, 37798269). Protein localisation in sour taste cells and the loss of acid responses in knockouts are mouse data (PMID 31543453, 31543264).
evidence.limitations: Sources exist and say what is claimed, but no cited source shows OTOP1 in human taste tissue. PMID 29371428 identifies murine OTOP1 in acid-detecting taste cells; PMID 37798269 shows human OTOP1 carries NH4Cl currents only when expressed in HEK-293 cells; PMID 31543453 and 31543264 are mouse knockouts. UniProt Q7RTM1 marks the sour-receptor role 'by similarity'. The assays are gene-specific (knockout, heterologous expression) and the function is very likely conserved, but the in-tissue evidence is mouse-only.

evidence.tissue: kidney; heart; intestine; tubular epithelial cells; macrophages
evidence.finding: OTUD6A is reported to rise in kidney tissue of nephropathy patients and angiotensin II-treated mice, located mainly in tubular epithelial cells; knockout mice are protected from angiotensin II kidney injury, cardiac hypertrophy and colitis. Knockouts are healthy at baseline, so the gene acts in disease-induced states rather than normal physiology.
evidence.limitations: Sources exist and match the claim. The human data are diseased tissue: nephropathy kidney (PMID 38105755) and hypertrophic heart (PMID 38342418). The rest is angiotensin II, aortic constriction and colitis models in mice, where knockouts are protected rather than harmed. No evidence of expression or function in healthy adult human tissue; detection is antibody-based and all three organ papers come from one Wenzhou group.

evidence.tissue: small intestine and colon; epithelial cells (luminal membrane)
evidence.finding: P2Y4-null mice lose UTP/ATP-induced chloride secretion in jejunal epithelium, the first demonstrated physiological role of the receptor; mice are otherwise grossly normal. Mouse data; receptor mRNA was detected in mouse liver, stomach and intestine.
evidence.limitations: PMID 12644577 says exactly this: P2Y4-null mice lose UTP/ATP-induced jejunal chloride secretion and are otherwise grossly normal, with mRNA loss checked in liver, stomach and intestine. PMID 15718265 adds colonic K+ secretion shared with P2Y2. It is mouse only, and the abstract notes the human receptor differs pharmacologically (UTP only). No human gut expression evidence is cited.

evidence.finding: Adult P2Y4-null mice have microcardia; the receptor is expressed in cardiac endothelial cells, not cardiomyocytes, and the authors also detected P2Y4 in human cardiac microvessels. Loss of the receptor alters the response to cardiac ischemia in mice.
evidence.limitations: PMID 22437266 supports microcardia in adult P2Y4-null mice and expression in cardiac endothelial cells, not cardiomyocytes. The phenotype arises from reduced post-natal heart growth, so it is developmental, and PMID 25595790 shows the knockout is protected in infarction. The human part is one sentence in the abstract ('We also detected P2Y4 expression in human cardiac microvessels') with no method or tissue status given there.

evidence.source_title: PMID 11690642; PMID 8617367 for the pancreas-restricted counter-evidence
evidence.tissue: skin; skeletal muscle; pancreas; brain; keratinocytes; muscle fibre sarcolemma
evidence.finding: Human keratinocytes express P2Y4 mRNA by RT-PCR with functional evidence in HaCaT cells; immunolabelling placed P2Y4 on the sarcolemma of human vastus lateralis fibres; a quantitative RT-PCR survey reported widespread, subtype-selective P2Y4 mRNA across human peripheral tissues and brain regions. UniProt lists pancreas, where the gene was cloned.
evidence.limitations: All four sources exist. PMID 12603858: RT-PCR in cultured keratinocytes and HaCaT, with the functional P2Y4 signature seen only in a subpopulation of HaCaT cells, not in normal keratinocytes. PMID 22052557: antibody labelling of vastus lateralis sarcolemma, no specificity control mentioned in the abstract. PMID 11690642: qRT-PCR survey reporting widespread expression. PMID 8617367 contradicts the breadth, reporting expression exclusively in pancreas, and states the gene is intronless, so RT-PCR signal can come from genomic DNA unless controlled. Cultured cells and antibodies, not normal tissue in situ.

evidence.finding: Human dental pulp tissue and odontoblast-like cells express PANX3 mRNA and protein (RT-PCR and immunofluorescence), where it mediates ATP release on cold stimulus.
evidence.limitations: PMID 26263540 abstract states Panx3 mRNA and protein were found in human dental pulp tissue and cultured odontoblast-like cells by RT-PCR and immunofluorescence, and that Panx3 overexpression or shRNA changes cold-evoked ATP release. Caveats: the functional work is in cultured cells, donor age is not given in the abstract (pulp usually comes from extracted teeth of young adults), and it is a single unreplicated study.

evidence.source_title: PMID 22947051 (human skin immunostaining); PMID 36813158 (mouse knockout)
evidence.finding: Panx3 is expressed in mammalian epidermis and regulated during keratinocyte differentiation; global Panx3-knockout mice have thinner dermis and hypodermis, reduced epidermal barrier function and more dermatitis with age, and show delayed wound healing. TNF-alpha induces PANX3 in human HaCaT keratinocytes.
evidence.limitations: The sources say what is claimed. PMID 36813158: knockout mice have reduced dermal and hypodermal area, reduced barrier function and more dermatitis with age. PMID 30389492: delayed wound healing in knockouts and TNF-alpha induction in HaCaT. Human normal-skin evidence comes from PMID 22947051, which reports PANX3 protein in human epidermis, hair follicles, sebaceous and eccrine glands and blood vessels. Caveats: the human evidence is antibody staining (diffuse intracellular, with a ~70 kDa species whose identity needed separate confirmation), and the functional data are mouse.

evidence.tissue: bone and cartilage; osteoblasts, osteoprogenitors, chondrocytes
evidence.finding: Panx3 is an ER calcium channel and hemichannel that promotes osteoblast and chondrocyte differentiation; mouse knockouts have altered long-bone growth and altered susceptibility to osteoarthritis and disc degeneration. Mostly mouse data; UniProt assigns the function to human by similarity, and human noncoding PANX3 variants associate with chronic back pain.
evidence.limitations: Sources exist, but the evidence is mouse and largely developmental. PMID 21690309 uses C2C12 and primary calvarial cells and metatarsal explants. PMID 26138248 states global Panx3 deletion gives no overt phenotype and no obvious effect on early skeletal development; PMID 26749194 and 33426805 report only shorter long bones, plus opposite effects on injury-induced versus ageing osteoarthritis. Human evidence is immunostaining in osteoarthritic lesions (disease tissue) and a noncoding-variant association with back pain (PMID 36448979). UniProt Q96QZ0 assigns the function by similarity.

evidence.tissue: skeletal muscle; muscle fibres and myoblasts
evidence.finding: Immunoblotting detected PANX3 species in adult human skeletal muscle tissue and in primary human myoblasts, where it regulates proliferation and differentiation. Antibody-based; the paper notes several immunoreactive species.
evidence.limitations: PMID 25239622 exists and says Panx3 is present in adult human skeletal muscle and primary myoblasts. The evidence is immunoblot with several immunoreactive species, including a ~70 kDa band the authors describe only as 'likely' modified Panx3; the functional work is in cultured myoblasts. No RNA or in situ confirmation in muscle tissue is cited, so the tissue claim rests on antibody specificity. In the cochlea paper (PMID 19009624) Panx3 labelling was only in cochlear bone, in mouse and rat.

evidence.finding: Group 1 and 2 POTEs including POTEC are testis-specific; Table 1 marks POTEC (POTE18, group 2) as testis-specific.
evidence.quote: We conclude that Groups 1 & 2 POTE s ( A , B , B2 , C , D ) have normal tissue expression consistent with CTAs, while Group 3 POTEs ... do not
evidence.limitations: Based on GTEx RNA-seq (the same kind of data as the catalog's numeric filter), so partly circular; multi-mapping among POTEB/B2/B3/C/D is not discussed; GTEx has no eye tissue.

evidence.source_title: Bera TK et al. POTE, a highly homologous gene family ... expressed in prostate, ovary, testis, placenta, and prostate cancer. PNAS 2002
evidence.assay: multiple-tissue RNA dot blot (76 samples) and RT-PCR on normal tissue cDNA panel
evidence.tissue: brain, heart, liver, kidney, lung, pancreas, colon (negative); testis, prostate, placenta, ovary (positive)
evidence.finding: No signal in essential organs; RT-PCR positive only in testis, prostate, placenta and weakly ovary.
evidence.quote: The expression of the C34AG cluster was not detected in any of the essential organs, including brain, heart, liver, and kidney.
evidence.limitations: Probe/primers derive from POTE-21 (POTED) and paralogs are 90-98% identical, so the assay is family-level; no eye tissue in panel.

evidence.source_title: Bera TK et al. PNAS 2002 (same paper, paralog cloning)
evidence.assay: RT-PCR cloning and sequencing of >24 clones from prostate and testis cDNA
evidence.finding: Expressed paralogs mapped to chromosomes 2, 14, 15, 21, 22; chromosome 18 (POTEC) not among them.
evidence.quote: POTE RNAs are transcribed from chromosomes 2, 14, 15, 21, and 22 in both prostate and testis.
evidence.limitations: Small clone sample (>24), so a low-abundance chr18 transcript could be missed.

evidence.source_title: Bera TK et al. POTE paralogs are induced and differentially expressed in many cancers. Cancer Res 2006 (PubMed abstract)

evidence.quote: The expression of POTE genes in normal tissues is restricted to prostate, ovary, testis, and placenta.

evidence.source_title: PMID 12475935 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC139254/)
evidence.tissue: prostate; basal and terminal epithelial cells
evidence.finding: Human: UniProt (Q86YR6, citing PMID 12475935) records POTED expression in normal prostate, in basal and terminal epithelial cells, alongside ovary, testis and placenta. The same source lists POTEC (B2RU33) as expressed in prostate and testis.
evidence.limitations: UniProt Q86YR6 and Bera 2002 (PMID 12475935, full text opened) do report POTE in normal prostate, with in situ signal in basal and terminal epithelial cells. Two weaknesses. First, the in situ probe was a 1-kb 5' fragment and the paralogs are 90-98% identical, so the cell-type localisation is family-level, not POTED-specific; the dot blot, Northern and 16-tissue PCR were also not paralog-resolved. The only paralog-resolved evidence is cloning and sequencing of prostate and testis cDNA, which found transcripts from chromosomes 2, 14, 15, 21 and 22; chromosome 21 is POTED, so POTED transcription in prostate is supported, but without quantitation. Second, prostate is a male reproductive accessory gland, so this is a finding only if the screen does not exempt prostate. The same paper found no signal in brain, heart, kidney, liver, lung, colon, pancreas, spleen, thymus, small intestine or peripheral blood leukocytes, which supports the candidate. Separately, the POTEC (chromosome 18) prostate claim conflicts with the paper, which did not find chromosome 18 transcripts among the sequenced prostate and testis clones.

entries.summary: Family-level assays in the original POTE papers (dot blot, RT-PCR, Northern) found signal only in prostate, testis, placenta and weakly ovary, with brain, heart, liver, kidney negative, but those primers/probes were not paralog-specific and were built on the chr21 paralog. Conversely, Barger et al. 2018 state from GTEx RNA-seq that Group 3 POTE-actin genes (which include POTEF) show widespread normal-tissue expression and are not testis-specific; that is bulk RNA-seq subject to the same paralog (and actin) cross-mapping concern. No POTEF-specific protein assay in a vital normal tissue was found (one IHC paper is in ovary and cannot separate POTEE from POTEF).
entries.decision_reason: Reports conflict, cannot separate the gene from paralogs, or come from cultured, diseased or fetal samples.

evidence.source_title: POTE, a highly homologous gene family located on numerous chromosomes and expressed in prostate, ovary, testis, placenta, and prostate cancer (PNAS 2002, PMC139254)
evidence.assay: Multi-tissue dot blot, RT-PCR, Northern blot; in situ hybridization on prostate only
evidence.tissue: prostate, testis, placenta, ovary positive; brain, heart, liver, kidney (dot blot) and brain, heart, liver, lung, pancreas, colon (RT-PCR) negative
evidence.finding: POTE family transcripts not detected in essential organs.
evidence.quote: was not detected in any of the essential organs, including brain, heart, liver, and kidney.
evidence.limitations: Reference cDNA is the chr21 paralog ('aligns almost 100% to human chromosome 21q11.2'); primers described as amplifying all forms of POTE; chr2 POTE-actin paralogs such as POTEF are not separately resolved. Second quote: RT-PCR band 'detected in testis (lane 3), prostate (lane 7), and placenta (lane 8), and very weakly in ovary (lane 9)'.

evidence.source_title: Evolution and expression of chimeric POTE-actin genes in the human genome (PNAS 2006, PMC1693842)
evidence.assay: Northern blot; RT-PCR with forward primer in exon 10 conserved across POTE-2alpha/beta/gamma and reverse primer in the actin insert; Western blot in breast cancer lines
evidence.tissue: prostate and testis positive; brain negative (Northern)
evidence.finding: POTE-actin transcript signal in prostate and testis, none in brain or the MCF-10A normal breast line; 120-kDa fusion protein shown only in breast cancer cell lines.
evidence.quote: there are no detectable bands in MCF-10A and in brain
evidence.limitations: Detects POTE-2alpha (POTEF), 2beta and 2gamma together, not POTEF alone; very limited normal-tissue panel; no normal-tissue Western. Family statement in the paper: 'members of the POTE family have expression restricted to a few normal tissues (prostate, testis, ovary, and placenta)'.

evidence.source_title: Barger et al., Expression of the POTE gene family in human ovarian cancer (Sci Rep 2018) - lab-hosted PDF
evidence.assay: GTEx bulk RNA-seq per paralog (via GeneCards)
evidence.tissue: 'several normal tissues' (not itemized in main text; Supplementary Fig. S1)
evidence.finding: Group 3 POTEs, listed as E, F, G, H, I, J, KP, M, do not show testis-specific expression; POTE-actin genes show widespread normal-tissue expression. Table 1 marks POTEF (POTE2alpha, Group 3, actin fusion) as not testis-specific.
evidence.quote: In contrast to Group 1 & 2 POTEs, Group 3, and particularly the POTE-actin genes, showed widespread normal tissue expression
evidence.limitations: This is GTEx bulk RNA-seq, i.e. the same data class already used as a numeric filter, and is exposed to cross-mapping among POTEE/F/I/J and actin-derived 3' sequence. Authors themselves note 'A caveat to our analysis is that GTEx used bulk tissues'. Specific vital tissues are not named in the text I read.

evidence.source_title: Primate-specific POTE-actin gene could play a role in human folliculogenesis by controlling the proliferation of granulosa cells (Cell Death Discov 2021, PMID 34285194) - Europe PMC abstract record
evidence.finding: POTEE/POTEF protein staining in granulosa and luteal cells.
evidence.quote: Using immunohistochemistry (IHC) with human ovarian tissue, POTEE or POTEF was weakly seen in the granulosa cells

entries.summary: The human gene was characterised by Liu et al. 2005 (Mol Biol Rep) as expressed specifically in testis, and UniProt annotates it 'Testis-specific' on that basis. Mouse RT-PCR across heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidney, brain, testis and ovary also found Ppp3r2 mRNA only in testis, with protein in testis and sperm validated by knockout. A few rodent hippocampus/cartilage papers mention Ppp3r2 as a regulated or predicted target (abstract-level only, not opened in full), which is not gene-specific evidence of normal adult human expression; note the gene sits inside GRIN3A on the same strand.

entries.toxicity_reports: No therapy targeting PPP3R2 itself was found. Europe PMC abstracts note that calcineurin inhibitors affect sperm calcineurin (PMID 26429887: 'male mice lacking Ppp3cc or Ppp3r2 genes (knockout mice) are infertile'), i.e. the knockout phenotype reported is male infertility; abstracts only, not opened in full.
