entries.reported_tissue: brain, kidney, skin (RT-PCR, Ikeda 1997 as curated by UniProt; full text not opened); adrenal cortex (IHC, Lezcano 2021); each contradicted by the Kaczorowski 2022 IHC panel. No report in normal retina or uvea.
entries.summary: Reports conflict. Positive side: UniProt, citing the discovery paper (Ikeda 1997), says PRAME is expressed in testis and 'detected in samples of kidney, brain and skin'; the paper's abstract says only 'some normal tissues, albeit at a lower level' and I could not open its full text (publisher 403, no open copy), so tissue-level amounts are unverified. Later reviews cite the same paper for low RNA in adrenal, ovary and endometrium, and Lezcano 2021 (abstract only) reports PRAME protein by IHC 'at low levels in the endometrium, adrenal cortex, and adult as well as fetal ovary'. Negative side: Kaczorowski 2022 (full text; EP461 antibody, 70 normal tissues) found nuclear staining only in testis, endometrium, placental decidua and corpus luteum granulosa cells, and states kidney, adrenal, liver, lung alveoli and brain were negative; a SAGE plus real-time PCR study (Boon 2003, abstract) lists PRAME among genes with little or no expression in normal adult brain regions; HPA IHC (Enhanced) annotates testis only. Eye: no source reports PRAME in normal retina, choroid or uveal melanocytes; short-term cultured normal uveal melanocytes had undetectable PRAME RNA with a hypermethylated promoter, and conjunctival/cutaneous findings are limited to rare PRAME-positive junctional melanocytes in nevi, solar lentigines and sun-damaged skin (lesional or adjacent-to-melanoma tissue). Kidney: PRAME-specific T cells showed low reactivity to cultured kidney epithelial cells (Amir 2011) and the IMA203 TCR gave a very low signal on cultured renal cortical epithelial cells from one of two donors. No human loss-of-function disease is listed in UniProt. Clinically, PRAME TCR-T cells (IMA203, 40 patients, up to 8.8e9 cells) were reported safe with no specific renal toxicity; the trial papers do not attribute any event to on-target, off-tumour recognition.
entries.decision_reason: Conflicting reports, so no rule fires. Brain, kidney and skin are attributed to the 1997 discovery paper only through UniProt's annotation; its full text was not opened, so tissue levels are unverified. A 70-tissue IHC series (Kaczorowski 2022) found no staining in brain, kidney or adrenal, and Boon 2003 found little or no RNA in normal brain. Low adrenal staining (Lezcano 2021, abstract) is contradicted by the same series. No report in normal eye. PRAME-directed T-cell therapy trials report no dose-limiting on-target toxicity in these tissues. Neither negative series excludes a 1-4% neuronal subpopulation.

evidence.source_title: UniProt P78395 (PRAME_HUMAN) tissue specificity
evidence.assay: curated annotation with experimental evidence code, citing PubMed 9047241 (RT-PCR/northern in the original paper)
evidence.finding: States testis expression and detection in kidney, brain and skin samples; disease field empty.
evidence.quote: TISSUE SPECIFICITY: Expressed in testis. Detected in samples of kidney, brain and skin. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:9047241}.
evidence.limitations: Curated summary, not the primary data; gives no level, sample number or donor age. Does not mention adrenal, ovary or endometrium, which reviews attribute to the same paper.

evidence.source_title: Ikeda H et al. Characterization of an antigen that is recognized on a melanoma showing partial HLA loss by CTL expressing an NK inhibitory receptor. Immunity 1997 (PubMed abstract)
evidence.assay: abstract only (paper used RT-PCR; details not in abstract)
evidence.finding: PRAME expressed in many tumours and in some normal tissues at lower level.
evidence.quote: It is expressed in a large proportion of tumors and also in some normal tissues, albeit at a lower level.
evidence.limitations: FULL TEXT NOT OPENED: cell.com returned HTTP 403 and the only repository copy (UCLouvain DIAL) is restricted. The tissue list and levels (adrenal, ovary, endometrium, kidney, brain, skin) are therefore known only through UniProt and reviews.

evidence.source_title: Kaczorowski M et al. PRAME Expression in Cancer. A Systematic Immunohistochemical Study of >5800 Epithelial and Nonepithelial Tumors. Am J Surg Pathol 2022 (full text)
evidence.assay: IHC, EP461 monoclonal, 70 normal tissues in multi-tissue blocks/TMAs; IHC cross-validated by qPCR in 23 tumours
evidence.tissue: kidney, adrenal, liver, colon, thyroid, prostate, breast, salivary gland (negative)
evidence.finding: Vital-organ epithelia and mesenchyme including kidney and adrenal were negative.
evidence.quote: Neither epithelial nor mesenchymal structures of the colonic mucosa, liver, kidney, prostate, breast, thyroid, adrenal and salivary glands were positive.
evidence.limitations: Number of samples per normal tissue not given (70 normal tissues in total); TMA cores could miss focal or rare-cell expression; directly contradicts Lezcano 2021 for adrenal cortex. No eye tissue listed. (PMC full text read through NCBI E-utilities efetch, tags stripped.)

evidence.source_title: Kaczorowski 2022 (same paper), brain and lung
evidence.finding: No staining in brain; alveolar epithelium negative, respiratory epithelium only apical cilia staining; sebaceous glands cytoplasmic staining.
evidence.quote: No staining was present in the brain, peripheral ganglia, and nerves.
evidence.limitations: Brain region and number of samples not stated; a 1-4% subpopulation of cortical neurons with weak nuclear signal could be missed on tissue cores.

evidence.source_title: Kaczorowski 2022 (same paper), positive normal tissues
evidence.tissue: testis, endometrium, placenta decidua, ovarian corpus luteum
evidence.finding: Positive normal tissues were all reproductive.
evidence.quote: Focal and weak PRAME expression was observed in decidua basalis of the placenta and granulosa cells of the ovarian corpus luteum.
evidence.limitations: Abstract summarises as 'In normal tissues, PRAME was expressed in the testis and proliferative endometrium.'

evidence.source_title: Lezcano C et al. Immunohistochemical Detection of Cancer-Testis Antigen PRAME. Int J Surg Pathol 2021 (PubMed abstract)
evidence.assay: IHC with a monoclonal antibody on FFPE normal and tumour tissues (antibody clone not named in abstract)
evidence.tissue: testis; endometrium, adrenal cortex, adult and fetal ovary (low)
evidence.finding: PRAME protein at low levels in adrenal cortex, a vital tissue.
evidence.quote: PRAME protein expression in normal tissues is congruent with original molecular data being present in the testis, and at low levels in the endometrium, adrenal cortex, and adult as well as fetal ovary.
evidence.limitations: Abstract only; full text not open access. Extent/intensity in adrenal, number of adrenal samples and which other normal tissues (brain, eye, kidney) were tested are not in the abstract. Contradicted by Kaczorowski 2022 (adrenal negative).

evidence.source_title: Lezcano C et al. PRAME Expression in Melanocytic Tumors. Am J Surg Pathol 2018 (full text, author manuscript)
evidence.assay: IHC, EPR20330 monoclonal, 400 melanocytic tumours plus solar lentigines and non-lesional skin
evidence.finding: Rare isolated PRAME-positive junctional melanocytes in solar lentigines and benign non-lesional sun-damaged skin; no nuclear labelling of other skin cells; sebaceous cytoplasmic labelling judged artefact.
evidence.quote: Rare isolated junctional melanocytes with immunoreactivity for PRAME were also seen in solar lentigines and benign nonlesional skin.
evidence.limitations: Non-lesional skin came from re-excisions of lentigo maligna (sun-damaged, adjacent to melanoma), so not strictly normal. Paper's statement that normal expression includes 'testis, ovary, placenta, adrenals, and endometrium' is cited from earlier RNA work, not tested here. No eye tissue. (PMC full text read through NCBI E-utilities efetch, tags stripped.)

evidence.source_title: Boon K et al. Comparison of medulloblastoma and normal neural transcriptomes identifies a restricted set of activated genes. Oncogene 2003 (PubMed abstract)
evidence.assay: SAGE across normal adult and paediatric brain regions, real-time PCR verification of selected genes
evidence.tissue: normal cerebellum and other brain regions
evidence.finding: PRAME named among genes highly expressed in medulloblastoma within a set selected for little or no expression in normal brain.
evidence.quote: revealing 30 transcripts with high expression in multiple tumors and little or no expression in the normal cerebellum and other adult and pediatric brain regions
evidence.limitations: Abstract only; it does not state that PRAME itself was one of the genes verified by real-time PCR in normal brain. SAGE is not gene-specific and is insensitive to rare cells.

evidence.source_title: Gentien D et al. Multi-omics comparison of malignant and normal uveal melanocytes reveals molecular features of uveal melanoma. Cell Rep 2023 (full text)
evidence.assay: RNA-seq and promoter methylation of short-term cultures of normal uveal (choroidal) melanocytes versus uveal melanoma PDX
evidence.finding: PRAME RNA undetectable and promoter hypermethylated in normal uveal melanocytes.
evidence.quote: PRAME is associated with a particularly high fold change from undetectable in NM to highly expressed in both PDXs
evidence.limitations: Cultured cells and RNA-seq, so not a gene-specific assay on tissue; authors note in vivo profiles remain to be verified. Bears on the donor with PRAME-positive eye melanocytes: literature gives no support for normal uveal melanocyte expression. (PMC full text read through NCBI E-utilities efetch, tags stripped.)

evidence.source_title: LeBlanc RE et al. PRAME immunohistochemistry is useful in the evaluation of conjunctival melanomas, nevi, and primary acquired melanosis. J Cutan Pathol 2021 (PubMed abstract)
evidence.finding: Scattered faintly PRAME-positive intraepithelial melanocytes in 6 conjunctival nevi.
evidence.quote: Scattered, faintly PRAME-positive intraepithelial melanocyte nuclei were identified in six nevi.
evidence.limitations: Abstract only; lesional (nevus) tissue, not normal eye; conjunctiva, not retina or uvea. A larger series (Mudhar 2023, abstract, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36804828/) scored 96% of conjunctival nevi and 96% of benign melanoses PRAME score 0.

evidence.source_title: Amir AL et al. PRAME-specific Allo-HLA-restricted T cells with potent antitumor reactivity useful for therapeutic T-cell receptor gene transfer. Clin Cancer Res 2011 (PubMed abstract)
evidence.assay: T-cell reactivity against a panel of non-malignant cell types, with PRAME expression measured in the reactive cells
evidence.tissue: kidney epithelial cells, mature dendritic cells
evidence.finding: High-avidity PRAME-specific T cells spared most non-malignant cells but showed low reactivity to kidney epithelial cells and mature DCs, attributed to low PRAME expression.
evidence.quote: These T cells, however, also exerted low reactivity against mature dendritic cells (DC) and kidney epithelial cells, which was shown to be because of low PRAME expression.
evidence.limitations: Abstract only; cultured primary cells, not tissue (rubric: cultured samples do not count). Unfavourable signal nonetheless, and consistent with UniProt's 'kidney'.

evidence.source_title: Wermke M et al. Autologous T cell therapy for PRAME+ advanced solid tumors in HLA-A*02+ patients: a phase 1 trial (IMA203). Nat Med 2025 (full text), preclinical section
evidence.assay: Mass-spectrometry immunopeptidomics of HLA-A*02 normal tissues; IFN-gamma release against primary normal cells
evidence.tissue: 41 normal tissue types (peptide not quantifiable); renal cortical epithelial cells (very low signal)
evidence.finding: PRAME SLLQHLIGL peptide not quantifiable by MS on normal tissues; TCR unreactive to normal primary cells except very low signal on renal cortical epithelial cells from 1 of 2 donors.
evidence.quote: Abundant PRAME-004 presentation could be demonstrated on patient-derived native (that is, unmodified, shock-frozen) primary tumor tissue and metastases while not quantifiable on 41 different normal tissue types
evidence.limitations: Sponsor-authored; 'not quantifiable' is a sensitivity-limited statement about one HLA-A*02 peptide, not absence of the protein; the list of 41 tissues is in a supplement I did not open. Introduction of the same paper states expression 'is limited to testis and at low RNA levels in the endometrium, ovaries, adrenal glands and a few other tissues'. (PMC full text read through NCBI E-utilities efetch, tags stripped.)

evidence.source_title: Human Protein Atlas PRAME (JSON record and tissue page)
evidence.assay: IHC, reliability Enhanced (antibodies HPA045153, HPA068562, CAB080138); RNA summaries
evidence.finding: Protein annotated in testis seminiferous ducts only; RNA tissue enriched testis 102.1 nTPM; single-nuclei brain 'Cell type enriched' inhibitory neurons 2.3 nCPM.
evidence.quote: Cytoplasmic expression in seminiferous ducts in testis.
evidence.limitations: Read through a summarising fetch tool; per-tissue staining for adrenal, kidney, cortex and skin is shown only graphically and was not extracted; retina marked N/A. Cytoplasmic rather than nuclear pattern differs from the diagnostic antibodies. RNA values are database counts, not literature.

evidence.source_title: NCBI Gene 23532 PRAME (RefSeq summary)
evidence.finding: RefSeq summary asserts testis-only expression.
evidence.quote: It is not expressed in normal tissues, except testis.
evidence.limitations: Database annotation; contradicted by every primary source above for endometrium/ovary.

evidence.source_title: PMID 34023098 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8152939/)
evidence.tissue: skin; melanocytes (sun-damaged skin); stromal cells in scars
evidence.finding: Human: nuclear PRAME staining in non-neoplastic skin is usually absent or limited to a few scattered melanocytes, most often in actinically damaged skin; the authors also note occasional weak nuclear staining of stromal cells in scars. This fits the catalog's existing dismissed rare-cell hit in eye melanocytes and hints at damage- or wound-associated expression.
evidence.limitations: Lezcano 2021 says it as claimed: in non-neoplastic skin nuclear PRAME staining is 'usually absent' or 'limited to few scattered melanocytes most frequently encountered in actinically damaged skin', and 'occasional weak nuclear immunoreactivity of stromal cells in scars'. This is the nuclear pattern with the diagnostic antibody, in human non-neoplastic tissue. Caveats: it is a review reporting the authors' observations without counts; the tissue is damaged or scarred rather than strictly normal; and the larger 2022 IHC study found all cutaneous structures other than sebaceous glands negative. So it is real but rare, focal and weak. The link to the catalog's eye-melanocyte hit is the flagger's inference, not in the source.

evidence.source_title: PMID 35973038 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9588667/); PMID 34023098 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8152939/)
evidence.finding: Human: IHC across 70 normal tissues found cytoplasmic PRAME staining in sebaceous glands of the skin; a second review reports the same in sebocytes, consistently with clone EPR20330 but not with all anti-PRAME antibodies, and calls its significance unclear. Staining is cytoplasmic, not the nuclear pattern scored in tumors, so it may be clone-specific cross-reactivity.
evidence.limitations: Both sources say this. Kaczorowski 2022 (70 normal tissues): 'Cytoplasmic staining was seen in sebaceous glands of the skin whereas other cutaneous structures were negative'. Lezcano 2021: cytoplasmic staining of sebocytes, 'consistently observed with the EPR20330 clone, but not with all anti-PRAME antibodies', significance unclear. One addition to the claim: the 2022 study used a different clone (EP461, with E7I1B giving nearly identical patterns), so the staining is seen with more than one clone. It is still cytoplasmic rather than the nuclear pattern, has no RNA or knockout validation, and cross-reactivity is not excluded, so it is not gene-specific proof of PRAME protein.

evidence.source_title: PMID 23460923 / PMC3584020 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3584020/)
evidence.finding: Human: the curated UniProt entry for PRAME (P78395) records that PRAME is up-regulated by interferon gamma and bacterial PAMPs, citing PMID 23460923. This is inducible rather than constitutive expression.
evidence.limitations: The UniProt induction annotation exists and cites PMID 23460923, but the paper (Wadelin 2013, PLoS One; abstract and full text opened) shows induction only in leukaemic cell lines, mainly HL60, with U937 used for localisation. No primary PBMC, monocytes, neutrophils or healthy-donor leukocytes were tested. IFN-gamma or LPS alone did not significantly change PRAME; induction needed a PAMP plus IFN-gamma and was transient. The authors only speculate that inducibility might explain low levels in normal tissue. This is not evidence of expression in normal activated immune cells.

evidence.source_title: PMID 35973038 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9588667/) for protein-level negatives; UniProt P78395 citing PMID 9047241 for the RNA statement
evidence.finding: Human: UniProt's tissue-specificity annotation (citing the original cloning paper, PMID 9047241) lists expression in kidney, brain and skin in addition to testis. The large 2022 IHC study (PMID 35973038) found kidney, brain and adrenal negative at protein level, so this is low-level RNA not confirmed as protein; a search summary also indicated adrenocortical staining varies by antibody clone, but I did not open that source.
evidence.limitations: UniProt P78395 does say 'Expressed in testis. Detected in samples of kidney, brain and skin', citing PMID 9047241. I could not open the Ikeda 1997 full text (publisher returned 403); its abstract says only 'expressed ... in some normal tissues, albeit at a lower level'. Secondary reviews of that paper name testis, adrenal, ovary and endometrium as the normal sites, not kidney, brain or skin, so those three rest on the UniProt curation alone and I marked the adult/normal and gene-specific flags from that annotation, not from the paper. The 2022 IHC study on 70 normal tissues found kidney, brain and adrenal negative, and skin negative apart from sebaceous glands. At most this is trace RNA without protein, as the flagger concedes. The 'adrenocortical staining varies by clone' remark is unsourced and should be disregarded.

entries.toxicity_reports: IMA203 / anzutresgene autoleucel (affinity-enhanced PRAME TCR-T; Wermke et al., Nat Med 2025, full text https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12283372/; 41 in safety set, 40 infused, up to 8.8e9 cells): 'IMA203 T cells were safe, and the MTD was not reached.' 'The most common TEAEs with higher severity (≥grade 3) were cytopenias associated with lymphodepletion'; CRS in 92.7% (grade 3 in 4.9%, 'grade 3 CRS being defined by grade 3 rash and grade 4 transaminitis, respectively'); ICANS in 12.2%, 'No grade 3 or higher neurotoxicities occurred'; 'A single dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) was observed with a patient treated at DL2 experiencing grade 3 atrial fibrillation, hypotension with hemodynamic instability'; 'no treatment-related patient deaths were reported'. On kidney: 'no reactivity toward non-malignant human primary cells ..., except for a very low signal on human cortical renal epithelial cells with one of two donors. It is noteworthy that, so far, no specific renal toxicity has been observed in patients of the ongoing clinical trial.' The paper does not use the phrase on-target/off-tumour for any event and does not discuss adrenal, ocular or testicular toxicity. Unexplained in the main text (preferred terms are in a supplement I did not open): Table 2 lists Endocrine disorders 2 patients (1 grade ≥3), Eye disorders 1 patient (grade ≥3), Renal and urinary disorders 6 (2 grade ≥3, at least one after a second infusion), Skin disorders 9 (2 grade ≥3), 'regardless of relatedness'. MDG1011 (PRAME TCR-T, myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms, 9 treated; Cancers 2025, full text https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12468345/): 'The treatment was well tolerated. No dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) were observed, and the most common serious adverse events were associated with lymphodepleting chemotherapy and/or disease progression.' Brenetafusp / IMC-F106C (PRAME x CD3 ImmTAC): no peer-reviewed report found; only news coverage of conference abstracts, read through a summarising fetch tool. OncLive on ESMO 2022 (https://www.onclive.com/view/imc-f106c-shows-potential-as-t-cell-receptor-driven-therapy-in-melanoma): 77% of 55 patients had CRS in the first 3 doses, 35% had a grade ≥3 adverse event, and the investigator is quoted '[Overall, there was] no treatment-related discontinuation nor grade 5 toxicity [originating] from this therapy.' JNCCN360 on ASCO 2024 abstract 9507 (https://jnccn360.org/advanced-skin-cancers/news/asco-2024-phase-i-findings-on-novel-bispecific-protein-for-cutaneous-melanoma): 'Cytokine-release syndrome of grades 1 and 2 (50%) was the most common adverse event.' Search snippets (not opened) add rash as a frequent treatment-related event; none of the coverage attributes an event to normal-tissue PRAME. The ESMO abstract page returned 404. Preclinical warning: Amir 2011 (abstract) 'Clinical studies have to determine the significance of the reactivity observed against mature DCs and kidney epithelial cells'; Gezgin 2017 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5509351/) 'This reactivity could lead to nephrotoxicity and long-term depletion of mature dendritic cells'. No clinical report opened confirms either.

I read the PubMed abstract of Manchev et al., Blood 2014: a consanguineous family with severe autosomal recessive macrothrombocytopenia and thrombocytopathy, homozygous c.222C>G (p.Ile74Met) in PRKACG, with a marked proplatelet-formation defect and low filamin A in megakaryocytes, rescued in vitro by lentiviral wild-type PRKACG in patient megakaryocytes. Caveats: it is a single family with one missense variant; the evidence is functional in patient megakaryocytes, not a direct measurement of expression in normal tissue; the full text did not load, so the paper's megakaryocyte/platelet expression data remain unchecked.

evidence.source_title: Lin DC et al., J Biol Chem 2002;277(22):19276-80, PMID 11886876 (abstract only); see also Soga T et al., Biochim Biophys Acta 2002, PMID 12427552
evidence.tissue: gastrointestinal tract, endocrine glands, brain, spleen, pancreas; not resolved (glandular epithelium, stroma and vascular endothelium shown only in decidua)
evidence.finding: Human: UniProt Q8TCW9 lists PROKR1 (prokineticin receptor 1, a Gq-coupled GPCR) as expressed in stomach, throughout the small intestine, colon, rectum, thyroid, pituitary, salivary gland, adrenal gland, brain, spleen, prostate and pancreas, besides testis and ovary, citing Evans et al., Endocrinology 2008. It is a signalling receptor with widespread low-level non-reproductive expression, not a germline-restricted gene.
evidence.limitations: UniProt Q8TCW9 does list this tissue panel, but it attributes it to Evans et al. 2008 (PMID 18339712), which is a decidua/early-pregnancy paper; a search of its open-access full text found none of pituitary, salivary, small intestine or spleen as an expression result. The list matches Lin et al., JBC 2002 (PMID 11886876), whose abstract says prokineticin receptor mRNA is 'expressed in gastrointestinal organs, endocrine glands, and other tissues'. A second cloning paper (Soga 2002, PMID 12427552) reports a different PK-R1 distribution (testis, medulla oblongata, skeletal muscle, skin) and notes PK-R1 and PK-R2 are 87% identical, so paralog cross-detection in these 2002 RT-PCR tissue panels cannot be excluded from the abstracts alone. The evidence is bulk mRNA only, with no cell type, no quantitation and no protein outside decidua, so it does not contradict the atlas maximum of 1.6 TPM. Real low-level non-reproductive expression is plausible but weaker and less well sourced than claimed. I did not check mouse knockout literature.

evidence.source_title: UniProt P85298 (ARHGAP8); Johnstone CN et al., Gene 2004;336(1):59-71, PMID 15225876 (parent gene only)
evidence.tissue: kidney, colon, small intestine, stomach, skeletal muscle
evidence.finding: Human: PRR5-ARHGAP8 is a readthrough locus with no function or tissue annotation of its own in UniProt (B1AHC3, B1AHC4). Its downstream parent ARHGAP8 (UniProt P85298) is 'highly expressed in kidney and placenta' and also in colon, skeletal muscle, small intestine and stomach (Johnstone et al., Gene 2004). Any peptide from the ARHGAP8 portion of the fusion would therefore be presented in normal kidney and gut.
evidence.limitations: The sources say what is claimed, but about the parent gene, not this one. UniProt P85298 (ARHGAP8) reads 'Highly expressed in kidney and placenta. Also expressed in colon, skeletal muscle, small intestine, stomach, and testis. Not detected in brain, liver or spleen', citing Johnstone et al. 2004 (PMID 15225876), whose abstract confirms transcripts in normal mammary gland and colon. The readthrough entries (B1AHC3, B1AHC4, H0Y9T8) are unreviewed with no function or tissue annotation. There is no direct evidence that the fusion transcript or protein exists in normal tissue. The valid point is narrower: peptides from the ARHGAP8-derived sequence are shared with a parent gene expressed in normal kidney and gut, which is a sequence-overlap (mapping_risk) issue rather than a missed function of the readthrough gene. I did not check the degree of sequence overlap.

evidence.source_title: PMID 33719563, DOI 10.1152/ajplung.00022.2020 (Europe PMC abstract); UniProt Q8N7X1 https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q8N7X1.txt (function curated from that paper only; caution note on RBMX retrogene origin; HPA testis-enriched)
evidence.tissue: lung; bronchoalveolar / alveolar type II-like epithelial cells (human cell lines)
evidence.finding: Human: RBMXL3 was pulled out by proteomics as a protein binding a hairpin element in the surfactant protein B (SFTPB) mRNA 3'UTR, and siRNA against RBMXL3 reduced dexamethasone-induced SP-B mRNA in human bronchoalveolar cells; UniProt curates this as its function. The evidence is from cultured lung epithelial lines (A549 and HEK293 are in the indexing), and the abstract shows no endogenous expression in normal adult lung tissue, so this is a glucocorticoid-dependent, cell-line-level lead only.
evidence.limitations: The source exists and says what the finding reports: PMID 33719563 (Am J Physiol Lung Cell Mol Physiol 2021, L942-L957) identifies RBMXL3 by proteomics as a protein binding the 30-nt hairpin element in the human SP-B mRNA 3'UTR, and siRNA against RBMXL3 reduced dexamethasone-induced SP-B mRNA in 'human bronchoalveolar cells'. UniProt Q8N7X1 curates this as the function from that single paper. But it is not evidence of expression or function in normal adult human lung. The abstract describes only cultured cells (MeSH indexing lists A549 and HEK293 cells, plus mouse lung epithelial cells in which RBMXL3 was expressed exogenously with a plasmid reporter); it reports no endogenous RBMXL3 RNA or protein in normal lung tissue or primary alveolar type II cells. A549 is a lung adenocarcinoma line, so endogenous expression there is tumor-line expression, which is expected for a cancer/testis gene. UniProt's own cross-reference gives HPA 'Tissue enriched (testis)'. Gene specificity is also unproven from the abstract: UniProt cautions that RBMXL3 is an RBMX-derived retrogene, and neither the proteomic peptide assignment nor the siRNA is shown in the abstract to discriminate it from RBMX or other RBMX-like paralogs. I read only the abstract and the UniProt entry, not the full text, so the paper may contain specificity controls or tissue data I did not see. As it stands this is a single-lab, cell-line, glucocorticoid-dependent mechanistic lead, as the finding itself concedes, and does not show a normal-tissue liability.

No human olfactory mucosa data found.

entries.summary: SCGB1D1 (lipophilin A) is an established secreted tear protein: it was purified and sequenced from normal human tears as a heterodimer with lipophilin C (SCGB2A1), and HPA single-cell data put its top RNA signal in lacrimal acinar cells, matching the Census 'eye: acinar cell' signal. UniProt additionally lists thymus, kidney, testis, ovary and salivary gland, and the 1999 cDNA paper says lipophilins were 'widely expressed in normal tissues', but I could only open that abstract and could not confirm that the assay separates lipophilin A from its close paralog lipophilin B (SCGB1D2). HPA MS data flag pancreas (large ducts) and thyroid/parathyroid, without IHC.
entries.decision_reason: The protein was purified and sequenced from normal human tears (Lehrer 1998); our donor-level data detect it in acinar cells of the eye. Read at abstract level; the producing cells are inferred from the secretion.

evidence.limitations: Primary abstract (Choi et al., J Immunol 2004, PMID 15034037) says IIS is expressed in virtually all tissues, highest in lymph nodes, tonsil, cultured lymphoblasts and ovary, is augmented by IFN-gamma in lymphoblast cells, and is markedly elevated in activated CD8+ and CD19+ cells versus resting lymphoid cells. Independent support for cytokine induction: Lu et al. 2011 (PMC3063214) found IL-1beta, TNF-alpha and IFN-gamma increased SCGB1D4 in normal human nasal explants using sequenced qRT-PCR products. Caveats: only the abstract of the 2004 paper was read, so I could not check whether its probes exclude the close paralogs SCGB1D1/SCGB1D2; and HPA disagrees on the resting pattern (enriched in fallopian tube, cervix and epididymis, not lymphoid tissue), so the 'all tissues' breadth is doubtful while the induction claim stands.

evidence.source_title: PMID 20579626 (Lapunzina 2010, Am J Hum Genet); UniProt Q8TDD2; PMID 15474293 (Gao 2004, Gene) for the limits of the human expression data
evidence.tissue: bone (and tooth root); osteoblasts, osteocytes; odontoblasts and cementoblasts
evidence.finding: Human: a homozygous SP7/Osterix frameshift (c.1052delA) causes recessive osteogenesis imperfecta (OI type XII) with recurrent fractures, bone deformity and delayed tooth eruption; UniProt curates SP7 as a transcriptional activator essential for osteoblast differentiation, with expression restricted to bone-derived cells.
evidence.limitations: PMID 20579626 exists and says what is claimed: homozygous c.1052delA in SP7/OSX in an Egyptian child with recessive osteogenesis imperfecta (recurrent fractures, mild bone deformities, delayed tooth eruption). UniProt Q8TDD2 does say 'essential for osteoblast differentiation' and 'Restricted to bone-derived cell'. Two caveats. The patient is a child and the paper frames it as bone development, so this is human loss-of-function evidence, not adult expression evidence. UniProt's tissue line rests on PMID 15474293, where SP7 mRNA was restricted to bone-derived cell lines in vitro and was undetectable by Northern in any adult tissue including mandibular bone; in vivo osteoblast expression was shown only by in situ on human embryonic tissue. So direct adult human expression is not shown by these sources. SP7 has no close paralog confusion here (genetic mapping plus sequencing).

evidence.source_title: PMID 20615976 (Zhou 2010, PNAS)
evidence.finding: Mouse: postnatal conditional deletion of Osx (Sp7) at several time points showed it is essential for osteoblast differentiation and new bone formation in growing and adult bones, and severely disrupted osteocyte maturation, morphology and function. This is an adult homeostatic role, not only an embryonic one.
evidence.limitations: The source is real and accurately quoted: PMID 20615976 reports that postnatal conditional deletion of Osx at several time points blocks osteoblast differentiation and new bone formation in growing and adult bones and disrupts osteocyte maturation, morphology and function. Weakened only because it is mouse-only; it is a gene-specific conditional knockout and does show an adult, not just embryonic, role. No human adult data in this source.

evidence.source_title: PMID 26599722 (He 2016, Int Endod J), a review of mouse primary studies
evidence.finding: Mouse (review): Osx is expressed in odontoblasts and cementoblasts from late embryonic to postnatal stages, and odontoblast-specific conditional knockout gives short, thin tooth roots. Evidence is for postnatal root formation, not shown for mature adult teeth.
evidence.limitations: PMID 26599722 is a review and says what is claimed: Osx expression from late embryonic to postnatal stages in odontoblasts and cementoblasts, and odontoblast conditional knockout mice with short, thin roots. It is mouse, developmental/postnatal root formation, and a review rather than primary data; nothing about mature adult human teeth. The only human hint is delayed tooth eruption in the OI patient (PMID 20579626).

evidence.finding: Mouse only: Spam1 RNA (RT-PCR, in situ) and protein (Western, IHC) were detected in kidney cortex, mainly proximal tubules and glomeruli, and Spam1-null mice had reduced urine volume and failed to raise urine osmolality after water deprivation. evidence.limitations: Both mouse sources exist and say what is claimed. PMID 17446714: Spam1 RNA (RT-PCR, in situ) and protein (Western, IHC) in mouse kidney cortex, mainly proximal tubules and glomeruli; Spam1-null mice had reduced urine volume and no rise in urine osmolality after 24 h water deprivation. PMID 9933825: PH-20 transcripts in normal mouse kidney and tubular cells. The null mouse makes it gene-specific, but it is mouse-only. The one human source checked, PMID 8575780, found a single 2.4 kb transcript strictly limited to testis across 16 tissues by Northern, which agrees with the human RNA atlases. No human kidney evidence was found, and Northern would not detect very low expression.

evidence.finding: Human: Kouprina et al. report that SPANX-N genes, unlike SPANX-A/D, are expressed at a low level in several nongametogenic adult tissues, attributed to lower promoter CpG methylation. The abstract does not name the tissues or resolve individual SPANX-N members; the full text was not read.
evidence.limitations: Full text of PMID 17406683 (PMC1831492) read. RT-PCR used pan-SPANX-N primers, then products were cloned and sequenced to assign members (Table 2). For SPANX-N1 the only positive normal tissues were testis and cervix; prostate, placenta, lung, colon, brain, liver, muscle, spleen, heart, kidney and lymph node were negative. Only 4 of 120 clones from normal tissues were N1, while 95 of 103 clones from tumors and cancer lines were N1. Cervix is a reproductive-tract tissue, so there is no non-reproductive normal expression for this member; the family-level abstract statement does not apply to N1. The paper also notes N1 has a frameshift in exon 2.

evidence.source_title: PMID 17406683 full text, Table 2 (PMC1831492)
evidence.tissue: several nongametogenic adult tissues (not named in abstract)
evidence.finding: Human: SPANX-N family reported as expressed at a low level in several nongametogenic adult tissues, in contrast to SPANX-A/D. Family-level statement from the abstract; member-specific tissues not verified.
evidence.limitations: Full text of PMID 17406683 read. In Table 2, SPANX-N4 transcripts were found in testis and prostate only; cervix, placenta, lung, colon, brain, liver, muscle, spleen, heart, kidney and lymph node were negative. So the family-level 'several nongametogenic tissues' statement reduces to prostate alone for this member, a male reproductive accessory gland, at roughly 50 to 100 times below testis. Counts as a finding only if prostate is treated as non-reproductive.

entries.summary: SPATA3 (TSARG1) is described as testis/spermatid restricted. A 2025 study (Mol Med Rep) surveyed adult mouse tissues by Western blot (muscle, brain, heart, liver, spleen, lung, colon, kidney, breast, uterus, ovary, testis) and found the SPATA3-I2 protein specifically in testis, localised to round and elongated spermatids; HPA reports testis-enriched RNA and IHC 'Selective cytoplasmic expression in spermatozoa'. No direct gene-specific assay of normal human somatic tissues was opened; the human statements rest on atlas data.
entries.decision_reason: Sources describe germline, placental or embryonic restriction, or did not test adult somatic tissue.

evidence.source_title: PMID 28264649 (PMC5338094), Bekpen et al., BMC Genomics 2017
evidence.tissue: skin / connective tissue (primary fibroblasts); broad tissues; primary foreskin fibroblasts
evidence.finding: Human/primate: the SPATA31A/C family 'broadened the expression into many tissues' relative to the testis-only mouse gene; antibody staining shows the protein in human fibroblast nucleoli with relocalisation to the whole nucleus after UV, and CRISPR reduction of SPATA31A copies in human primary fibroblasts increased UV sensitivity. Antibody and knockout are family-level, so this applies to the SPATA31A copies in the batch (A1, A3, A5, A6, A7), not demonstrably to the D or F subfamilies.
evidence.limitations: Source exists and the abstract of PMID 28264649 (Bekpen et al., BMC Genomics 2017) says the family 'broadened the expression into many tissues', that the protein relocalises from nucleolus to whole nucleus after UV, and that CRISPR reduction of copies in human primary fibroblasts increased UV sensitivity. PMID 29676996 exists but is about SPATA31A1 overexpression causing premature senescence and copy number versus longevity, not normal-tissue expression. Weaknesses on full-text check (PMC5338094): (1) not gene-specific: the RT-PCR/qPCR detects A and C types together, and the antibody was raised against peptides shared by A and C types, with western bands at 170-200 kD versus 157/130 kD predicted; nothing distinguishes SPATA31A1 from A3/A5/A6/A7 or the C copies. (2) Expression outside testis is described by the authors as 'quite low' with testis still highest, from commercial pooled total RNA (brain, liver, kidney, heart, lung, thymus, spleen, cerebellum) with no donor/age details. (3) The functional evidence is in cultured HFF foreskin fibroblast lines (ATCC CRL-2703/CRL-2450), i.e. in vitro cells of neonatal-type origin, not adult tissue in situ. (4) The only tissue IHC (lung and sinus epithelium, tonsil) uses sections labelled 'Lung CF' and 'Tonsil allergic', i.e. apparently diseased tissue, with the same family-level antibody and no quantification. Real family-level signal that the atlases cannot exclude because of multi-mapping, but it is not demonstrated for SPATA31A1 specifically nor in normal adult tissue.

evidence.source_title: PMID 11807770 (Klein et al., Eur J Immunol 2002) for the knockout; PMID 11591116 for the induced transcript
evidence.tissue: lymphoid (spleen B cells); activated B cells undergoing class switch recombination
evidence.finding: Mouse: a lymphocyte-specific Spo11 transcript (alternative 5' exon) is induced more than eightfold by RT-PCR in LPS/cytokine-stimulated B cells undergoing class switching. However, Spo11-deficient mice have normal somatic hypermutation and class switching, so the induced transcript has no required function.
evidence.limitations: All three sources exist and match. PMID 10873300 (Tokuyama & Tokuyama, Cell Immunol 2000): mouse Spo11 detected by RT-PCR on day 3 in normal mu+ B cells under IgA/IgG1 class-switch stimuli. PMID 11591116 (same authors, 2001): lymphocyte-derived Spo11 cDNA with a novel 5' portion, exons 2-12 identical to testis form, 'strongly induced (above eightfold)' with LPS + retinoic acid + IL-4; note this paper also claims antisense oligo inhibited class switching 60-90%, which the finding omitted. PMID 11807770 (Klein et al., Eur J Immunol 2002): Spo11-/- mice have normal somatic hypermutation and normal serum levels of all Ig isotypes, 'Spo11 is not required for Ig hypermutation or class switch recombination', which contradicts the antisense result and removes any required function. Spo11 is single-copy and the cDNA was sequenced, so the assay is gene-specific, but the evidence is mouse only, in vitro stimulated cells, RT-PCR without protein, from a single two-author group and not independently replicated; no human activated-B-cell data. Accurately described by the finder as low priority.

evidence.source_title: PMID 37523817 (Kikuchi et al., BBRC 2023); PMID 7935409 (Kohmura et al., MCB 1994)
evidence.tissue: small intestine (ileum); broad tissues in mouse; ileal epithelium / stem-progenitor cells
evidence.finding: Mouse: Srm transcripts were described as 'rather ubiquitous' across tissues and the single knockout has no apparent phenotype; triple knockout of Brk/Ptk6, Srms and Frk impairs ileal homeostasis and recovery from radiation-induced mucosal damage, whereas single or double knockouts do not, indicating a redundant epithelial role.
evidence.limitations: Both sources exist and say what is claimed. PMID 7935409 (Kohmura et al., Mol Cell Biol 1994): mouse Srm, 'expression of two transcripts is rather ubiquitous and changes according to tissue and developmental stage'; knockout mice 'displayed no apparent phenotype'. PMID 37523817 (Kikuchi et al., BBRC 2023): Brk/Ptk6-Srms-Frk triple-knockout mice have reduced ileal stem/progenitor population and defective recovery from radiation-induced mucosal damage; 'single- or double-knockout of BFK genes did not elicit such abnormalities'. The knockouts are gene-targeted so the genetics are gene-specific, but all evidence is mouse; the phenotype requires loss of all three kinases, so it does not show that Srms itself is expressed or needed in ileal epithelium (the triple-KO effect could be carried by Ptk6/Frk, which are the well-established gut epithelial members); the 1994 'ubiquitous' statement is Northern-level and includes developmental stages. No human adult data. Low-priority, as the finding itself concedes.

evidence.source_title: Czech et al. 2012, J Neurochem 122:260: The human testis-determining factor SRY localizes in midbrain dopamine neurons (PubMed abstract)
evidence.tissue: human male and female substantia nigra, post-mortem controls
evidence.finding: SRY protein in a subset of male nigral dopamine neurons.
evidence.quote: SRY immunoreactivity was detected in the human male, but not female substantia nigra pars compacta, within a sub-population of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) positive neurons.
evidence.limitations: One sheep polyclonal antibody; two female negative controls.

evidence.source_title: PMID 22568433 (PMC3529967), Czech et al., J Neurochem 2012
evidence.tissue: brain (midbrain: substantia nigra, ventral tegmental area); tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons; GAD-positive neurons in substantia nigra pars reticulata
evidence.finding: Human: SRY immunoreactivity was detected in adult male (not female) substantia nigra pars compacta within a subpopulation of TH-positive neurons, and in VTA and pars reticulata neurons. In human cell lines SRY knockdown reduced TH, DDC, DBH and MAO-A, so the authors propose it positively regulates catecholamine synthesis in the male midbrain; UniProt also annotates a role in maintaining motor function of dopaminergic neurons (by similarity to rat).
evidence.limitations: Source exists and says what is claimed. PubMed abstract of PMID 22568433 (Czech et al., J Neurochem 2012;122:260-71): SRY immunoreactivity in human male but not female SNc within a subpopulation of TH-positive neurons, co-localisation with TH in VTA and with GAD in SNr; SRY knockdown in M17 cells reduced TH, DDC, DBH, MAO-A. Full text (PMC3529967): post-mortem brains from 7 donors listed as 'Control' (5 male aged 48-69, 2 female), 43% (+/-9%) of male SNc TH+ neurons SRY-positive; VTA is from a single male. SRY is single-copy and Y-linked, and absence of signal in female SNc argues against cross-reaction with autosomal/X SOX proteins, so the assay is reasonably gene-specific. Caveats that keep this from being strong: one laboratory, one sheep polyclonal antibody (C-terminal peptide aa 189-204), only 2 female negative controls, no peptide block, no western blot and no SRY mRNA (RT-PCR/ISH) on the human brain tissue; the antibody was validated by siRNA/overexpression only in cell lines, and the authors themselves say further studies are required. The functional evidence is cell-line only, and the UniProt motor-function annotation is by similarity to rat. So: expression claim confirmed at antibody level in adult human normal brain; a required function in human is not shown.

evidence.source_title: PMID 19914267 (PMC2891862), Ely et al., Steroids 2010 (rat review)
evidence.finding: Rat (SHR model): a review states Sry is expressed in brain, kidney and adrenal gland of adult males and links the Sry locus to blood-pressure regulation via the sympathetic and renin-angiotensin systems. Rat carries multiple Sry copies, so transfer to human is uncertain.
evidence.limitations: Source exists and says it: abstract of PMID 19914267 (Ely et al., Steroids 2010) states Sry 'is expressed in the brain, kidney and adrenal gland of adult males' and links the SHR Y chromosome/Sry locus to blood pressure via the sympathetic and renin-angiotensin systems. But it is a review of rat work (SHR/WKY), the rat has multiple functional Sry copies (stated in the abstract) so the data are about a multi-copy locus with no one-to-one human orthologue, and the hypertension model is a disease strain. The only human content is Y-chromosome association with blood pressure, not SRY expression in kidney or adrenal. No human adult kidney/adrenal expression is shown. The finding was already framed as rat-only and 'possible'; that is accurate, and it does not bear on human normal-tissue expression beyond the brain claim covered separately.

evidence.tissue: bone marrow; undifferentiated mesenchymal stem cells
evidence.finding: Human: SSX (with NY-ESO-1 and N-RAGE) is expressed in undifferentiated bone-marrow mesenchymal stem cells and falls on osteocyte/adipocyte differentiation; SSX protein is cytoplasmic and co-distributes with MMP2 and vimentin. The abstract says 'SSX' without a family member, the cells are culture-expanded (the abstract does not state adult versus fetal origin), and in vivo marrow expression is not shown. Abstract only read.

evidence.source_title: UniProt Q8TC36; PMID 12621555
evidence.finding: Human: UniProt records conflicting tissue specificity, 'widely expressed' per PubMed:12621555 against testis-specific per PubMed:21711156, with protein shown in sperm. I read the UniProt entry, not the papers; the human disease phenotype is male infertility only (spermatogenic failure 16).
evidence.limitations: UniProt Q8TC36 records the conflict exactly as stated. PMID 12621555 (2003, Chinese-language cloning paper) does say human TSARG4 mRNA 'is expressed in a wide range of adult tissues, including testis', with no assay detail in the abstract; SUN5 is 45% identical to SPAG4. The abstract of PMID 21711156 only confirms protein in human testis and does not itself state testis specificity. Later protein data (sperm) and the infertility-only loss-of-function phenotype point to a testis-restricted role, so the wide-expression report is most likely superseded.

evidence.tissue: blood; polymorphonuclear leukocytes, T cells, B cells
evidence.finding: Human: functional TAAR2 (with TAAR1) in blood PMN, T and B cells; siRNA knockdown showed both receptors are needed for chemotaxis toward 2-phenylethylamine, tyramine and T1AM, and for amine-triggered cytokine and immunoglobulin secretion.
evidence.limitations: PMID 23315425 exists and the abstract matches the claim: functional expression of TAAR1 and TAAR2 in isolated human blood PMN, T and B cells, with siRNA showing both are needed for amine-induced leukocyte functions. Weakened because it is a single-laboratory report resting on RT-PCR, antibodies and siRNA in primary cells, with implausibly low sub-nanomolar potencies, and the catalog's atlases show 0.0 TPM; I found no independent replication in this check. Abstract only read.

evidence.source_title: UniProt Q9P1P5
evidence.finding: Human: UniProt annotates TAAR2 as an orphan olfactory receptor for trace amines signalling through G(s); it also records no expression in several brain regions or liver (PubMed:10684976). Olfactory-epithelium expression is inferred from the function annotation, not a human tissue assay I opened.
evidence.limitations: UniProt Q9P1P5 does carry the 'orphan olfactory receptor' function, but it is annotated by similarity to a mouse protein (ECO:0000250, Q5QD04), not from a human assay. The only human tissue line is a negative one (not expressed in listed brain regions or liver, PubMed:10684976). Olfactory expression in humans is an inference, as the finding itself admits.

evidence.finding: Mouse: MIN6 cells and mouse islets express T1R2, T1R3 and gustducin; artificial sweeteners stimulated insulin secretion via calcium and cAMP, blocked by gurmarin. Mouse only.
evidence.limitations: PMID 19352508 exists and says what is claimed, but it is mouse only (MIN6 line and mouse islets). T1R2 mRNA was detected by RT-PCR, while function was shown with sweeteners and gurmarin, which act on the receptor complex rather than T1R2 alone. No human data.

evidence.source_title: PMID 17724330; UniProt Q8TE23 for taste function
evidence.finding: Human: duodenal L cells express sweet taste receptors, alpha-gustducin and other taste signalling elements; in the human L-cell line NCI-H716, sugar- and sucralose-driven GLP-1 release was blocked by the sweet receptor antagonist lactisole. The abstract says 'sweet taste receptors' (T1R2/T1R3 heterodimer) rather than naming TAS1R2 alone.
evidence.limitations: PMID 17724330 exists and the abstract says human duodenal L cells express 'sweet taste receptors', gustducin and other taste elements, and that lactisole blocked GLP-1 release in NCI-H716 cells. The abstract does not name TAS1R2; lactisole acts on TAS1R3, so the functional block is not TAS1R2-specific, the function is in a tumour-derived cell line, and the tissue evidence is antibody staining. Abstract only read. Taste-bud function with TAS1R3 is well established (UniProt Q8TE23) but UniProt has no tissue-specificity entry.

entries.reported_tissue: taste receptor cells of tongue and palate epithelium (taste buds)
entries.summary: UniProt places TAS2R1 in gustducin-positive taste receptor cells of tongue and palate. Extra-oral reports I could open are from cultured cells only: RT-PCR, western blot and immunofluorescence in cultured human pulmonary artery and airway smooth muscle cells (Upadhyaya 2014), and reviews citing qRT-PCR in keratinocytes/epidermis and mammary cell lines; no opened source shows TAS2R1 specifically in intact adult brain, heart or lung tissue (Foster 2013 found many TAS2Rs in failing human heart but the text does not name TAS2R1).
entries.decision_reason: Evidence is from another species, a database annotation or an assay shared with a paralog, or the tissue is reproductive.

evidence.finding: Canonical expression in taste receptor cells.
evidence.quote: Expressed in subsets of taste receptor cells of the tongue and palate epithelium and exclusively in gustducin-positive cells.
evidence.limitations: Curated comment; underlying primary paper not opened (and may rest partly on rodent in situ data).

evidence.source_title: Upadhyaya JD et al. Dextromethorphan mediated bitter taste receptor activation in the pulmonary circuit causes vasoconstriction. PLoS One 2014 (PMC4207743)
evidence.assay: RT-PCR, qPCR, shRNA knockdown, western blot and immunofluorescence with polyclonal anti-T2R1
evidence.tissue: Cultured human pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells and airway smooth muscle cells (ATCC or gift)
evidence.finding: TAS2R1 transcript among 21 of 25 T2Rs detected; T2R1 protein reduced ~50% by T2R1 shRNA; ~3-fold higher in PASMC than ASMC (per fetch summary).
evidence.quote: Immunoblot analysis revealed a decrease of ∼50% in T2R1 protein expression
evidence.limitations: Cultured cells only; no human tissue examined ('Due to feasibility concerns in obtaining intact human lung tissues' porcine rings were used). Intronless GPCR RT-PCR is prone to genomic DNA signal; antibody specificity supported only by partial knockdown.

evidence.source_title: Jaggupilli A et al. Analysis of the expression of human bitter taste receptors in extraoral tissues. Mol Cell Biochem 2017 (PMID 28012014), abstract
evidence.tissue: Cell lines/cultured cells: CuFi-1, NuLi-1 bronchial epithelial, airway and pulmonary artery smooth muscle, mammary epithelial, breast cancer
evidence.finding: TAS2R1 is not among the moderately or highly expressed TAS2Rs listed in the abstract (a search snippet said TAS2R1 was at low level; not verified in full text).

evidence.source_title: PMID 25573083 (Wolfle et al. 2015, Skin Pharmacol Physiol)
evidence.finding: Human: TAS2R1 (with TAS2R38) protein was shown by double immunostaining with alpha-gustducin in human skin, HaCaT cells and primary keratinocytes; bitter agonists triggered calcium influx and raised differentiation markers (keratin 10, involucrin, transglutaminase).
evidence.limitations: PMID 25573083 exists and its abstract says what is claimed: TAS2R1 and TAS2R38 expression in human skin, colocalisation with alpha-gustducin in HaCaT cells and primary keratinocytes, and calcium influx and differentiation markers after diphenidol or amarogentin. Weakened because the protein evidence is antibody immunostaining only (TAS2R antibodies are not knockout-validated in the abstract), the functional work is mostly in the HaCaT line, and the agonists are promiscuous across TAS2Rs, so the function is not attributable to TAS2R1 specifically. I read the abstract only, not the full text.

evidence.source_title: PMID 20972434 full text, Table 1 (PMC3066567)
evidence.tissue: airway and thyroid; airway smooth muscle cells; thyrocytes
evidence.finding: Family-level, human: TAS2Rs are expressed and functional on human airway smooth muscle (bronchodilation, PMID 20972434) and in human thyrocytes, where agonists reduce TSH-dependent calcium and iodide efflux (PMID 25342133). The abstracts do not name which subtypes, so this applies to TAS2R13, TAS2R41, TAS2R50, TAS2R60, TAS2R7 and TAS2R1 only as a family-level caution; human bronchus studies that name subtypes point to TAS2R5/10/14/31 (PMID 24266887, 30365340), not these.
evidence.limitations: Both papers exist and say what is claimed at family level. The full text of PMID 20972434 (PMC3066567, Table 1) does name subtypes, by qRT-PCR in cultured human airway smooth muscle cells relative to ADRB2: TAS2R50 0.48, TAS2R13 0.26, TAS2R1 0.17 (all low, against 3.4 to 4.0 for TAS2R10/14/31), while TAS2R7, TAS2R41, TAS2R60 and TAS1R2 were not detected; the text states TAS2R7 'is not expressed in ASM'. So the family-level caution is wrong for TAS2R7/41/60 in airway and holds only as low transcript in cultured cells for TAS2R13/50/1. Function was shown with promiscuous agonists and TAS2R10 knockdown only. For thyroid (PMID 25342133) I could read only the abstract, which names TAS2R38 and TAS2R42 but not these genes.

Weakened because the macrophages came from lung resections of carcinoma patients (not normal donors), the evidence is transcript only, and the paper's functional conclusion implicates TAS2Rs 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 14, 30, 39 and 40, not TAS2R7, in cytokine inhibition. evidence.source_title: PMID 18003842 (Behrens et al., J Neurosci 2007; PMCID PMC6673335)
evidence.tissue: tongue and palate taste epithelium; gustducin-positive taste receptor cells
evidence.finding: Human: UniProt curates TAS2R8 as a bitter taste receptor expressed in subsets of taste receptor cells of the tongue and palate epithelium, exclusively in gustducin-positive cells; it may also sense gastrointestinal contents.
evidence.limitations: UniProt Q9NYW2 does carry the quoted tissue-specificity text, but that sentence has no evidence tag and is identical word for word in the TAS2R9 entry: it is a family-level statement copied from the abstract of Adler et al. 2000 (PMID 10761934), whose in situ localisation and gustducin co-expression were done in rodent taste tissue. The companion paper PMID 10761935 characterised mT2R-5, hT2R-4 and mT2R-8 (a mouse gene, not human TAS2R8). The UniProt function line is hedged ('may play a role'), and the gastrointestinal role is speculative. So the cited source is not gene-specific human evidence. The underlying claim is nonetheless supported by a better source: Behrens et al. 2007 report all 25 human TAS2R genes expressed in taste receptor cells of human circumvallate papillae by in situ hybridisation with gene-specific probes (abstract read; per-gene levels for TAS2R8 not checked).

evidence.source_title: PMID 18003842 (Behrens et al., J Neurosci 2007) for expression; PMID 23599216 for function in adults
evidence.tissue: tongue and palate taste epithelium; gustducin-positive taste receptor cells
evidence.finding: Human: UniProt curates TAS2R9 as a gustducin-coupled bitter taste receptor expressed in subsets of taste receptor cells of the tongue and palate epithelium; the gastrointestinal role is annotated by similarity only. Human TAS2R9 polymorphisms predict perceived bitterness of acesulfame potassium, supporting a working receptor in adults.
evidence.limitations: UniProt Q9NYW1 does carry the quoted text, but the tissue-specificity sentence is the same untagged family-level boilerplate as in TAS2R8, derived from rodent in situ data in Adler et al. 2000 (PMID 10761934), and the function line is 'by similarity'. PMID 23599216 (Allen et al., Chem Senses 2013) is real and gene-specific: TAS2R9 alleles predicted acesulfame-K bitterness in 108 adults, and the abstract also cites a TAS2R9 allele effect on ofloxacin response in vitro. That is a genetic association in living adults (possible linkage with neighbouring TAS2R genes in the chr12 cluster), not a tissue expression assay, so it supports a working receptor only indirectly. The claim is real but the cited expression evidence is weaker than stated; the direct human evidence is Behrens et al. 2007, in situ hybridisation of all 25 human TAS2R genes in human circumvallate papillae (abstract read; per-gene level for TAS2R9 not checked).

evidence.source_title: Yamakoshi et al. 2013, Biochem Biophys Res Commun 432:66: Trichohyalin-like 1 protein, a member of fused S100 proteins, is expressed in normal and pathologic human skin (PubMed abstract)
evidence.finding: TCHHL1 protein in basal keratinocytes.
evidence.quote: An immunohistochemical study showed that TCHHL1 proteins were expressed in the basal layer of the normal epidermis.
evidence.limitations: Abstract only; donor age not stated.

evidence.finding: Human: immunohistochemistry with TCHHL1 antibodies shows protein in the basal layer of normal epidermis and in cultured growing keratinocytes, with mRNA detected in normal skin and cultured keratinocytes.
evidence.limitations: PMID 23376073 (Yamakoshi et al., BBRC 2013) exists and its abstract says this directly: antibodies raised against the TCHHL1 C-terminus stained the basal layer of normal human epidermis and the perinuclear area of cultured growing keratinocytes, and TCHHL1 mRNA was detected in normal skin and cultured keratinocytes. The C-terminal immunogen makes cross-reaction with other fused S100 proteins (TCHH, hornerin, filaggrin) less likely. Caveats: abstract only was read; a single laboratory with an in-house polyclonal antibody; no knockout or peptide-block validation is mentioned in the abstract; donor age is not stated.

evidence.source_title: PMID 21614011 (title and MeSH only)
evidence.finding: A 2011 letter is titled as identifying TCHHL1 as an S100 fused-type protein selectively expressed in hair follicles (record indexed for human and goat). Only the title was available, so species and method are unconfirmed.
evidence.limitations: PMID 21614011 (Wu, Latendorf, Meyer-Hoffert, Schroder, J Invest Dermatol 2011;131:1761-3) exists with exactly that title and is MeSH-indexed for Hair Follicle, Humans, Goats and Antibody Specificity. It is a letter with no abstract, and I could not retrieve the body (publisher page returned no readable text), so species of the tissue stained, the assay and the follicle compartment remain unverified. The goat indexing may refer to the antibody host rather than goat tissue, but I could not check that. Note that 'selectively expressed in hair follicles' conflicts with the Toyama group's basal-epidermis localisation (PMID 23376073), so the two antibody studies disagree about where the protein is. Flags set conservatively because the text was not read.

evidence.source_title: PMID 33133644 (PMCID PMC7591909)
evidence.finding: Human: siRNA knockdown of TCHHL1 in normal human keratinocytes reduced proliferation and increased early apoptosis, and skin-equivalent models built from knockdown cells had a hypoplastic epidermis.
evidence.limitations: PMID 33133644 (Makino et al., Cell Death Discov 2020) exists and its abstract states the claim as written: TCHHL1 siRNA inhibited proliferation and induced early apoptosis of normal human keratinocytes, and skin-equivalent models built from knockdown cells had a markedly hypoplastic epidermis. The siRNA is gene-specific. It is weakened because the evidence is entirely in vitro (cultured primary keratinocytes and 3D skin equivalents, which are often of neonatal origin), not adult tissue in vivo, and there is no human loss-of-function disease or mouse knockout. Same laboratory as the other TCHHL1 papers; abstract only was read.

evidence.finding: Human skin xenotransplants: UVB irradiation raised TCHHL1 mRNA two days after exposure, and immunohistochemistry showed the signal spreading from the basal into the spinous layer.
evidence.limitations: PMID 30610764 (Makino et al., Clin Exp Dermatol 2019) exists and its abstract matches the claim: TCHHL1 mRNA rose 2 days after UVB, and immunohistochemistry signal spread from the basal layer (sham) into basal and spinous layers, alongside more Ki67-positive cells. Weakened because the tissue is human skin grafted onto mice, not skin in a person, and the abstract gives no fold change. The induction tracks keratinocyte proliferation, so it is an extension of the basal-layer finding rather than an independent one. Abstract only was read.

evidence.source_title: PMID 12097419 (Wang et al., J Immunol 2002)
evidence.finding: Human: UniProt curates TFDP3 as predominantly testis-expressed with a low level of expression in pancreas, citing the original cloning papers. The catalog shows 0.0 off-target TPM.
evidence.limitations: The UniProt Q5H9I0 line is quoted accurately, and the primary source supports it: Wang et al. 2002 (PMID 12097419) state that HCA661 (= TFDP3, per the UniProt synonym) was 'predominantly detected in testis, but not in other normal tissues, except for a weak expression in normal pancreas'. Weakened because it is a single 2002 SEREX paper, the signal is described as weak, and the abstract does not give the method (likely RT-PCR on a commercial normal-tissue panel) or say whether the product was sequenced. TFDP3 is an intronless retrogene closely related to TFDP1, so genomic DNA contamination or TFDP1 cross-amplification cannot be excluded, and pancreas RNA is prone to such artefacts. Modern atlases showing 0 TPM argue against it. PMID 16418725's abstract says nothing about tissue distribution. Primary full texts were not read.

evidence.source_title: PMID 20559320 (PMCID PMC3131880)
evidence.finding: Human: UniProt annotates TFDP3 as induced in response to DNA damage, citing a paper on E2F-1 regulation by a DNA damage-responsive DP partner. The evidence is likely from cell lines, so induction in normal tissue is unproven.
evidence.limitations: UniProt Q5H9I0 does annotate 'INDUCTION: In response to DNA damage' citing PMID 20559320, and that paper (Ingram et al., Cell Death Differ 2011) says DP-4 (= TFDP3) 'is induced in DNA-damaged cells' and that depleting it restores E2F-1 activity, so it is gene-specific. But the abstract refers only to 'cells', which means cultured (almost certainly tumour-derived) lines; there is no evidence of induction in normal adult human tissue. The finding itself conceded this. It stays a hypothesis for normal tissue, not a documented off-target liability.

evidence.source_title: PMID 30420784 (PMC6294671), Full et al., Nat Microbiol 2019;4:164-176, Fig. 1d-g, Supplementary Figs. 1c and 3a; UniProt Q96BQ3
evidence.tissue: any herpesvirus-infected somatic tissue (not tissue-restricted; shown in cultured human cells only); herpesvirus-infected cells (cell type not named in the abstract)
evidence.finding: Human TRIM43 is strongly upregulated during herpesvirus infection (including KSHV reactivation) through the transcription factor DUX4, and acts as a centrosomal E3 ligase that degrades pericentrin to restrict herpesviruses (Full et al., Nat Microbiol 2019). UniProt Q96BQ3 curates this as 'induced by DUX4 during herpesvirus infection'. Evidence is from cell culture; the abstract gives no human tissue data.
evidence.limitations: The source exists and says what is claimed. The PubMed abstract of Full et al., Nat Microbiol 2019 states TRIM43 shows 'profound upregulation during herpesvirus infection as part of a germline-specific transcriptional program mediated by the transcription factor DUX4' and ubiquitinates pericentrin for proteasomal degradation; UniProt Q96BQ3 curates 'induced by DUX4 during herpesvirus infection'. The open-access full text (PMC6294671) is stronger than the claim's 'cell culture only': induction by HCMV in primary human foreskin fibroblasts, higher TRIM43 mRNA in HSV-1-positive versus HSV-1-negative patient bronchoalveolar lavage samples (18 vs 16), and TRIM43 protein moderate or high in 10 of 17 AIDS Kaposi sarcoma skin biopsies with minimal staining in healthy skin. The paper's own tissue qRT-PCR also reports very low ubiquitous mRNA with higher levels in brain, thymus and testis (Supplementary Fig. 3a). Caveats: this is infected or diseased tissue, not normal steady-state adult tissue, so it is an induced-expression flag only (HFF are neonatal, KS is a tumor in immunosuppressed patients). Paralog specificity is not established: the methods say the RNA-seq analysed TRIM43A, TRIM43B and TRIM43C together, and the qRT-PCR, siRNA and polyclonal antibody (ab80460) are unlikely to separate near-identical copies. Healthy skin was minimal, which limits the practical off-target concern to actively infected cells.

evidence.source_title: PMID 30420784 (PMC6294671), methods RNA-seq section; UniProt A6NCK2 (no annotation)
evidence.tissue: any herpesvirus-infected somatic tissue; herpesvirus-infected cells
evidence.finding: Human TRIM43B is a near-identical paralog of TRIM43, which is induced by DUX4 during herpesvirus infection; the same induction is plausible for TRIM43B but the abstract does not mention it and UniProt A6NCK2 has no annotation. Family-level inference only.
evidence.limitations: The claim is honestly labelled as a family-level inference, and that is all it is. The abstract of PMID 30420784 does not mention TRIM43B and UniProt A6NCK2 has no induction, tissue or function annotation. The only mention in the full text is one methods sentence: 'the transcripts of the three TRIM43 gene copies found in humans (TRIM43A, TRIM43B and TRIM43C), were analyzed' in the RNA-seq of HSV-1-infected and DUX4-transfected HEK 293T cells. That makes it plausible that TRIM43B reads contribute to the reported induction (and TRIM43B is a known DUX4 target in the FSHD literature), but the paper gives no TRIM43B-specific result, and none of its assays separates the copies. No evidence in normal adult uninfected tissue.

evidence.source_title: PMID 40609779 (Wu et al., Cell Signal 2025, doi 10.1016/j.cellsig.2025.111973); UniProt Q8IWZ4; PMID 29186683
evidence.tissue: virus-infected somatic tissue (shown only in the A549 human lung carcinoma line); A549 cells after dsRNA transfection or Rift Valley fever reporter virus infection
evidence.finding: Human TRIM48 is described as an induced negative-feedback regulator of RIG-I signaling, upregulated after dsRNA transfection or RNA virus infection in A549 cells (Cell Signal 2025); UniProt Q8IWZ4 curates 'induced upon RIG-I/DDX58 stimulation'. A separate paper (PMID 29186683) shows it degrades PRMT1 to promote ASK1 activation and cell death under oxidative stress, but in cancer cells and a xenograft with forced expression, not normal tissue.
evidence.limitations: Both sources exist and say what is claimed, but neither is normal tissue. PMID 40609779 (Wu et al., Cell Signal 2025;134:111973) is an siRNA screen of 616 E3 ligases in A549 cells; the abstract says 'TRIM48 acts as an induced feedback regulator upon infection' and names it a negative feedback regulator of RIG-I, with overexpression and deficiency experiments. UniProt Q8IWZ4 curates 'induced upon RIG-I/DDX58 stimulation'. PMID 29186683 (Hirata et al., Cell Rep 2017) shows TRIM48 degrades PRMT1 to promote oxidative-stress ASK1 activation, using knockdown and forced expression in a cancer xenograft. All evidence is from tumor cell lines; I only read the abstract of the 2025 paper, so the magnitude of induction and absolute expression level are unchecked. Induction in normal infected human epithelium or immune cells is untested, so this stays a hypothesis, not a documented normal-tissue function. The assays are directed at TRIM48, though it sits in the chr11 TRIM48/TRIM49/TRIM51/TRIM64 cluster of similar genes and cross-reactivity of the siRNAs or primers was not verified.

evidence.source_title: PMID 33184450 (Gu et al., Cell Mol Immunol 2021;18:1981, PMC8322076); UniProt Q8VI40 also notes mouse Trim60 expression is restricted to embryos up to the 8-cell stage (PMID 11424210)
evidence.tissue: innate immune system (response to LPS and bacterial infection); not stated in the UniProt summary; innate immune cells implied
evidence.finding: UniProt annotates human TRIM60 (Q495X7) as an E3 SUMO ligase that SUMOylates TAB2 and suppresses NF-kB and MAPK signalling, citing PMID 33184450. The mouse entry (Q8VI40) reports that Trim60 knockout mice mount a stronger immune response to LPS septic shock and L. monocytogenes infection, so the in vivo evidence is mouse.
evidence.limitations: The sources exist and say what is claimed: UniProt Q495X7 and Q8VI40 both carry the TAB2 SUMOylation function citing PMID 33184450, and the mouse entry carries the knockout phenotype. But the paper (Gu et al., Cell Mol Immunol 2021, PMC8322076) is entirely mouse or overexpression: Trim60 knockout mice, mouse bone-marrow-derived macrophages, mouse embryonic fibroblasts, the RAW 264.7 mouse macrophage line, and tagged TRIM60 transfected into HEK293T. No expression of endogenous TRIM60 in human macrophages or any normal adult human tissue is shown, and the human UniProt function is inferred from the mouse work. One correction to the claim: the paper's full text says knockout mice were more susceptible to LPS shock but more resistant to Listeria, not simply an 'elevated response' to both. The assay is gene-specific (knockout, shRNA with qPCR), so this is a real mouse macrophage function with no human normal-tissue evidence.

evidence.source_title: PMID 40593606 (Sun et al., Nat Commun 2025;16:5591, PMC12219730); mouse tissue RT-PCR in PMID 17499049 and ependymal cilia in PMID 23897886 via UniProt A4Q9F6
evidence.tissue: heart (mouse); dividing cells generally; mitotic cells (spindle poles)
evidence.finding: UniProt states that TTLL13 is a tubulin polyglutamylase that, with CFAP100, glutamylates spindle-pole microtubules and is needed for proper spindle assembly (PMID 40593606, cited on both the human A6NNM8 and mouse A4Q9F6 entries). Mouse Ttll13 expression is reported highest in heart and testis.
evidence.limitations: The UniProt statements are as claimed on both A6NNM8 and A4Q9F6. I opened the cited paper (Sun et al., Nat Commun 2025, PMC12219730), which answers the researcher's open question: the spindle-pole evidence is from the HaCaT immortalised human keratinocyte line, HEK293T and HeLa cells, plus primary keratinocytes from mice. It is not from normal adult human tissue. The knockout in the paper is Cfap100, not Ttll13; TTLL13 evidence is co-immunoprecipitation of the endogenous protein in HaCaT, localisation of TTLL13-GFP (and TTLL13 in mouse primary keratinocytes) at spindle poles, and rescue by TTLL13 overexpression. So endogenous TTLL13 protein is detected by antibody in a human keratinocyte line, which is suggestive for dividing epidermal cells but is cell-line evidence with no TTLL13 loss-of-function. Mouse heart expression (PMID 17499049) is mouse RT-PCR only. Skin is already in the bulk panel.

There is no human data, no protein-level data, no knockout phenotype, and the enzyme activity is annotated only as 'probable'. The human annotation directly disagrees with broad somatic expression, so this is most likely a species difference or low-level RT-PCR signal, not evidence of a human normal-tissue function.

evidence.finding: Mouse Ttll8 (UniProt A4Q9F1) is a tubulin monoglycylase that, with TTLL3, glycylates cilia as well as sperm flagella; expression is highest in testis but also reported in brain, heart, kidney, liver, lung, muscle, spleen and trachea. The Ttll3/Ttll8 double knockout phenotype listed is subfertility from abnormal flagellar beating (PMID 33414192), so no vital somatic phenotype is documented.
evidence.limitations: UniProt A4Q9F1 (mouse) does say this: highly expressed in testis, also expressed in brain, heart, kidney, liver, lung, muscle, spleen and trachea, and in brain specifically in ependymal cilia (PMID 23897886), and the Ttll3/Ttll8 double knockout is subfertile (PMID 33414192, abstract confirms a male fertility phenotype only). All of it is mouse. The human entry A6PVC2 has no tissue annotation and its function text is inferred by similarity from the mouse protein. The mouse data are gene-specific RT-PCR, but the only knockout phenotype is reproductive, so no vital somatic role is documented. The ependymal-cilia detail strengthens the researcher's point that a rare-ciliated-cell signal could be diluted in bulk, but it remains an unverified possibility in human.

Family-level inference only.

evidence.source_title: PMID 18076704 and PMID 18194880 (contradicting follow-ups); original claim PMID 10903929
evidence.finding: Human: deletion mapping in 15 males with Xp22.3 deletions narrowed an X-linked nonspecific mental retardation interval to about 15 kb containing only VCX-A (VCX3A); it was deleted in all patients with mental retardation and retained in all with normal intelligence. This implies a neurodevelopmental or brain role, although UniProt still lists expression as exclusively testis and the paralogues VCX, VCX2 and VCX3B showed no such correlation.
evidence.limitations: PMID 10903929 exists, is specific to VCX-A (VCX3A) and says what is claimed: a 15 kb critical interval, deleted in all patients with mental retardation and retained in all with normal intelligence. But it is deletion mapping, not evidence of expression in adult brain, and later studies contradict it. PMID 18076704 found VCX3A deleted in 62 of 80 X-linked ichthyosis patients with normal intelligence and concluded the deletion is not sufficient for mental retardation. PMID 18194880 reports a male with all VCX genes and NLGN4X deleted and normal intelligence. UniProt lists expression as exclusively testis. Any role would be developmental, and the causal link is disputed.

entries.summary: The VCX/Y family paper (Lahn and Page 2000) states that all members appear to be expressed exclusively in male germ cells; UniProt and NCBI RefSeq repeat this for VCX3B. HPA IHC (two antibodies, reliability Supported) shows nuclear staining in spermatogonia, spermatocytes and spermatids, with a caution that the antibodies target more than one gene. No opened source reports VCX3B or any VCX member in adult retina or brain; the proposed link of the paralog VCX3A (VCX-A) to intellectual disability is genetic (deletion mapping), not expression evidence in the abstracts opened.
entries.decision_reason: Sources describe germline, placental or embryonic restriction, or did not test adult somatic tissue.

evidence.finding: Human: the VHL-like protein cDNA was originally isolated by RT-PCR from human cerebellum (and cancer cell lines), with the transcript most abundant in placenta; the protein binds HIF-alpha and acts as a dominant-negative VHL. This gene-specific cloning supports the catalog's 4.4 TPM cerebellum value being real expression rather than mis-mapped VHL reads.
evidence.limitations: PMID 14757845 exists and its abstract states a 676-bp partial cDNA was isolated by RT-PCR from human brain cerebellum and several cancer cell lines, with the transcript most abundant in placenta. That is qualitative detection by PCR cloning with no quantification and no protein evidence; the abstract does not state donor age or status. The cloned product was sequenced (78% similar to VHL), so it is distinct from VHL, though VHLL is an intronless retrogene and genomic DNA contamination cannot be excluded from the abstract. It supports low-level cerebellar transcript presence, not a documented function in adult brain; the dominant-negative VHL function was shown by overexpression.

entries.summary: WFDC13 has no dedicated human expression paper that I could open, but sources agree it is a male reproductive tract gene: HPA classifies RNA as 'Tissue enriched (Epididymis)' in epididymal principal cells, and a 2024 PNAS study lists WFDC13 among 'reproductive tract-specific genes in humans' (mouse cluster knockout affects sperm motility). evidence.finding: Human: UniProt (citing the chromosome 20 WAP-locus RT-PCR study) annotates WFDC8 as expressed ubiquitously, highest in epididymis, then testis and trachea. The abstract states this pattern for 'most' genes in the locus, which also includes WFDC9, WFDC10A and WFDC13, and notes some have high transcript levels in neural tissues; a proposed role is mucosal host defence.
evidence.limitations: PMID 12206714 exists, but its abstract describes the 14-gene locus collectively: 'several of the genes appear to be expressed ubiquitously, but, in most cases, the highest transcript levels are found in epididymis followed by testis and trachea', and 'some' genes are high in neural tissues. It does not name WFDC8 for trachea or neural expression. UniProt Q8IUA0 does carry the per-gene annotation 'expressed ubiquitously, highest in epididymis followed by testis and trachea', but it appears to restate the locus-level sentence. I could not retrieve the full text (PMC1222987) to check the WFDC8-specific data. This is one 2002 RT-PCR survey with no protein evidence and no cell type; the host-defence role is speculative in the source.
