evidence.source_title: PMID 16083862 (primary); PMID 33962015 for the statement that in vivo protein expression is not consistently demonstrated
evidence.tissue: brain (hippocampus, striatum, amygdala, thalamus); hippocampal CA3 pyramidal neurons; dentate gyrus polymorphic layer
evidence.finding: Human: ZACN (L2/ZAC, zinc-activated ligand-gated cation channel) cDNA was cloned from adult caudate nucleus; RT-PCR confirmed mRNA in adult hippocampus, striatum, amygdala and thalamus, and an antipeptide antibody stained protein mainly in hippocampal CA3 pyramidal cells and the dentate gyrus polymorphic layer. The same tissue cDNA panels also detected mRNA in pancreas, liver, lung, heart, kidney and skeletal muscle.
evidence.limitations: The source exists and its abstract says what is claimed: L2/ZAC cDNA cloned from human caudate nucleus, RT-PCR mRNA in adult hippocampus, striatum, amygdala and thalamus, plus brain, pancreas, liver, lung, heart, kidney and skeletal muscle on tissue cDNA panels, and antipeptide-antibody staining in hippocampal CA3 pyramidal cells and the dentate gyrus polymorphic layer. ZACN has no close paralog (about 15% identity to 5-HT3A/B), so the RT-PCR is gene-specific. The protein part is weaker than 'documented': the abstract itself calls it 'L2-like immunoreactivity' from a single unvalidated antipeptide antibody, and the main ZAC laboratory wrote in 2021 (PMID 33962015) that 'expression of the ZAC protein in vivo has yet to be consistently demonstrated'. The RT-PCR is non-quantitative and agrees with the low atlas RNA. I read only the abstract (full text is paywalled), so the species of the stained sections is confirmed only through a later paper (PMID 26872532) that describes them as human. No physiological function or loss-of-function phenotype is known. Net: gene-specific low-level brain RNA is real; neuronal protein expression is unconfirmed.

evidence.finding: Human: the original cloning paper detected ZAC transcripts in adult trachea, spinal cord and stomach (plus placenta and fetal brain), and showed the expressed channel is functional (spontaneous currents, activated by Zn2+, blocked by tubocurarine). The gene is absent from mouse and rat, so no rodent knockout exists to reveal a phenotype.
evidence.limitations: The source exists and the abstract states: 'Transcripts of ZAC subunits were detected in human placenta, trachea, spinal cord, stomach, and fetal brain', the gene is lost from mouse and rat, and the HEK293-expressed channel shows spontaneous current, Zn2+ activation and tubocurarine block. All of that matches the claim. Weakened because: the abstract does not say the trachea, spinal cord and stomach samples were adult (likely commercial adult RNA panels, but I did not verify this in the full text); detection is qualitative with no level, cell type or protein; channel function is shown only in transfected cells, not native tissue; and no physiological role or human loss-of-function phenotype is known. The rodent-orthologue point is correct. This is gene-specific evidence of low-level transcript, not a documented function in these tissues.

evidence.source_title: PMID 28656966 (full text PMC5493756)
evidence.tissue: blood / innate immune system; monocytes / macrophages
evidence.finding: ZNRF4 is an ER-anchored E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades RIP2 and negatively regulates NOD2 signalling: Znrf4-knockdown monocytes showed sustained NF-kB activation, and Znrf4-knockdown mice had reduced NOD2-induced tolerance to MDP and cleared Listeria monocytogenes better. The abstract does not state the species of the monocytes, and the in vivo data are mouse knockdown, not a human expression measurement.
evidence.limitations: The source exists and supports the claim; the full text (PMC5493756) is stronger than the abstract-only reading. The monocytes are human: THP-1 cells and primary CD14+ monocytes and monocyte-derived macrophages from human PBMC. Knockdown of endogenous ZNRF4 in human primary monocytes raised RIP2 protein and NF-kB activation; endogenous ZNRF4 co-immunoprecipitated with RIP2 in primary human monocytes, at a low level unstimulated and more after MDP; ZNRF4 silencing increased IL-8, TNF and IL-1beta secretion in primary human macrophages. Expression is induced: the paper reports ZNRF4 upregulation by NOD2/MDP stimulation and Listeria infection, and enhanced ZNRF4 in peritoneal macrophages of MDP-tolerised mice. The in vivo data are mouse morpholino knockdown, as the claim says. Caveats: endogenous protein detection relies on commercial antibodies (Abcam ab173954/ab67951, Santa Cruz sc-169900) whose specificity is supported by siRNA knockdown shown in cell lines; this is a single laboratory's report with no independent replication found, and it conflicts with near-zero ZNRF4 RNA in sorted immune-cell atlases. ZNRF4 has no close paralog likely to confound the siRNA or qPCR.
